chapters.title: There Is No One Left
paragraphs: Everyone said that Mary Lennox was the most disagreeable-looking child they had ever seen. They said it when she was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle, and it was true. She had a thin little face and a thin little body, with thin, light hair and a sour look. Her hair was yellow, and so was her face, because she had been born in India and had always been sick with one thing or another. Her father had worked for the English Government and had always been busy and unwell himself. Her mother had been a great beauty who cared only about going to parties and having fun with cheerful people. She had not wanted a little girl at all. When Mary was born, she handed her over to an Ayah, who was made to understand that if she wanted to please the Mem Sahib, she must keep the child out of sight as much as she could. So when Mary was a sickly, fussy, ugly baby, she was kept out of the way. When she grew into a sickly, fussy toddler, she was kept out of the way too. The only faces she ever remembered seeing every day were the dark faces of her Ayah and the other native servants. They always obeyed her and let her have her own way in everything, because the Mem Sahib would be angry if her crying disturbed her. So by the time Mary was six years old, she was as bossy and selfish a little pig as ever lived. The young English governess who came to teach her to read and write disliked her so much that she quit after three months. When other governesses came to fill the job, they always left even sooner than the first. So if Mary had not decided that she really wanted to learn to read books, she would never have learned her letters at all.
One terribly hot morning, when she was about nine years old, she woke up feeling very cross. She became even crosser when she saw that the servant standing by her bed was not her Ayah.
“Why did you come?” she said to the strange woman. “I won’t let you stay. Send my Ayah to me.”

The woman looked frightened, but all she could do was stammer that the Ayah could not come. When Mary flew into a rage and hit and kicked her, the woman only looked more frightened and repeated that it was not possible for the Ayah to come to Missie Sahib.

There was something mysterious in the air that morning. Nothing was done in its usual order, and several of the native servants seemed to be missing. The ones Mary did see crept or hurried about with gray, scared faces. But no one would tell her anything, and her Ayah did not come. As the morning went on, she was left completely alone. At last she wandered out into the garden and began to play by herself under a tree near the veranda. She pretended she was making a flower bed, and she stuck big scarlet hibiscus blossoms into little heaps of earth. All the while she grew angrier and angrier, muttering to herself the things she would say and the names she would call Saidie when she came back.
“Pig! Pig! Daughter of Pigs!” she said, because to call a native a pig is the worst insult of all.

She was grinding her teeth and saying this over and over when she heard her mother come out onto the veranda with someone. It was a fair young man, and they stood talking together in low, strange voices. Mary knew the fair young man, who looked like a boy. She had heard that he was a very young officer who had just come from England. The child stared at him, but she stared most at her mother. She always did this when she had the chance to see her, because the Mem Sahib (Mary called her that more often than anything else) was such a tall, slim, pretty person and wore such lovely clothes. Her hair was like curly silk, and she had a delicate little nose that seemed to look down on things, and large, laughing eyes. All her clothes were thin and floaty, and Mary said they were “full of lace.” They looked even fuller of lace than ever this morning, but her eyes were not laughing at all. They were large and scared, and they were lifted pleadingly to the face of the fair boy officer.
“Is it really so bad? Oh, is it?” Mary heard her say.
“Dreadful,” the young man answered in a shaking voice. “Dreadful, Mrs. Lennox. You should have gone to the hills two weeks ago.”
The Mem Sahib wrung her hands.
“Oh, I know I should have!” she cried. “I only stayed to go to that silly dinner party. What a fool I was!”

At that very moment, such a loud wailing broke out from the servants’ quarters that she clutched the young man’s arm, and Mary stood shivering from head to foot. The wailing grew wilder and wilder. “What is it? What is it?” Mrs. Lennox gasped.
“Someone has died,” answered the boy officer. “You didn’t tell me it had broken out among your servants.”
“I didn’t know!” the Mem Sahib cried. “Come with me! Come with me!” And she turned and ran into the house.

After that, terrible things happened, and the mystery of the morning was explained to Mary. The cholera had broken out in its deadliest form, and people were dying like flies. The Ayah had fallen ill in the night, and the servants had wailed in the huts because she had just died. Before the next day, three other servants were dead, and others had run away in terror. There was panic on every side, and there were dying people in all the bungalows.

During the confusion and bewilderment of the second day, Mary hid in the nursery, and everyone forgot about her. Nobody thought of her, nobody wanted her, and strange things happened that she knew nothing about. Mary cried and slept by turns through the hours. She only knew that people were sick and that she kept hearing mysterious, frightening sounds. Once she crept into the dining room and found it empty. A half-finished meal was still on the table, and the chairs and plates looked as if they had been shoved back in a hurry when the diners suddenly got up for some reason. The child ate some fruit and biscuits, and because she was thirsty, she drank a glass of wine that stood almost full. It was sweet, and she did not know how strong it was. Very soon it made her terribly drowsy. She went back to her nursery and shut herself in again, frightened by the cries she heard in the huts and the hurrying sound of feet. The wine made her so sleepy that she could hardly keep her eyes open. She lay down on her bed and knew nothing more for a long time.
Many things happened during the hours when she slept so heavily. But she was not disturbed by the wailing or by the sound of things being carried in and out of the bungalow.

When she woke up, she lay there and stared at the wall. The house was perfectly still. She had never known it to be so quiet before. She heard no voices and no footsteps, and she wondered if everybody had recovered from the cholera and the trouble was over. She also wondered who would take care of her now that her Ayah was dead. There would be a new Ayah, and perhaps she would know some new stories. Mary had grown rather tired of the old ones. She did not cry because her nurse had died. She was not an affectionate child and had never cared much for anyone. The noise and rushing about and wailing over the cholera had frightened her, and she had been angry because no one seemed to remember she was alive. Everyone was too panicked to think of a little girl nobody was fond of. When people had the cholera, it seemed they remembered nothing but themselves. But if everyone had gotten well again, surely someone would remember her and come looking for her.

But no one came, and as she lay waiting, the house seemed to grow quieter and quieter. She heard something rustling on the matting, and when she looked down, she saw a little snake gliding along and watching her with eyes like jewels. She was not frightened, because he was a harmless little thing that would not hurt her, and he seemed to be in a hurry to get out of the room. He slipped under the door as she watched him.
“How strange and quiet it is,” she said. “It sounds as if there is no one in the bungalow but me and the snake.”

Almost the next minute, she heard footsteps in the compound, and then on the veranda. They were men’s footsteps, and the men came into the bungalow and talked in low voices. No one went to meet them or speak to them, and they seemed to be opening doors and looking into rooms.
“What a sad, empty place!” she heard one voice say. “That pretty, pretty woman! I suppose the child, too. I heard there was a child, though no one ever saw her.”

Mary was standing in the middle of the nursery when they opened the door a few minutes later. She looked like an ugly, cross little thing, and she was frowning because she was starting to feel hungry and shamefully neglected. The first man to come in was a large officer she had once seen talking to her father. He looked tired and troubled, but when he saw her he was so startled that he almost jumped back.
“Barney!” he cried out. “There is a child here! A child alone! In a place like this! Heaven help us, who is she?”

“I am Mary Lennox,” the little girl said, drawing herself up stiffly. She thought the man was very rude to call her father’s bungalow “a place like this!” “I fell asleep when everyone had the cholera, and I only just woke up. Why does nobody come?”
“It’s the child no one ever saw!” exclaimed the man, turning to his companions. “She has actually been forgotten!”
“Why was I forgotten?” Mary said, stamping her foot. “Why does nobody come?”
The young man named Barney looked at her with great sadness. Mary even thought she saw him blink, as if he were blinking away tears.
“Poor little kid!” he said. “There is nobody left to come.”

That was the strange and sudden way Mary found out that she had neither father nor mother left. They had died and been carried away in the night. The few native servants who had not died had also left the house as fast as they could get out of it, and not one of them had remembered that there was a Missie Sahib. That was why the place was so quiet. It was true that there was no one in the bungalow but herself and the little rustling snake.

chapters.title: Mistress Mary Quite Contrary
paragraphs: Mary had liked to watch her mother from far away, and she had thought her very pretty. But she hardly knew her, so no one could have expected her to love her, or to miss her much now that she was gone. In fact, she did not miss her at all. Mary was a child who thought only of herself, and she went on thinking only of herself, as she always had. If she had been older, she would surely have been frightened to find herself alone in the world. But she was very young, and since people had always looked after her, she assumed they always would. What she really wondered was whether she was going to live with nice people, who would be polite to her and let her have her own way, as her Ayah and the other native servants had done.

She knew she would not be staying at the English clergyman’s house, where she had been taken at first. She did not want to stay there anyway. The clergyman was poor, and he had five children, all nearly the same age. They wore shabby clothes, and they were always quarreling and snatching toys from one another. Mary hated their messy little bungalow, and she was so unpleasant to the children that after a day or two nobody would play with her. By the second day they had given her a nickname, and it made her furious.

Basil was the one who thought of it first. He was a small boy with cheeky blue eyes and a turned-up nose, and Mary hated him. She was playing by herself under a tree, just as she had been playing on the day the cholera broke out. She was piling up heaps of earth and making paths for a garden, and Basil came and stood close by to watch her. After a while he grew rather interested, and all at once he had an idea to offer.
“Why don’t you put a heap of stones there and pretend it’s a rockery?” he said. “There, in the middle.” And he leaned over her to point.
“Go away!” cried Mary. “I don’t want boys around. Go away!”
For a moment Basil looked angry, and then he started to tease her. He was always teasing his sisters. He danced around and around her, making faces, singing and laughing.

“Mistress Mary, quite contrary,
How does your garden grow?
With silver bells, and cockle shells,
And marigolds all in a row.”

He kept singing it until the other children heard him and laughed too. The angrier Mary got, the more they sang “Mistress Mary, quite contrary.” After that, for as long as she stayed with them, they called her “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary” whenever they talked about her to each other, and often when they talked to her.
“You’re going to be sent home,” Basil told her, “at the end of the week. And we’re glad of it.”
“I’m glad of it too,” Mary answered. “Where is home?”

“She doesn’t even know where home is!” said Basil, with all the scorn of a seven-year-old. “It’s England, of course. Our grandmama lives there, and our sister Mabel was sent to her last year. But you’re not going to your grandmama. You don’t have one. You’re going to your uncle. His name is Mr. Archibald Craven.”
“I don’t know anything about him,” Mary snapped.

“I know you don’t,” Basil answered. “You don’t know anything. Girls never do. I heard Father and Mother talking about him. He lives in a huge, lonely old house in the country, and nobody goes near him. He’s so cross that he won’t let them, and they wouldn’t come even if he did. He’s a hunchback, and he’s horrible.”
“I don’t believe you,” said Mary. She turned her back and stuck her fingers in her ears, because she would not listen to another word.

But she thought about it a great deal afterward. That night Mrs. Crawford told her she would be sailing to England in a few days to live with her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, at Misselthwaite Manor. Mary looked so stony and stubbornly uninterested that they did not know what to make of her. They tried to be kind to her, but she simply turned her face away when Mrs. Crawford tried to kiss her, and she held herself stiff when Mr. Crawford patted her shoulder.

“She’s such a plain child,” Mrs. Crawford said afterward, with pity in her voice. “And her mother was such a pretty creature, with such a pretty manner too. Mary has the most unattractive ways I have ever seen in a child. The children call her ‘Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,’ and though it’s naughty of them, you can’t help understanding why.”

“Perhaps if her mother had brought her pretty face and her pretty manners into the nursery more often, Mary might have learned some pretty ways too. It’s very sad, now that the poor beautiful woman is gone, to think that many people never even knew she had a child at all.”

“I believe she hardly ever looked at her,” sighed Mrs. Crawford. “When her Ayah died, there was nobody left to spare a thought for the poor little thing. Imagine the servants running away and leaving her all alone in that empty bungalow. Colonel McGrew said he nearly jumped out of his skin when he opened the door and found her standing by herself in the middle of the room.”

Mary made the long voyage to England in the care of an officer’s wife, who was taking her own children to leave them at a boarding school. The woman was wrapped up in her own little boy and girl, and she was rather glad to hand Mary over to the woman Mr. Archibald Craven had sent to meet her in London. That woman was his housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor, and her name was Mrs. Medlock. She was a stout woman with very red cheeks and sharp black eyes. She wore a very purple dress, a black silk cape trimmed with shiny black beads, and a black bonnet with purple velvet flowers that stuck up and trembled whenever she moved her head. Mary did not like her at all. But Mary seldom liked anyone, so that was nothing unusual, and it was plain enough that Mrs. Medlock did not think much of her either.
“My word! She’s a plain little thing, isn’t she?” she said. “And we’d heard her mother was a beauty. She hasn’t passed much of it down, has she, ma’am?”
“Perhaps she’ll improve as she grows older,” the officer’s wife said kindly. “If she weren’t so sallow, and had a nicer expression, her features are really quite good. Children change so much.”
“She’ll have to change a good deal,” answered Mrs. Medlock. “And there’s nothing at Misselthwaite likely to improve children—if you ask me!”

They thought Mary was not listening, because she was standing a little apart from them at the window of the private hotel where they had gone. She was watching the buses and cabs and people go by, but she heard every word, and it made her very curious about her uncle and the place where he lived. What sort of place was it, and what would he be like? What was a hunchback? She had never seen one. Perhaps there were none in India.

Ever since she had been living in other people’s houses, with no Ayah, she had begun to feel lonely and to have strange thoughts that were new to her. She had begun to wonder why she had never seemed to belong to anyone, even when her father and mother were alive. Other children seemed to belong to their fathers and mothers, but she had never really seemed to be anyone’s little girl. She had had servants, and food, and clothes, but nobody had paid any attention to her. She did not know this was because she was a disagreeable child. Of course, she did not know she was disagreeable. She often thought other people were, but she had no idea that she was too.

She thought Mrs. Medlock was the most disagreeable person she had ever seen, with her common, brightly colored face and her common, fancy bonnet. The next day they set out on their journey to Yorkshire. Mary walked through the station to the train carriage with her head held high, trying to stay as far away from Mrs. Medlock as she could, because she did not want to seem to belong to her. It would have made her angry to think that people took her for Mrs. Medlock’s little girl.

But Mrs. Medlock was not in the least bothered by Mary or her thoughts. She was the kind of woman who would “stand no nonsense from young ones.” At least, that is what she would have said if anyone had asked her. She had not wanted to go to London just when her sister Maria’s daughter was about to be married. But she had a comfortable, well-paid job as housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor, and the only way to keep it was to do at once whatever Mr. Archibald Craven told her to do. She never dared even to ask a question.

“Captain Lennox and his wife died of the cholera,” Mr. Craven had told her in his short, cold way. “Captain Lennox was my wife’s brother, and I am their daughter’s guardian. The child is to be brought here. You must go to London and bring her yourself.”
So she packed her small trunk and made the journey.

Mary sat in her corner of the railway carriage, looking plain and fretful. She had nothing to read and nothing to look at, so she folded her thin little black-gloved hands in her lap. Her black dress made her look more yellow than ever, and her limp, light hair straggled out from under her black crêpe hat.

“I never saw a more marred-looking young one in my whole life,” Mrs. Medlock thought. (Marred is a Yorkshire word, and it means spoiled and pettish.) She had never seen a child who could sit so still and do nothing. At last she got tired of watching her and began to talk in a brisk, hard voice.
“I suppose I may as well tell you something about where you’re going,” she said. “Do you know anything about your uncle?”
“No,” said Mary.
“You never heard your father and mother talk about him?”
“No,” said Mary, frowning. She frowned because she remembered that her father and mother had never talked to her about anything in particular. They had certainly never told her things.
“Humph,” muttered Mrs. Medlock, staring at her odd, unresponsive little face. She said nothing more for a few moments, and then she began again.
“I suppose you might as well be told something, to get you ready. You’re going to a strange place.”
Mary said nothing at all. Mrs. Medlock seemed rather put out by her obvious lack of interest, but after taking a breath she went on.

“Not that it isn’t a grand big place in a gloomy way, and Mr. Craven is proud of it in his way—and that’s gloomy enough too. The house is six hundred years old, and it stands on the edge of the moor. There are nearly a hundred rooms in it, though most of them are shut up and locked. And there are paintings and fine old furniture and things that have been there for ages, and a big park around it, with gardens and trees whose branches trail to the ground—some of them do.” She paused and took another breath. “But there’s nothing else,” she finished suddenly.

Mary had begun to listen in spite of herself. It all sounded so unlike India, and anything new rather appealed to her. But she did not mean to look interested. That was one of her unhappy, disagreeable ways. So she sat still.
“Well,” said Mrs. Medlock. “What do you think of it?”
“Nothing,” she answered. “I don’t know anything about such places.”
That made Mrs. Medlock give a short laugh.
“Eh!” she said. “But you talk like an old woman. Don’t you care?”
“It doesn’t matter,” said Mary, “whether I care or not.”

“You’re right about that,” said Mrs. Medlock. “It doesn’t. I don’t know why you’re to be kept at Misselthwaite Manor, unless it’s because that’s the easiest way. _He’s_ not going to trouble himself about you, that’s certain. He never troubles himself about anyone.”
She stopped herself, as if she had just remembered something in time.
“He has a crooked back,” she said. “That’s what soured him. He was a sour young man and got no good out of all his money and his big house until he was married.”

Mary’s eyes turned toward her, in spite of her plan not to seem to care. She had never thought of a hunchback being married, and she was a little surprised. Mrs. Medlock saw this, and since she was a talkative woman, she went on with more interest. At any rate, it was one way of passing the time.

“She was a sweet, pretty thing, and he’d have walked the whole world over to get her a blade of grass she wanted. Nobody thought she’d marry him, but she did, and people said she married him for his money. But she didn’t—she didn’t,” she said firmly. “When she died—”
Mary gave a little jump, without meaning to.

“Oh! She died?” she exclaimed, quite without meaning to. She had just remembered a French fairy story she had once read, called “Riquet à la Houppe.” It was about a poor hunchback and a beautiful princess, and it suddenly made her feel sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven.

“Yes, she died,” Mrs. Medlock answered. “And it made him stranger than ever. He cares about nobody. He won’t see people. Most of the time he goes away, and when he is at Misselthwaite he shuts himself up in the West Wing and won’t let anyone see him but Pitcher. Pitcher is an old fellow, but he took care of Mr. Craven when he was a child, and he knows his ways.”

It sounded like something from a book, and it did not make Mary feel cheerful. A house with a hundred rooms, nearly all of them shut up with their doors locked—a house on the edge of a moor, whatever a moor was—sounded dreary. And a man with a crooked back who shut himself up too! She stared out of the window with her lips pressed tightly together. It seemed only natural that the rain should have begun to pour down in gray slanting lines, splashing and streaming down the window panes. If the pretty wife had been alive, she might have made things cheerful. She might have been something like Mary’s own mother, running in and out and going to parties, as her mother had done, in dresses “full of lace.” But she was not there any more.

“You needn’t expect to see him, because ten to one you won’t,” said Mrs. Medlock. “And you mustn’t expect people to talk to you. You’ll have to play about and look after yourself. You’ll be told which rooms you can go into and which you’re to keep out of. There are gardens enough. But when you’re in the house, don’t go wandering and poking about. Mr. Craven won’t have it.”

“I won’t want to go poking about,” said sour little Mary. And just as suddenly as she had begun to feel a little sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven, she stopped feeling sorry and decided he was unpleasant enough to deserve everything that had happened to him.

She turned her face toward the streaming panes of the carriage window and gazed out at the gray rainstorm, which looked as if it would go on forever and ever. She watched it so long and so steadily that the grayness grew heavier and heavier before her eyes, and she fell asleep.

chapters.title: Across the Moor
paragraphs: She slept for a long time. When she woke, Mrs. Medlock had bought a lunch basket at one of the stations, and they ate some chicken, cold beef, bread and butter, and drank hot tea. The rain seemed to be pouring down harder than ever, and everyone in the station wore wet, shining waterproof coats. The guard lit the lamps in the carriage, and Mrs. Medlock grew very cheerful over her tea, chicken and beef. She ate a great deal and then fell asleep herself. Mary sat and stared at her, watching her fine bonnet slide to one side, until she dozed off again in her own corner of the carriage, lulled by the rain splashing against the windows. It was quite dark when she woke the next time. The train had stopped at a station, and Mrs. Medlock was shaking her.
“You’ve had a good sleep!” she said. “Time to open your eyes! We’re at Thwaite Station, and we’ve got a long drive ahead of us.”

Mary stood up and tried to keep her eyes open while Mrs. Medlock gathered her parcels. The little girl did not offer to help. In India, native servants always picked things up and carried them, and it seemed perfectly proper to her that other people should wait on you.

The station was small, and nobody but the two of them seemed to be getting off the train. The station-master spoke to Mrs. Medlock in a rough, friendly way. He pronounced his words in a strange, broad manner that Mary later learned was Yorkshire.
“I see you’ve got back,” he said. “And you’ve brought the young one with you.”
“Aye, that’s her,” answered Mrs. Medlock. She spoke with a Yorkshire accent herself, and she jerked her head back over her shoulder toward Mary. “How’s your Missus?”
“Well enough. The carriage is waiting outside for you.”

A brougham stood on the road in front of the little open platform. Mary saw that it was a smart carriage, and that the footman who helped her in was smart too. His long waterproof coat and the waterproof cover on his hat were shining and dripping with rain, just like everything else, including the burly station-master.

The footman shut the door and climbed up beside the coachman, and they drove off. The little girl found herself in a comfortably cushioned corner, but she did not feel like going back to sleep. She sat looking out of the window. She was curious to see something of the road that was taking her to the strange place Mrs. Medlock had talked about. She was not a timid child at all, and she was not exactly frightened. But she felt that anything might happen in a house with a hundred rooms, nearly all of them shut up—a house standing at the edge of a moor.
“What is a moor?” she asked Mrs. Medlock suddenly.

“Look out of the window in about ten minutes and you’ll see,” the woman answered. “We have to drive five miles across Missel Moor before we reach the Manor. You won’t see much, because it’s a dark night, but you’ll see something.”

Mary asked no more questions. She waited in the darkness of her corner, keeping her eyes on the window. The carriage lamps threw light a little way ahead, and she caught glimpses of the things they passed. After leaving the station, they had driven through a tiny village, and she had seen whitewashed cottages and the lights of a public house. Then they had passed a church and a vicarage. In one cottage there was a little shop window with toys, sweets and odd things set out for sale. Then they were on the highroad, and she saw hedges and trees. After that there seemed to be nothing different for a long time—or at least it felt like a long time to her.

At last the horses began to slow down, as if they were climbing uphill. Soon there seemed to be no more hedges and no more trees. In fact, she could see nothing but thick darkness on either side. She leaned forward and pressed her face against the window just as the carriage gave a big jolt.
“Eh! We’re on the moor now, sure enough,” said Mrs. Medlock.

The carriage lamps cast a yellow light on a rough road that seemed to be cut through bushes and low, scrubby plants. Beyond them lay the great dark expanse that spread out in front of them and all around. A wind was rising, and it made a strange, wild, low, rushing sound.
“It’s—it’s not the sea, is it?” said Mary, looking around at her companion.

“No, not at all,” answered Mrs. Medlock. “It isn’t fields or mountains either. It’s just miles and miles and miles of wild land where nothing grows but heather and gorse and broom, and nothing lives but wild ponies and sheep.”
“I feel as if it might be the sea, if there were water on it,” said Mary. “It sounds like the sea right now.”
“That’s the wind blowing through the bushes,” Mrs. Medlock said. “It’s a wild, dreary sort of place, if you ask me, though plenty of people like it—especially when the heather’s in bloom.”

On and on they drove through the darkness. The rain stopped, but the wind rushed past and whistled and made strange sounds. The road went up and down, and several times the carriage crossed a little bridge, with water rushing very fast and noisily underneath. Mary felt as if the drive would never end. The wide, bleak moor seemed to her like a vast black ocean, and she was crossing it on a narrow strip of dry land.
“I don’t like it,” she said to herself. “I don’t like it,” and she pressed her thin lips more tightly together.
The horses were climbing a hilly stretch of road when she first caught sight of a light. Mrs. Medlock saw it just as soon as she did, and she let out a long sigh of relief.
“Eh, I’m glad to see that bit of light twinkling,” she exclaimed. “It’s the light in the lodge window. We’ll get a good cup of tea before long, at any rate.”

It was “before long,” as she had said, but not very soon. When the carriage passed through the park gates, there were still two miles of avenue to drive through. The trees nearly met overhead, so it felt as if they were driving through a long, dark tunnel.

They drove out of the tunnel into an open space and stopped in front of an immensely long but low house that seemed to ramble around a stone courtyard. At first Mary thought there were no lights at all in the windows. But as she got out of the carriage, she saw that one room in a corner upstairs showed a dull glow.

The front door was huge, made of massive, oddly shaped panels of oak, studded with big iron nails and bound with great iron bars. It opened into an enormous hall, so dimly lit that the faces in the portraits on the walls and the figures in the suits of armor made Mary not want to look at them. As she stood on the stone floor, she looked like a very small, odd little black figure, and she felt as small and lost and odd as she looked.
A neat, thin old man stood near the manservant who opened the door for them.
“You are to take her to her room,” he said in a husky voice. “He doesn’t want to see her. He’s going to London in the morning.”
“Very well, Mr. Pitcher,” Mrs. Medlock answered. “As long as I know what’s expected of me, I can manage.”
“What’s expected of you, Mrs. Medlock,” Mr. Pitcher said, “is that you make sure he isn’t disturbed, and that he doesn’t see what he doesn’t want to see.”

Then Mary Lennox was led up a broad staircase, down a long corridor, up a short flight of steps, and through one corridor after another. At last a door opened in a wall, and she found herself in a room with a fire burning and a supper laid out on a table.
Mrs. Medlock said bluntly:
“Well, here you are! This room and the next one are where you’ll live—and you must stay in them. Don’t you forget that!”
That was how Mistress Mary arrived at Misselthwaite Manor, and she had perhaps never felt so contrary in all her life.

chapters.title: Martha
paragraphs: Mary woke the next morning because a young housemaid had come in to light the fire. The girl was kneeling on the hearth-rug, noisily raking out the cinders. Mary lay still and watched her for a few moments, and then she began to look around the room. She had never seen a room like it, and she thought it was strange and gloomy. The walls were hung with tapestry, embroidered with a scene from a forest. Under the trees stood people in fantastic costumes, and far off she could see the turrets of a castle. There were hunters and horses and dogs and ladies. Mary felt as if she were in the forest with them. Through a deep window she could see a great stretch of land that climbed up and away. It seemed to have no trees at all, and it looked rather like an endless, dull, purplish sea.
“What is that?” she said, pointing out of the window.
Martha, the young housemaid, had just gotten to her feet. She looked out and pointed too.
“That over there?” she said.
“Yes.”
“That’s the moor,” she said with a friendly grin. “Do you like it?”
“No,” answered Mary. “I hate it.”
“That’s only because you’re not used to it,” said Martha, going back to her hearth. “You think it’s too big and bare right now. But you will like it.”
“Do you?” asked Mary.

“Aye, I do,” answered Martha cheerfully, scrubbing away at the grate. “I love it. It’s not bare at all. It’s covered with growing things that smell sweet. It’s lovely in spring and summer, when the gorse and broom and heather are in flower. It smells of honey, and there’s so much fresh air—and the sky looks so high, and the bees and skylarks make such a nice noise, humming and singing. Eh! I wouldn’t live away from the moor for anything.”

Mary listened to her with a serious, puzzled look. The native servants she had known in India were nothing like this. They were fawning and humble, and they never dared to talk to their masters as if they were equals. They bowed low and called them “protector of the poor” and names like that. Indian servants were given orders, never asked. It was not the custom to say “please” or “thank you,” and when Mary was angry she had always slapped her Ayah in the face. She wondered a little what this girl would do if someone slapped her. Martha was a round, rosy, good-natured looking creature, but she had a sturdy way about her. It made Mistress Mary wonder whether she might even slap back—if the person who slapped her was only a little girl.
“You are a strange servant,” she said from her pillows, rather haughtily.
Martha sat back on her heels with her blacking-brush in her hand. She laughed, and she did not seem the least bit angry.

“Eh! I know that,” she said. “If there was a grand Missus at Misselthwaite, I’d never have been even one of the under housemaids. Maybe they’d have let me be a scullerymaid, but I’d never have been allowed upstairs. I’m too common, and I talk too much Yorkshire. But this is a funny house, for all it’s so grand. It seems like there’s no Master or Mistress, except Mr. Pitcher and Mrs. Medlock. Mr. Craven won’t be bothered about anything when he’s here, and he’s nearly always away. Mrs. Medlock gave me the job out of kindness. She told me she could never have done it if Misselthwaite had been like other big houses.”
“Are you going to be my servant?” Mary asked, still in her bossy little Indian way.
Martha started to rub her grate again.
“I’m Mrs. Medlock’s servant,” she said firmly. “And she’s Mr. Craven’s. But I’m to do the housemaid’s work up here and wait on you a bit. You won’t need much waiting on, though.”
“Who is going to dress me?” demanded Mary.
Martha sat back on her heels again and stared. In her amazement she spoke in broad Yorkshire.
“Can’t you dress yourself!” she said.
“What do you mean? I don’t understand your language,” said Mary.
“Eh! I forgot,” Martha said. “Mrs. Medlock told me I’d have to be careful, or you wouldn’t know what I was saying. I mean, can’t you put on your own clothes?”
“No,” answered Mary, quite indignantly. “I never did in my whole life. My Ayah dressed me, of course.”

“Well,” said Martha, plainly not aware at all that she was being rude, “it’s time you learned. You can’t start too young. It’ll do you good to wait on yourself a bit. My mother always said she couldn’t see why grand people’s children didn’t turn out to be fools. What with nurses, and being washed and dressed and taken out to walk as if they were puppies!”
“It is different in India,” said Mistress Mary scornfully. She could hardly stand this.
But Martha was not crushed at all.

“Eh! I can see it’s different,” she answered, almost sympathetically. “I expect it’s because there are so many blacks there instead of proper white people. When I heard you were coming from India, I thought you were a black too.”
Mary sat up in bed, furious.
“What!” she said. “What! You thought I was a native. You—you daughter of a pig!”
Martha stared at her and turned red.

“Who are you calling names?” she said. “You needn’t be so upset. That’s not the way for a young lady to talk. I’ve nothing against the blacks. When you read about them in religious pamphlets, they’re always very devout. You always read that a black is a man and a brother. I’ve never seen a black, and I was really pleased to think I was going to see one up close. When I came in to light your fire this morning, I crept up to your bed and carefully pulled back the cover to look at you. And there you were,” she said, disappointed, “no more black than me—for all you’re so yellow.”
Mary did not even try to control her rage and humiliation.

“You thought I was a native! You dared! You don’t know anything about natives! They are not people—they’re servants who must bow to you. You know nothing about India. You know nothing about anything!”

She was in such a rage, and she felt so helpless before the girl’s plain stare. Somehow she also felt suddenly and horribly lonely, far away from everything she understood and everything that understood her. So she threw herself face down on the pillows and burst into passionate sobbing. She sobbed so wildly that good-natured Yorkshire Martha was a little frightened and quite sorry for her. She went to the bed and bent over her.

“Eh! You mustn’t cry like that!” she begged. “You really mustn’t. I didn’t know you’d be so upset. I don’t know anything about anything—just like you said. I beg your pardon, Miss. Please stop crying.”

There was something comforting and truly friendly in her odd Yorkshire speech and her sturdy ways, and it had a good effect on Mary. She gradually stopped crying and grew quiet. Martha looked relieved.

“It’s time for you to get up now,” she said. “Mrs. Medlock said I was to carry your breakfast and tea and dinner into the room next to this one. It’s been made into a nursery for you. I’ll help you with your clothes if you’ll get out of bed. If the buttons are at the back, you can’t button them up yourself.”
When Mary finally decided to get up, the clothes Martha took from the wardrobe were not the ones she had worn when she arrived the night before with Mrs. Medlock.
“Those are not mine,” she said. “Mine are black.”
She looked over the thick white wool coat and dress, and then she added with cool approval:
“These are nicer than mine.”

“These are the ones you have to put on,” Martha answered. “Mr. Craven ordered Mrs. Medlock to get them in London. He said, ‘I won’t have a child dressed in black wandering about like a lost soul. It would make the place sadder than it is. Put some color on her.’ Mother said she knew what he meant. Mother always knows what a person means. She doesn’t hold with black herself.”
“I hate black things,” said Mary.

The dressing taught them both something. Martha had “buttoned up” her little sisters and brothers, but she had never seen a child who stood still and waited for someone else to do things for her. It was as if Mary had neither hands nor feet of her own.
“Why don’t you put on your own shoes?” she said when Mary calmly held out her foot.
“My Ayah did it,” answered Mary, staring. “It was the custom.”

She said that very often—“It was the custom.” The native servants were always saying it. If you told them to do something their ancestors had not done for a thousand years, they gazed at you mildly and said, “It is not the custom,” and you knew that was the end of the matter.

It had never been the custom for Mistress Mary to do anything but stand and let herself be dressed like a doll. But before she was ready for breakfast, she began to suspect that life at Misselthwaite Manor would end up teaching her a number of things that were quite new to her. She would learn things like putting on her own shoes and stockings, and picking up what she dropped. If Martha had been a well-trained young lady’s maid, she would have been more humble and respectful. She would have known it was her business to brush hair, and button boots, and pick things up and put them away. But she was only an untrained Yorkshire country girl. She had been raised in a cottage on the moor with a swarm of little brothers and sisters. They had never dreamed of doing anything but waiting on themselves. They also waited on the younger ones, who were either babies in arms or just learning to totter about and tumble over things.

If Mary Lennox had been a child ready to be amused, she might have laughed at how readily Martha talked. But Mary only listened coldly, and she wondered at the girl’s free and easy manner. At first she was not interested at all. But gradually, as the girl rattled on in her good-tempered, homely way, Mary began to notice what she was saying.

“Eh! You should see them all,” she said. “There are twelve of us, and my father only gets sixteen shillings a week. I can tell you, my mother has a hard time getting porridge for them all. They tumble about on the moor and play there all day, and Mother says the air of the moor fattens them up. She says she believes they eat the grass, same as the wild ponies do. Our Dickon, he’s twelve years old, and he has a young pony he calls his own.”
“Where did he get it?” asked Mary.

“He found it on the moor with its mother when it was just a baby. He started making friends with it and giving it bits of bread and picking young grass for it. And it got to like him so much that it follows him about and lets him get on its back. Dickon’s a kind lad, and animals like him.”

Mary had never owned a pet of her own, and she had always thought she would like one. So she began to feel a slight interest in Dickon. She had never before been interested in anyone but herself, so this was the dawning of a healthy feeling. She went into the room that had been made into a nursery for her, and she found it was rather like the one she had slept in. It was not a child’s room but a grown-up’s room, with gloomy old pictures on the walls and heavy old oak chairs. A table in the center was set with a good, solid breakfast. But she had always had a very small appetite, and she looked at the first plate Martha set before her with something more than indifference.
“I don’t want it,” she said.
“You don’t want your porridge!” Martha exclaimed in disbelief.
“No.”
“You don’t know how good it is. Put a bit of treacle on it, or a bit of sugar.”
“I don’t want it,” Mary repeated.
“Eh!” said Martha. “I can’t stand to see good food go to waste. If our children were at this table, they’d clean it bare in five minutes.”
“Why?” said Mary coldly.
“Why!” echoed Martha. “Because they hardly ever had their stomachs full in their lives. They’re as hungry as young hawks and foxes.”
“I don’t know what it is to be hungry,” said Mary, with the indifference of ignorance.
Martha looked indignant.

“Well, it would do you good to try it. I can see that plain enough,” she said bluntly. “I have no patience with folks who sit there and just stare at good bread and meat. My word! Don’t I wish Dickon and Phil and Jane and the rest of them had what’s here under their pinafores.”
“Why don’t you take it to them?” suggested Mary.
“It’s not mine,” answered Martha firmly. “And this isn’t my day out. I get my day out once a month, same as the rest. Then I go home and clean up for Mother and give her a day’s rest.”
Mary drank some tea and ate a little toast and some marmalade.
“You wrap up warm and run out and play,” said Martha. “It’ll do you good and give you some appetite for your meat.”
Mary went to the window. There were gardens and paths and big trees, but everything looked dull and wintry.
“Go out? Why should I go out on a day like this?”
“Well, if you don’t go out, you’ll have to stay in, and what have you got to do?”
Mary glanced around. There was nothing to do. When Mrs. Medlock had prepared the nursery, she had not thought about amusement. Perhaps it would be better to go and see what the gardens were like.
“Who will go with me?” she asked.
Martha stared.

“You’ll go by yourself,” she answered. “You’ll have to learn to play like other children do when they haven’t got sisters and brothers. Our Dickon goes off on the moor by himself and plays for hours. That’s how he made friends with the pony. He’s got sheep on the moor that know him, and birds that come and eat out of his hand. However little there is to eat, he always saves a bit of his bread to coax his pets.”

It was really this mention of Dickon that made Mary decide to go out, though she did not realize it. There would be birds outside, even if there would not be ponies or sheep. They would be different from the birds in India, and it might amuse her to look at them.
Martha found her coat and hat and a pair of stout little boots, and she showed her the way downstairs.

“If you go around that way, you’ll come to the gardens,” she said, pointing to a gate in a wall of shrubbery. “There are lots of flowers in summertime, but there’s nothing blooming now.” She seemed to hesitate a second before she added, “One of the gardens is locked up. No one has been in it for ten years.”
“Why?” asked Mary in spite of herself. Here was another locked door, added to the hundred in the strange house.

“Mr. Craven had it shut up when his wife died so suddenly. He won’t let anyone go inside. It was her garden. He locked the door and dug a hole and buried the key. There’s Mrs. Medlock’s bell ringing—I must run.”

After Martha was gone, Mary turned down the walk that led to the door in the shrubbery. She could not stop thinking about the garden that no one had been into for ten years. She wondered what it would look like and whether any flowers were still alive in it. She passed through the shrubbery gate and found herself in great gardens, with wide lawns and winding walks with clipped borders. There were trees and flower-beds, and evergreens clipped into strange shapes, and a large pool with an old gray fountain in the middle. But the flower-beds were bare and wintry, and the fountain was not playing. This was not the garden that was shut up. How could a garden be shut up? You could always walk into a garden.

She was just thinking this when she noticed a long wall at the end of the path she was following. Ivy was growing over it. She did not know England well enough to realize that she was coming to the kitchen-gardens, where the vegetables and fruit were grown. She went toward the wall and found a green door in the ivy, and it stood open. This was clearly not the closed garden, so she could go in.

She went through the door and found a garden with walls all around it. It was only one of several walled gardens that seemed to open into one another. She saw another open green door, showing bushes and pathways between beds of winter vegetables. Fruit-trees were trained flat against the wall, and over some of the beds there were glass frames. Mary stood and stared around her. The place was bare and ugly enough, she thought. It might be nicer in summer when things were green, but there was nothing pretty about it now.

Before long, an old man with a spade on his shoulder came through the door that led from the second garden. He looked startled to see Mary, and he touched his cap. His old face was sour and grumpy, and he did not seem the least bit glad to find her there. But Mary was annoyed with his garden and was wearing her “quite contrary” look, and she certainly was not glad to see him either.
“What is this place?” she asked.
“It’s one of the kitchen gardens,” he answered.
“What is that?” said Mary, pointing through the other green door.
“Another one,” he said shortly. “There’s one more on the other side of that wall, and the orchard is on the far side of that.”
“May I go into them?” asked Mary.
“If you like. But there’s nothing to see.”

Mary did not answer. She walked down the path and through the second green door. On the other side she found more walls, along with winter vegetables and glass frames. In the second wall, though, there was one more green door, and it was closed. Maybe it led into the garden that no one had seen for ten years. Mary was not a timid child, and she had always done whatever she pleased, so she went up to the door and turned the handle. She half hoped it would not open, because then she could be sure she had found the mysterious garden. But it opened easily, and she stepped through into an orchard. It had walls all around it as well, with trees trained against them, and bare fruit trees stood in the brown winter grass. There was no green door anywhere in sight. Mary searched for one. Yet when she first came into the upper end of the garden, she had noticed that the wall did not seem to stop at the orchard. It seemed to go on past it, as if it closed in some other place beyond. She could see the tops of trees above the wall. As she stood still, she spotted a bird with a bright red breast perched on the highest branch of one of them. All at once he burst into his winter song, almost as if he had seen her and was calling her.

She stopped to listen, and somehow his cheerful, friendly little whistle made her feel glad. Even a disagreeable little girl can be lonely. The huge closed-up house, the huge bare moor and the huge bare gardens had made this one feel as if she were the only person left in the world. If she had been an affectionate child, used to being loved, her heart would have broken. But though she was “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,” she was forlorn, and the little bird with the bright breast brought a look to her sour face that was very nearly a smile. She listened until he flew away. He was nothing like the birds of India, and she liked him. She wondered whether she would ever see him again. Perhaps he lived in the mysterious garden and knew all its secrets.

Perhaps she thought so much about the abandoned garden simply because she had nothing at all to do. It made her curious, and she wanted to know what it looked like. Why had Mr. Archibald Craven buried the key? If he had loved his wife so much, why did he hate her garden? She wondered if she would ever meet him. She knew that if she did, she would not like him, and he would not like her. She would only stand and stare and say nothing, even though she would be desperate to ask him why he had done such a strange thing.
“Nobody ever likes me, and I never like anybody,” she thought. “And I can’t chatter the way the Crawford children could. They were forever talking and laughing and making a racket.”
She thought about the robin and how he had seemed to sing his song to her. As she remembered the treetop where he had perched, she suddenly stopped short on the path.
“I’m almost certain that tree stood inside the secret garden,” she said. “The place had a wall all around it, and no door.”

She went back to the first kitchen garden, where the old man was still digging. She stopped beside him and watched for a few moments, cool and silent as ever. He took no notice of her, so finally she spoke up.
“I have been into the other gardens,” she said.
“Nothing stopped you,” he answered crossly.
“I went into the orchard.”
“There was no dog at the door to bite you,” he answered.
“There was no door into the other garden,” said Mary.
“What garden?” he said in a rough voice, pausing in his digging for a moment.
“The one beyond the wall,” answered Mistress Mary. “It has trees in it. I could see their tops. A bird with a red breast sat on one of them, singing.”

To her surprise, the gruff, weather-beaten old face changed. A slow smile spread across it, and the gardener looked like a different man. Mary thought it was strange how much nicer a person looked when he smiled. She had never noticed that before.
He turned to face the orchard and began to whistle, very low and soft. Mary could not imagine how a man so grumpy could make a sound so gentle and coaxing.

Almost at once, something wonderful happened. She heard a soft little rush of wings through the air. It was the bird with the red breast, flying toward them, and he landed on a big lump of earth right near the gardener’s foot.
“Here he is,” the old man chuckled, and then he spoke to the bird the way you would speak to a child.
“Where have you been, you cheeky little rascal?” he said. “I haven’t seen you before today. Have you started your courting this early in the season? You’re too forward.”

The bird cocked his tiny head and looked up at the old man with one soft, bright eye, round and black as a dewdrop. He seemed perfectly at ease and not at all afraid. He hopped around, pecking quickly at the ground for seeds and insects. Mary felt a strange tug in her heart, because he was so pretty and cheerful and so very like a person. His body was small and plump, his beak delicate, his legs thin and fine.
“Does he always come when you call him?” she asked, almost in a whisper.

“Aye, that he does. I’ve known him since he was a fledgling. He came out of the nest in the other garden, and when he first flew over the wall he was too weak to fly back for a few days, so we got friendly. When he went over the wall again, the rest of the brood was gone. He was lonely, and he came back to me.”
“What kind of bird is he?” Mary asked.

“Don’t you know? He’s a robin redbreast, and they’re the friendliest, nosiest birds alive. They’re nearly as friendly as dogs, if you know how to get along with them. Watch him pecking about there and looking round at us every now and then. He knows we’re talking about him.”
It was the oddest sight to see the old fellow gazing at the plump little bird in his scarlet waistcoat. He looked both proud of him and fond of him.

“He’s a conceited one,” he chuckled. “He likes to hear people talk about him. And nosy! Bless me, there never was his equal for curiosity and meddling. He’s always coming to see what I’m planting. He knows everything Mr. Craven never bothers to find out for himself. He’s the head gardener, he is.”

The robin kept hopping and pecking at the soil, and every so often he paused to look their way. Mary thought his black dewdrop eyes studied her with great interest. It truly seemed that he was learning everything about her. The strange tug in her heart grew stronger.
“Where did the rest of the brood fly to?” she asked.
“There’s no knowing. The old birds push the young ones out of the nest and make them fly, and they’re scattered before you know it. This one was a clever one, and he knew he was lonely.”
Mistress Mary stepped a little closer to the robin and looked at him very hard.
“I’m lonely,” she said.
Until now she had never realized that loneliness was part of what made her sour and cross. She found it out as the robin gazed at her and she gazed back.
Pushing his cap back from his bald head, the old gardener stared at her for a long minute.
“Are you the little lass from India?” he asked.
Mary nodded.
“Then it’s no wonder you’re lonely. You’ll be lonelier before you’re done,” he said.
He went back to digging, pushing his spade deep into the rich dark earth, while the robin hopped about, very busy with his own affairs.
“What is your name?” Mary asked.
He stood up straight to answer her.
“Ben Weatherstaff,” he said. Then, with a gruff chuckle, he added, “I’m lonely too, except when he’s around,” and he jerked a thumb at the robin. “He’s the only friend I have.”
“Friends? I have none,” said Mary. “I never did. My Ayah disliked me, and I never played with anyone.”
Yorkshire people have a habit of saying exactly what they think, bluntly and plainly, and old Ben Weatherstaff was a Yorkshire moor man.
“You and me are a good deal alike,” he said. “We were cut from the same cloth. Neither of us is good-looking, and we’re both as sour as we look. We’ve both got nasty tempers, I’ll warrant.”

This was plain speaking, and Mary Lennox had never once in her life heard the truth about herself. The native servants had always bowed low and given in to her, no matter what she did. She had never thought much about her looks. Now she wondered whether she was as plain as Ben Weatherstaff, and whether she looked as sour as he had looked before the robin came. She even began to wonder whether she was “nasty-tempered.” She felt uncomfortable.

Suddenly a clear, rippling sound rang out close by, and she turned around. She was standing a few feet from a young apple tree. The robin had flown onto one of its branches and burst into a snatch of song. Ben Weatherstaff laughed out loud.
“Why did he do that?” asked Mary.
“He’s decided he wants to be your friend,” replied Ben. “Blast me, if he hasn’t gone and taken a liking to you.”
“To me?” said Mary. She moved softly toward the little tree and looked up.

“Will you be my friend?” she asked the robin, just as though she were talking to a person. “Will you?” She did not use her hard little voice or her bossy Indian voice. Her tone was so soft and eager and coaxing that Ben Weatherstaff was just as surprised as she had been when she heard him whistle.
“Well, I never,” he cried. “You said that so sweetly and kindly, like a real child and not a sharp old woman. You said it nearly the way Dickon talks to his wild creatures out on the moor.”
“Do you know Dickon?” Mary asked, turning around in a hurry.

“Everybody knows him. Dickon wanders about everywhere. Even the blackberries and the heather-bells know him. I’d wager the foxes show him where their cubs are, and the skylarks don’t hide their nests from him.”

Mary would have asked more. She was nearly as curious about Dickon as she was about the forgotten garden. But just then the robin finished his song, shook his wings, opened them and flew off. His visit was over, and he had other business.
“He’s gone over the wall!” Mary cried, watching him fly. “Into the orchard, and then over the other wall, into the garden that has no door!”
“That’s where he lives,” said old Ben. “He hatched there. If he’s out courting, he’s sweet-talking some young madam of a robin among the old rose trees in there.”
“Rose trees?” said Mary. “Are there rose trees?”
Ben Weatherstaff picked up his spade again and began to dig.
“There were ten years ago,” he mumbled.
“I’d love to see them,” said Mary. “Where is that green door? A door must be somewhere.”
Ben thrust his spade deep and looked every bit as unfriendly as he had when she first laid eyes on him.
“There was ten years ago, but there isn’t now,” he said.
“No door!” cried Mary. “There must be one.”

“None that anyone can find, and none that’s anyone’s business. Don’t you be a nosy lass and poke your nose where it doesn’t belong. Here, I must get on with my work. Off with you and go play. I’ve no more time.”
And he really did stop digging. He swung his spade onto his shoulder and stalked away without a glance at her or a word of good-bye.

chapters.title: The Cry in the Corridor
paragraphs: At first, every day that passed was exactly like the one before for Mary Lennox. Each morning she woke in her tapestried room and found Martha kneeling at the hearth, building the fire. Each morning she ate breakfast in the nursery, which had nothing in it to amuse her. After every breakfast she gazed out the window at the huge moor, which seemed to stretch out in every direction and climb right up to the sky. After staring for a while, she realized that if she did not go outside she would have to stay in and do nothing—so out she went. She did not know it was the best thing she could have done. She did not know that when she began to walk fast, or even run, along the paths and down the avenue, she was stirring up her slow blood. She was making herself stronger by struggling against the wind that swept down from the moor. She ran only to get warm, and she hated the wind that rushed at her face, roared, and held her back as if it were some giant she could not see. But the big breaths of rough, fresh air blowing over the heather filled her lungs with something good for her whole thin body. They whipped some red into her cheeks and brightened her dull eyes, and she had no idea it was happening.

But after a few days spent almost entirely outdoors, she woke one morning knowing what it was to be hungry. When she sat down to breakfast, she did not look scornfully at her porridge and push it away. She picked up her spoon, began to eat, and kept on eating until her bowl was empty.
“You did well with that this morning, didn’t you?” said Martha.
“It tastes good today,” said Mary, feeling a little surprised herself.

“It’s the air of the moor that’s giving you a stomach for your food,” answered Martha. “It’s lucky for you that you’ve got food as well as appetite. There’s been twelve in our cottage with the stomach for it and nothing to put in it. You keep on playing out of doors every day and you’ll get some flesh on your bones, and you won’t be so yellow.”
“I don’t play,” said Mary. “I have nothing to play with.”

“Nothing to play with!” exclaimed Martha. “Our children play with sticks and stones. They just run about and shout and look at things.” Mary did not shout, but she did look at things. There was nothing else to do. She walked round and round the gardens and wandered along the paths in the park. Sometimes she looked for Ben Weatherstaff. Though she saw him at work several times, he was either too busy to look at her or too grumpy. Once, when she was walking toward him, he picked up his spade and turned away, as if he did it on purpose.

There was one place she went to more often than any other. It was the long walk outside the gardens with the walls around them. There were bare flower beds on either side of it, and ivy grew thickly against the walls. In one spot, the creeping dark green leaves were bushier than anywhere else. It looked as if that part had been neglected for a long time. The rest of the ivy had been clipped and made neat, but at this lower end of the walk it had not been trimmed at all.

A few days after she had talked to Ben Weatherstaff, Mary stopped to notice this and wondered why it was so. She had just paused and was looking up at a long spray of ivy swinging in the wind when she saw a gleam of scarlet and heard a bright chirp. There on top of the wall sat Ben Weatherstaff’s robin redbreast, leaning forward to look at her with his small head tilted to one side.
“Oh!” she cried out. “Is it you? Is it you?” It did not seem at all strange to her that she spoke to him as if she were sure he would understand and answer.

And he did answer. He twittered and chirped and hopped along the wall as if he were telling her all sorts of things. It seemed to Mistress Mary that she understood him, too, even though he was not speaking in words. It was as if he said:
“Good morning! Isn’t the wind nice? Isn’t the sun nice? Isn’t everything nice? Let’s both chirp and hop and twitter. Come on! Come on!”
Mary began to laugh. As he hopped and took little flights along the wall, she ran after him. Poor little thin, sallow, ugly Mary—for a moment she actually looked almost pretty.

“I like you! I like you!” she cried, pattering down the walk. She chirped and tried to whistle, though she had no idea how to do that at all. But the robin seemed quite satisfied, and he chirped and whistled back at her. At last he spread his wings and darted up to the top of a tree, where he perched and sang loudly.

That reminded Mary of the first time she had seen him. He had been swinging on a treetop then, and she had been standing in the orchard. Now she was on the other side of the orchard, standing on the path outside a wall—much lower down—and there was the same tree inside.
“It’s in the garden no one can go into,” she said to herself. “It’s the garden without a door. He lives in there. How I wish I could see what it’s like!”

She ran up the walk to the green door she had come through the first morning. Then she ran down the path through the other door and into the orchard. When she stood and looked up, there was the tree on the other side of the wall, and there was the robin, just finishing his song and starting to preen his feathers with his beak.
“It is the garden,” she said. “I’m sure it is.”

She walked all the way around and looked closely at that side of the orchard wall, but she found only what she had found before—there was no door in it. Then she ran through the kitchen gardens again and out into the walk beside the long ivy-covered wall. She walked to the end of it and looked, but there was no door. Then she walked to the other end, looking again, and still there was no door.
“It’s very strange,” she said. “Ben Weatherstaff said there was no door, and there is no door. But there must have been one ten years ago, because Mr. Craven buried the key.”

This gave her so much to think about that she began to be quite interested, and she felt she was not sorry after all that she had come to Misselthwaite Manor. In India she had always felt too hot and too listless to care much about anything. The truth was that the fresh wind from the moor had begun to blow the cobwebs out of her young brain and wake her up a little.

She stayed outdoors nearly all day. When she sat down to supper that night, she felt hungry and drowsy and comfortable. She did not feel cross when Martha chattered away. She felt she rather liked hearing her, and at last she thought she would ask her a question. She asked it after she had finished supper and sat down on the hearth rug in front of the fire.
“Why did Mr. Craven hate the garden?” she said.

She had made Martha stay with her, and Martha had not minded at all. She was very young and used to a crowded cottage full of brothers and sisters. She found it dull in the great servants’ hall downstairs, where the footman and the upper housemaids made fun of her Yorkshire speech, looked down on her as a common little thing, and sat whispering among themselves. Martha liked to talk, and the strange child who had lived in India and been waited on by “blacks” was novelty enough to attract her.
She sat down on the hearth herself, without waiting to be asked.
“Are you still thinking about that garden?” she said. “I knew you would. That was just how it was with me when I first heard about it.”
“Why did he hate it?” Mary persisted.
Martha tucked her feet under her and made herself quite comfortable.
“Listen to the wind wuthering round the house,” she said. “You could hardly stand up on the moor if you were out on it tonight.”

Mary did not know what “wuthering” meant until she listened, and then she understood. It must mean that hollow, shuddering sort of roar that rushed round and round the house, as if the giant no one could see were pounding on it and beating at the walls and windows to break in. But you knew he could not get in, and somehow it made you feel very safe and warm inside a room with a red coal fire.
“But why did he hate it so?” she asked, after she had listened. She meant to find out, if Martha knew.
Then Martha gave up her store of knowledge.

“Mind,” she said, “Mrs. Medlock said it’s not to be talked about. There’s lots of things in this place that’s not to be talked over. That’s Mr. Craven’s orders. His troubles are none of the servants’ business, he says. But if it weren’t for the garden he wouldn’t be like he is. It was Mrs. Craven’s garden. She made it when they were first married, and she just loved it, and they used to tend the flowers themselves. And none of the gardeners was ever let in. He and she used to go in and shut the door and stay there hours and hours, reading and talking. And she was just a bit of a girl, and there was an old tree with a branch bent like a seat on it. She made roses grow over it, and she used to sit there. But one day when she was sitting there, the branch broke and she fell to the ground and was hurt so badly that she died the next day. The doctors thought he’d go out of his mind and die, too. That’s why he hates it. No one’s ever gone in since, and he won’t let anyone talk about it.”
Mary did not ask any more questions. She looked at the red fire and listened to the wind “wuthering.” It seemed to be “wuthering” louder than ever.

At that moment, something very good was happening to her. In fact, four good things had happened to her since she came to Misselthwaite Manor. She had felt as if she understood a robin and he understood her. She had run in the wind until her blood grew warm. She had been healthily hungry for the first time in her life. And she had found out what it was to feel sorry for someone.

But as she listened to the wind, she began to listen to something else. She did not know what it was, because at first she could hardly tell it apart from the wind itself. It was a strange sound—it seemed almost as if a child were crying somewhere. Sometimes the wind sounded a good deal like a child crying, but soon Mistress Mary felt quite sure this sound was inside the house, not outside it. It was far away, but it was inside. She turned around and looked at Martha.
“Do you hear someone crying?” she said.
Martha suddenly looked confused.
“No,” she answered. “It’s the wind. Sometimes it sounds like someone’s lost on the moor and wailing. It’s got all sorts of sounds.”
“But listen,” said Mary. “It’s in the house—down one of those long corridors.”

And at that very moment a door must have been opened somewhere downstairs, because a great rushing draft blew along the passage. The door of the room where they sat was blown open with a crash. They both jumped to their feet, and the light went out. The crying sound was swept down the far corridor, so that it could be heard more plainly than ever.
“There!” said Mary. “I told you so! It is someone crying—and it isn’t a grown-up.”

Martha ran and shut the door and turned the key. But before she did, they both heard a door in some far passage shut with a bang, and then everything was quiet, because even the wind stopped “wuthering” for a few moments.
“It was the wind,” said Martha stubbornly. “And if it wasn’t, it was little Betty Butterworth, the scullery maid. She’s had the toothache all day.”
But something troubled and awkward in her manner made Mistress Mary stare hard at her. She did not believe Martha was telling the truth.

chapters.title: “There Was Someone Crying—There Was!”
paragraphs: Rain hammered down in torrents again the next day. When Mary looked out her window, gray mist and cloud had swallowed nearly all of the moor. Nobody would be going outdoors today.
“What do you all do in your cottage when it rains like this?” she asked Martha.

“Mostly we try not to trip over each other,” Martha answered. “Eh! There do seem a lot of us then. Mother’s a good-tempered woman, but she gets fair worn out and muddled. The biggest ones go out to the cow-shed and play there. Dickon doesn’t mind the wet. He goes out just the same as if the sun was shining. He says he sees things on rainy days that don’t show when it’s fair weather. One time he found a little fox cub half drowned in its hole, and he carried it home inside his shirt to keep it warm. Its mother had been killed close by, and the hole was washed out, and the rest of the litter was dead. He’s got it at home now. Another time he found a half-drowned young crow and brought that home, too, and tamed it. It’s called Soot because it’s so black, and it hops and flies about with him everywhere.”

By now Mary had stopped minding Martha’s friendly way of talking. She had even started to find it interesting, and she was sorry when Martha stopped or went away. The stories her Ayah had told her in India were nothing like Martha’s tales of the moorland cottage, where fourteen people lived in four little rooms and never quite had enough to eat. The children seemed to tumble about and amuse themselves like a litter of rough, good-natured collie puppies. Mary was most drawn to the mother and to Dickon. Whenever Martha told stories about what “mother” said or did, they always sounded comfortable.
“I could play with a raven or a fox cub, if I had one,” said Mary. “But I don’t have anything.”
Martha looked puzzled.
“Can you knit?” she asked.
“No,” answered Mary.
“Can you sew?”
“No.”
“Can you read?”
“Yes.”
“Then why don’t you read something, or learn a bit of spelling? You’re old enough to be learning from your books now.”
“I haven’t any books,” said Mary. “The ones I had were left in India.”
“What a shame,” said Martha. “If Mrs. Medlock would let you into the library, you’d find thousands of books in there.”

Mary did not ask where the library was. A new idea had struck her, and she decided to hunt for the place herself. Mrs. Medlock was no worry, since she seemed to stay in her cozy housekeeper’s sitting-room downstairs. In this odd house you almost never met anyone. Really, there were only the servants to meet, and while the master was away they lived in luxury down below. Their huge kitchen was hung with gleaming brass and pewter, and in their big servants’ hall they ate four or five hearty meals a day. Plenty of noisy, cheerful romping went on there whenever Mrs. Medlock was out of sight.

Mary’s meals were brought to her on time, and Martha waited on her, but no one bothered about her in the least. Mrs. Medlock looked in on her every day or two, but nobody asked what she did or told her what to do. She supposed this was just the English way of treating children. In India her Ayah had always looked after her, following her around and waiting on her hand and foot. Mary had often been tired of having her there. Now nobody followed her. She was learning to dress herself, because Martha looked as if she thought Mary was silly and stupid whenever she wanted things handed to her and put on for her.

“Haven’t you any common sense?” Martha said one day, after Mary had stood waiting for Martha to pull her gloves on for her. “Our Susan Ann is only four years old, and she’s twice as sharp as you. Some days you look fair soft in the head.”
Mary kept her sulky scowl for a whole hour afterward. Still, Martha’s words set her thinking, and she thought several things she had never thought before.

After Martha swept the hearth one last time and went downstairs, Mary stood at the window for some ten minutes this morning. The idea that came to her at the mention of the library was still on her mind. The library itself hardly interested her, since she had read very few books. But the word reminded her of the hundred rooms with their closed doors. Were they all truly locked? What might she find inside if she managed to get into one? Were there really a hundred? She could go and count how many doors she could find. That would give her something to do on a day when she could not go out. Nobody had ever taught her to ask leave before doing things, and she knew nothing whatever about authority. So even if she had met Mrs. Medlock, it would not have crossed her mind to ask whether she might walk around the house.

She opened her door, stepped into the corridor, and began to wander. The corridor was long, and it split into other corridors, and short flights of stairs took her up to yet more of them. Doors lined the way, one after another, and pictures hung on the walls. Some showed dark, curious landscapes, but mostly they were portraits of men and women dressed in strange, splendid costumes of satin and velvet. Soon she was standing in a long gallery with portraits covering every wall. She had never dreamed that a house could hold so many. She walked slowly along it, looking at the faces, and the faces seemed to look back. It felt as though they were asking what a little girl from India was doing in their house. Some portraits were of children. There were little girls in stiff satin frocks that reached their feet and spread out around them, and boys with puffed sleeves, lace collars and long hair, or with large ruffs about their necks. She always paused for the children. She wondered what they had been called, where they had gone, and why they dressed so oddly. One of them was a plain, stiff little girl who looked rather like Mary. She wore a green brocade dress and had a green parrot perched on her finger. Her eyes were sharp and curious.
“Where do you live now?” said Mary aloud to her. “I wish you were here.”

No other little girl can ever have had such a strange morning. The whole huge, rambling house seemed to hold nobody but Mary herself. She roamed up and down, along narrow passages and wide ones, and felt that she was the only person who had ever set foot there. All those rooms had been built, so people must once have lived in them. But everything looked so empty that she could scarcely believe it.

She did not think of turning the handle of a door until she climbed to the second floor. All the doors were shut, just as Mrs. Medlock had said they were. But at last Mary put her hand on the handle of one of them and turned it. For a moment she was almost frightened, because it turned easily, and when she pushed on the door itself, it opened slowly and heavily. It was a massive door, and it opened into a big bedroom. Embroidered hangings covered the wall, and inlaid furniture like the kind she had seen in India stood about the room. A broad window with leaded panes looked out over the moor. Above the mantel was another portrait of the stiff, plain little girl, who seemed to stare at her more curiously than ever.
“Maybe she slept in here once,” said Mary. “The way she stares at me gives me a strange feeling.”

After that she opened door after door. She saw so many rooms that she grew weary, and she began to believe there really were a hundred, though she had not counted. Every one of them held old pictures or old tapestries with odd scenes stitched into them. Almost all had curious furniture and curious ornaments as well.

One room looked like a lady’s sitting-room. Its hangings were all of embroidered velvet, and inside a cabinet stood roughly a hundred small ivory elephants. They came in many sizes. A few carried mahouts or palanquins on their backs. Some were far bigger than the rest, and some were so tiny they looked like babies. Mary had seen carved ivory in India, and elephants were nothing new to her. She opened the cabinet, climbed onto a footstool, and played with them for a good long while. When she grew tired, she lined the elephants up neatly again and closed the cabinet.

All through her wandering in the long corridors and empty rooms she had met nothing alive. In this room, though, she did. As soon as she had shut the cabinet, she heard a tiny rustle. She jumped and turned toward the sofa by the fireplace, where the noise seemed to come from. A cushion lay in the corner of the sofa, and the velvet cover had a hole in it. A small head with a pair of scared eyes was peeping out of the hole.
