Mary tiptoed across the room to see. The bright eyes belonged to a little gray mouse. She had gnawed her way into the cushion and built a cozy nest inside. Six baby mice lay curled up asleep beside her. Maybe nobody else was alive in the hundred rooms, but seven mice there did not look lonely in the least.
“If they weren’t so frightened, I would take them back with me,” said Mary.

She had wandered until she was too tired to go farther, so she started back. Two or three times she took the wrong corridor and had to walk back and forth until she found the right one. At last she came out on her own floor again. Even so, she was a good way from her room, and she was not sure where she was.
“I think I’ve taken the wrong turn again,” she said. She stood still where a short passage seemed to end in a wall hung with tapestry. “Which way do I go? It’s so quiet!”

She was standing there, just after she had said this, when a sound broke the stillness. It was another cry, but not quite like the one she had heard the night before. This one was short, a fretful, childish whine muffled by passing through walls.
“It’s closer than before,” said Mary, and her heart began to beat faster. “And it really _is_ crying.”

Without meaning to, she laid her hand on the tapestry beside her, and then she leaped back, badly startled. The tapestry hung over a door, and the door swung open. Behind it was another stretch of the corridor, and up it came Mrs. Medlock, with her bunch of keys in her hand and a very angry look on her face.
“What are you doing in this part of the house?” she said. She grabbed Mary by the arm and yanked her away. “Didn’t I warn you?”
“I took a wrong turn,” Mary explained. “I couldn’t tell which way to go, and then I heard someone crying.” At that moment she truly hated Mrs. Medlock, and a moment later she hated her still more.
“You heard nothing of the kind,” said the housekeeper. “Get back to your nursery this minute, or I’ll box your ears.”
Then she gripped Mary’s arm and hauled her, half pushing and half pulling, along one passage and down the next, until she shoved her through the door of her own room.

“Now listen,” she said. “You stay where you’re told, or you’ll find yourself locked in. The master had better find you a governess, as he promised he would. You’re the sort of child who needs somebody watching her closely, and I have plenty of other work.”
Mrs. Medlock marched out and slammed the door. Mary went and sat on the hearth-rug, white with rage. She did not cry. She ground her teeth instead.
“There _was_ someone crying—there _was_—there _was!_” she said to herself.

Twice now she had heard it, and one day she would find out what it was. She had learned a great deal this morning. It felt as if she had come back from a long journey. And in any case she had been entertained all through it. She had played with the ivory elephants, and she had met the gray mouse and her babies in their nest in the velvet cushion.

chapters.title: The Key to the Garden
paragraphs: Two days later, Mary opened her eyes in the morning and sat straight up in bed. She called out to Martha at once.
“Look at the moor! Look at the moor!”

The rainstorm was over. During the night the wind had swept away the gray mist and the clouds, and then it had died down too. A bright, deep blue sky now arched high above the moorland. Mary had never imagined a sky so blue. In India the skies were hot and glaring. This one was a deep, cool blue that seemed to sparkle like the water of a lovely lake with no bottom. Here and there, high up in all that blueness, small clouds of snow-white fleece floated by. The wide world of the moor itself looked softly blue, instead of gloomy purple-black or dreary gray.

“Aye,” said Martha with a cheerful grin. “The storm’s gone for a while. It does that around now each year. It slips away in the night, like it never came at all and never plans to come back. That’s because spring is on its way. It’s a good way off yet, but it’s coming.”
“I thought maybe it always rained or was dark in England,” Mary said.
“Eh! No!” said Martha, settling back on her heels among her black lead brushes. “Nowt of the sort!”

“What does that mean?” Mary asked, very serious. Back in India the natives had spoken many dialects that hardly anyone understood. So it did not surprise her that Martha used words she had never heard.
Martha laughed, just as she had on the first morning.

“There now,” she said. “I’ve gone and talked broad Yorkshire again, when Mrs. Medlock said I mustn’t. ‘Nowt of the sort’ means ‘nothing of the sort,’” she said slowly and carefully, “but it takes so long to say. Yorkshire is the sunniest place on earth when it is sunny. I told you you’d like the moor after a bit. Just wait till you see the gold gorse blossoms, and the broom blossoms, and the heather flowering, all purple bells, with hundreds of butterflies fluttering and bees humming and skylarks soaring up and singing. You’ll want to get out on it at sunrise and stay out all day, like Dickon does.”
“Could I ever go there?” Mary asked longingly. She gazed out of her window at the distant blue. It looked so new and huge and wonderful, a truly heavenly color.
“I don’t know,” answered Martha. “It seems to me you’ve never used your legs since the day you were born. You couldn’t walk five miles. And it’s five miles to our cottage.”
“I would like to see your cottage.”

For a moment Martha stared at her with curiosity. Then she took up her polishing brush and went back to rubbing the grate. She noticed that the small, plain face looked less sour right now than it had on that first morning. In fact it looked a bit like little Susan Ann’s face when she badly wanted something.

“I’ll ask Mother about it,” she said. “She’s the sort who nearly always finds a way. Today’s my day out, and I’m off home. Eh! I’m so glad. Mrs. Medlock thinks highly of Mother, so maybe Mother could speak to her.”
“I like your mother,” said Mary.
“I should think you do,” agreed Martha, polishing away.
“I’ve never seen her,” said Mary.
“No, you haven’t,” replied Martha.
She settled back on her heels once more and rubbed the end of her nose with the back of her hand, as though she were puzzled. But when she spoke, she sounded very sure.

“Well, she’s so sensible and hard-working and good-natured and clean that nobody could help liking her, whether they’d seen her or not. When I’m going home to her on my day out, I just jump for joy as I cross the moor.”
“I like Dickon,” added Mary. “And I’ve never seen him, either.”

“Well,” said Martha stoutly, “I’ve told you that even the birds like him, and the rabbits and wild sheep and ponies, and the foxes themselves. I wonder,” she said, staring at Mary thoughtfully, “what Dickon would think of you?”
“He wouldn’t like me,” said Mary in her stiff, cold little way. “Nobody does.”
Martha looked thoughtful again.
“How do you like yourself?” she asked, as if she really wanted to know.
Mary hesitated for a moment and thought it over.
“Not at all—really,” she answered. “But I never thought about it before.”
Martha grinned a little, as if at some homely memory.

“Mother said that to me once,” she said. “She was at her wash-tub, and I was in a bad temper and talking ill of folk. She turned round on me and said, ‘You young vixen, you! There you stand saying you don’t like this one and you don’t like that one. How do you like yourself?’ It made me laugh, and it brought me to my senses in a minute.”

As soon as Mary had eaten her breakfast, Martha hurried off, full of cheer. She had a five-mile walk across the moor to the cottage ahead of her. Once there, she would help her mother with the washing, bake for the week, and have a thoroughly good time.

Once Mary knew Martha was out of the house, she felt lonelier than ever. She got out into the garden as quickly as she could. First she ran around the fountain garden ten times, counting each lap carefully. When she was done, she felt much better. The sunshine made the whole place look different. The same high, deep blue sky stretched over Misselthwaite as over the moor. She kept tipping her face up to it and wondering how it would feel to lie on one of those little snow-white clouds and drift. Then she went into the first kitchen garden, where Ben Weatherstaff was working with two other gardeners. The change in the weather seemed to have done him good, and he spoke to her on his own.
“Springtime’s coming,” he said. “Can’t you smell it?”
Mary sniffed and thought she could.
“I smell something nice and fresh and damp,” she said.

“That’s the good rich earth,” he answered, digging away. “It’s in a good humor, getting ready to grow things. It’s glad when planting time comes. It’s dull in the winter, when it’s got nowt to do. Out in the flower gardens, things will be stirring down below in the dark. The sun’s warming them. You’ll see bits of green spikes sticking out of the black earth before long.”
“What will they be?” asked Mary.
“Crocuses and snowdrops and daffydowndillys. Have you never seen them?”
“No. In India everything is hot and wet and green after the rains,” said Mary. “I think plants shoot up overnight there.”

“These won’t shoot up overnight,” said Weatherstaff. “You’ll have to be patient. They’ll push a little higher here, send out a spike there, and open one leaf today and another tomorrow. Just keep watching.”
“I’m going to,” answered Mary.

Soon she heard the soft whirring of wings once more, and she knew right away that the robin was back. He was cheeky and full of life. He hopped around close to her feet, tilted his head to one side, and gave her such a sly look that she turned and asked Ben Weatherstaff a question.
“Do you think he remembers me?” she said.

“Remember you!” said Weatherstaff, offended. “He knows every cabbage stump in these gardens, never mind the people. He’s never seen a little lass here before, and he’s set on finding out everything about you. There’s no use trying to hide a thing from _him_.”
“Down in the dark, in the garden where he lives, are things starting to stir?” Mary asked.
“What garden?” grunted Weatherstaff, turning surly again.
“The garden with the old rose-trees.” She could not stop herself asking, she wanted so badly to know. “Did all the flowers die, or do some come back in summer? Are there ever roses?”
“Ask him,” said Ben Weatherstaff, nodding his hunched shoulders at the robin. “He’s the only one who can tell you. Nobody else has been inside it for ten years.”
Ten years was a long time, Mary thought. She had been born ten years ago.

Mary walked off slowly, deep in thought. She had started to like the garden, the same way she had started to like the robin, Dickon and Martha’s mother. She was starting to like Martha too. That seemed like a lot of people to like—for someone who was not used to liking anybody. To her, the robin was one of those people. She went to her usual walk beside the long, ivy-covered wall, from which she could see the tree-tops. The second time she paced up and down it, the most interesting and exciting thing happened to her, and it was all thanks to Ben Weatherstaff’s robin.

A chirp and a twitter reached her ears. She looked at the bare flower-bed on her left, and there he was, hopping around and acting as if he were pecking at the soil. He wanted her to think he had not followed her. But she knew he had. The surprise delighted her so much that she nearly shook.
“You remember me!” she cried. “You really do! You’re lovelier than anything in the whole world!”

She chirped and chatted and coaxed. He hopped, flicked his tail, and twittered, as if he were answering. His red waistcoat shone like satin, and he puffed out his small chest. He seemed so fine and grand and handsome that it was truly as if he were showing her how important, and how very like a person, a robin could be. Mistress Mary forgot she had ever been contrary. He let her creep nearer and nearer, bend down, talk to him, and try out some robin sounds of her own.

Oh, to think he would really let her come that close! He understood that nothing on earth would make her reach out a hand or give him the slightest fright. He understood it because he was a real person—just nicer than any other in the world. She was so happy she barely dared breathe.

The flower-bed was not entirely bare. No flowers grew in it, since the perennials had been cut back to rest over the winter. But tall and short shrubs grew together at the back of the bed. While the robin hopped about beneath them, she watched him cross a small heap of freshly dug earth. He paused on top to hunt for a worm. A dog had dug the earth up while trying to get at a mole, and had scratched out quite a deep hole.

Mary looked at the hole without understanding why it was there. Then she noticed something nearly buried in the fresh soil. It resembled a ring of rusty iron or brass. When the robin flew up into a nearby tree, she reached down and picked up the ring. It was more than a ring, though. It was an old key, and it looked as if it had lain buried for a long time.
Mistress Mary stood and gazed at it, her face almost frightened, as it swung from her finger.
“It could have been buried for ten years,” she whispered. “It might be the key to the garden!”

chapters.title: The Robin Who Showed the Way
paragraphs: Mary studied the key for quite a while. She turned it over and over in her hand, thinking. As I mentioned before, nobody had ever taught her to ask permission or to talk things over with grown-ups. All she thought about the key was this: if it belonged to the closed garden, and if she could find the door, she might be able to unlock it. Then she could see what was inside the walls, and what had become of the old rose trees. Because the garden had been shut up so long, she was dying to see it. It had to be different from any other place, she felt, and something strange must have happened there in ten years. Besides, if she liked it, she could slip inside every day and close the door behind her. She could invent a game of her own and play it all alone. Nobody would ever know where she was. They would think the door was still locked and the key buried in the ground. That thought pleased her very much.

Mary lived, so to speak, all by herself in a house with a hundred mysteriously locked rooms, and she had nothing at all to amuse her. This had started her idle mind working and was truly waking up her imagination. The fresh, strong, clean air from the moor surely had a lot to do with it. The moor air had given her an appetite, and wrestling with the wind had stirred her blood. In just the same way, it had stirred her thoughts. In India she had always been too hot, tired and weak to care much about anything. Here she was beginning to care, and to want to try new things. She already felt less “contrary,” though she could not have said why.

She slipped the key into her pocket and walked up and down her path. Nobody but herself ever seemed to come there, so she could stroll slowly and study the wall, or really the ivy that covered it. The ivy was what baffled her. However closely she looked, she saw only thick, glossy, dark green leaves. She was badly disappointed. A little of her old contrariness returned as she paced the path and gazed over the wall at the treetops inside. It seemed so silly, she told herself, to be this close and still not be able to get in. When she went back to the house, the key went with her in her pocket. She decided she would carry it whenever she went out, so that if she ever found the hidden door, she would be ready.
Mrs. Medlock had let Martha sleep at the cottage all night, but in the morning she was back at work, with cheeks redder than ever and in the best of spirits.

“I got up at four o’clock,” she said. “Eh! It was lovely on the moor, with the birds waking up and the rabbits scampering about and the sun coming up. I didn’t walk the whole way. A man gave me a ride in his cart, and I did enjoy myself.”

Martha was full of stories about her wonderful day off. Her mother had been happy to see her, and together they had gotten all the baking and washing done. Martha had even made every one of the children a doughcake with a little brown sugar inside.

“I had them all piping hot when they came in from playing on the moor. The whole cottage smelled of good, clean, hot baking, and there was a nice fire, and they just shouted for joy. Our Dickon said our cottage was good enough for a king to live in.”

That evening the whole family had gathered around the fire. Martha and her mother had stitched patches onto torn clothes and darned stockings, and Martha had told them all about the little girl from India. This girl, she said, had been looked after all her life by what Martha called “blacks,” so that she never even learned to put on her own stockings.
“Eh! They did like hearing about you,” said Martha. “They wanted to know all about the blacks, and about the ship you came on. I couldn’t tell them enough.”
Mary thought for a moment.

“I’ll tell you much more before your next day off,” she said, “so you’ll have more to talk about. I imagine they would love to hear about riding elephants and camels, and about the officers who go out hunting tigers.”
“My word!” cried Martha, delighted. “It would drive them clean out of their minds. Would you really do that, Miss? It would be just like the wild beast show we heard they had in York once.”
“India is nothing like Yorkshire,” Mary said slowly, as she turned the idea over in her mind. “I never realized that. Did Dickon and your mother enjoy hearing you talk about me?”

“Why, our Dickon’s eyes got so round they nearly popped out of his head,” answered Martha. “But Mother was upset that you seemed to be all alone like that. She said, ‘Hasn’t Mr. Craven got a governess for her, or a nurse?’ And I said, ‘No, he hasn’t. Mrs. Medlock says he will once he thinks of it, but she says he might not think of it for two or three years.’”
“I don’t want a governess,” said Mary sharply.

“But Mother says you should be learning your lessons by now, and you should have a woman to take care of you. She says, ‘Martha, just imagine how you’d feel in a big place like that, wandering around alone with no mother. You do your best to cheer her up,’ she says. And I told her I would.”
Mary gave her a long, steady look.
“You do cheer me up,” she said. “I like to hear you talk.”
After a little while Martha left the room and came back holding something under her apron.
“Guess what,” she said, with a cheerful grin. “I’ve brought you a present.”
“A present!” cried Mistress Mary. How in the world could a cottage packed with fourteen hungry people have a present to give anyone?

“A peddler was driving across the moor,” Martha explained. “He stopped his cart at our door. He had pots and pans and odds and ends, but Mother had no money to buy anything. Just as he was leaving, our ’Lizabeth Ellen called out, ‘Mother, he’s got skipping ropes with red and blue handles.’ And Mother called out all of a sudden, ‘Here, stop, mister! How much are they?’ And he says, ‘Tuppence.’ Mother started fumbling in her pocket, and she says to me, ‘Martha, you’ve brought me your wages like a good lass, and I’ve got four places to put every penny, but I’m going to take tuppence out of it to buy that child a skipping rope.’ And she bought one, and here it is.”

Martha pulled it out from under her apron and held it up with great pride. It was a strong, slim rope with a striped red and blue handle on each end. Mary Lennox had never seen a skipping rope in her life, and she gazed at it in bewilderment.
“What is it for?” she asked curiously.

“For!” cried Martha. “Do you mean they don’t have skipping ropes in India, even though they have elephants and tigers and camels! No wonder most of them are black. Here’s what it’s for. Just watch me.”

She ran to the middle of the room and, with a handle in each hand, began to skip, and skip, and skip. Mary turned around in her chair to stare. The strange faces in the old portraits seemed to stare too, wondering what on earth this common little cottage girl had the nerve to be doing right under their noses. But Martha never even saw them. She was delighted by the curiosity and interest in Mistress Mary’s face. She kept on skipping, counting as she went, until she reached a hundred.
“I can skip longer than that,” she said when she stopped. “When I was twelve I once got up to five hundred. But I wasn’t as plump then as I am now, and I was in practice.”
Mary got up from her chair, beginning to feel excited herself.
“It looks like fun,” said Mary. “Your mother must be a kind woman. Do you think I could ever learn to skip like that?”

“Just try it,” Martha urged, handing her the rope. “You won’t manage a hundred at first, but with practice you’ll build up. That’s what Mother said. She says, ‘Nothing will do her more good than a skipping rope. It’s the most sensible toy a child can have. Let her play outdoors in the fresh air, skipping, and it’ll stretch her arms and legs and put some strength into them.’”
Clearly, Mistress Mary’s arms and legs had very little strength in them when she first started to skip. She was not at all clever at it, but she enjoyed it so much that she hated to stop.
“Put your things on and run and skip outdoors,” said Martha. “Mother said I must tell you to stay outside as much as you can, even when it rains a bit, as long as you wrap up warm.”
Mary put on her coat and hat and slung the skipping rope over her arm. She opened the door to go out, but then she remembered something and turned back, rather slowly.

“Martha,” she said, “that was your own pay. It was really your two pennies. Thank you.” She said it stiffly, because she was not used to thanking anyone, or to noticing when people did things for her. “Thank you,” she said again, and she held out her hand, since she could not think what else to do.
Martha gave her hand an awkward little shake, as though she was not used to this sort of thing either. Then she burst out laughing.
“Eh! You’re a queer one, like a little old woman,” she said. “If you were our ’Lizabeth Ellen, you’d have given me a kiss.”
Mary looked stiffer than ever.
“Do you want me to kiss you?”
Martha laughed again.
“Nay, not me,” she answered. “If you were different, maybe you’d want to yourself. But you’re not. Run off outside and play with your rope.”

Mistress Mary felt a little awkward as she walked out of the room. Yorkshire people seemed strange to her, and Martha had always been something of a puzzle. At first she had disliked Martha very much, but not anymore. The skipping rope was a marvelous thing. She counted and skipped, and skipped and counted, until her cheeks glowed red and she was more interested in something than she had ever been in her life. The sun was out and a light wind was blowing. It was not a rough wind, but one that came in lovely little gusts, carrying the fresh smell of newly turned earth. She skipped around the fountain garden and up one path and down another. At last she skipped into the kitchen garden, where Ben Weatherstaff was digging and talking to his robin, who hopped about beside him. She skipped down the path toward him. He raised his head and gave her a curious look. She had wondered whether he would notice her. She wanted him to see her skip.

“Well!” he exclaimed. “Upon my word. Maybe you are a young ’un after all, and maybe you’ve got a child’s blood in your veins instead of sour buttermilk. You’ve skipped some red into those cheeks, as sure as my name’s Ben Weatherstaff. I wouldn’t have believed you had it in you.”
“I’d never skipped before,” said Mary. “I’m only just starting. I can only get to twenty.”

“Keep at it,” said Ben. “You’re not bad at it, for a young ’un who’s lived among heathens. Look how he’s watching you,” he said, jerking his head toward the robin. “He followed you yesterday, and he’ll be after you again today. He’s bound to find out what a skipping rope is, for he’s never seen one. Eh!” he said, shaking his head at the bird, “that curiosity of yours will be the death of you one day if you don’t watch out.”

Mary skipped around every garden and around the orchard, stopping to rest every few minutes. At last she went to her own special path and decided to see if she could skip all the way along it. It was a long stretch, and she started slowly. But before she was halfway down, she was so hot and breathless that she had to stop. She didn’t mind much, because she had counted all the way to thirty. She stopped with a happy little laugh, and there, lo and behold, was the robin, swaying on a long branch of ivy. He had followed her, and he greeted her with a chirp. As Mary skipped toward him, something heavy in her pocket had bumped against her with every jump. Now, seeing the robin, she laughed again.
“Yesterday you showed me where the key was,” she said. “Today you should show me the door. But I bet you don’t know where it is!”

The robin flew off his swaying spray of ivy and landed on top of the wall. He opened his beak and poured out a loud, lovely trill, purely to show off. Nothing in the world is as charming as a robin showing off, and they do it nearly all the time.
Back in India, Mary Lennox had heard plenty about Magic in her Ayah’s tales. She always insisted that what happened next, almost that very moment, was Magic.

One of those pleasant little gusts of wind came sweeping down the path, stronger than any before it. It was strong enough to set the tree branches waving, and far more than strong enough to sway the trailing sprays of untrimmed ivy that hung from the wall. Mary had stepped up close to the robin. All at once the gust tossed aside some loose strands of ivy, and in an instant she leaped forward and grabbed them. She had spotted something behind them: a round knob, hidden until now by the leaves that hung over it. It was the knob of a door.

She slid her hands under the leaves and began to pull and push them out of the way. The ivy hung thickly, but nearly all of it was a loose, swinging curtain, though a little had crept across the wood and iron. Mary’s heart started to pound, and her hands trembled a bit with joy and excitement. The robin went on singing and twittering, with his head cocked to one side, as though he were just as excited as she was. What was this beneath her hands, square and made of iron, with a hole her fingers could feel?

It was the lock of the door that had stood closed for ten years. She reached into her pocket, took out the key, and found that it fit the keyhole. She slid the key in and turned it. It took both hands, but it turned.

Then she drew a deep breath and glanced back along the path to make sure nobody was coming. Nobody was. Nobody ever came there, it seemed. She drew another deep breath, since she could not help it. Then she held back the swinging curtain of ivy and pushed the door open, slowly, slowly.
She slipped through the opening, closed the door behind her, and stood with her back against it. She looked all around, breathing fast with excitement and wonder and delight.
She was standing _inside_ the secret garden.

chapters.title: The Strangest House Anyone Ever Lived In
paragraphs: Nobody could have imagined a sweeter or more mysterious place. The high walls around it were covered with the bare stems of climbing roses, so thick that they were matted together. Mary Lennox knew they were roses because she had seen so many of them in India. The ground was all wintry brown grass, and clumps of bushes grew out of it that were surely rosebushes, if they were alive. There were plenty of standard roses whose branches had spread so wide that they looked like little trees. There were other trees in the garden too. One of the things that made the place look so strange and lovely was that climbing roses had run all over them and let long tendrils hang down, making light, swaying curtains. Here and there the tendrils had caught hold of one another, or of a far-reaching branch, and crept from one tree to the next, making lovely bridges. There were no leaves or roses on them now, and Mary did not know whether they were dead or alive. But their thin gray or brown branches and sprays looked like a hazy cloak spread over everything: the walls, the trees, and even the brown grass. In places the tendrils had fallen from their supports and run along the ground. This hazy tangle from tree to tree was what made it all look so mysterious. Mary thought it must be different from other gardens, because it had been left all alone for so long. And it truly was different from any other place she had ever seen in her life.
“How still it is!” she whispered. “How still!”

Then she waited a moment and listened to the stillness. The robin had flown up to his treetop, and he was as still as everything else. He did not even flutter his wings. He sat without moving and looked at Mary.
“No wonder it’s still,” she whispered again. “I’m the first person to speak in here for ten years.”

Stepping as softly as if she were afraid to wake someone, she moved away from the door. She was glad of the grass under her feet, because it kept her footsteps silent. She passed beneath one of the fairy-like gray arches between the trees and gazed up at the sprays and tendrils that made it.
“I wonder if they’re all completely dead,” she said. “Is it a completely dead garden? I wish it weren’t.”

If she had been Ben Weatherstaff, she could have told by looking at the wood whether it was alive. But all she could see was gray and brown sprays and branches, and not one of them showed even a tiny leaf-bud anywhere.
Still, she was _inside_ the wonderful garden. Any time she liked, she could come back through the door under the ivy, and it felt as though she had found a whole world of her own.

The sun was shining inside the four walls. The high arch of blue sky over this one corner of Misselthwaite seemed even brighter and softer than it did over the moor. The robin flew down from his treetop and hopped about, or flew after her from one bush to the next. He chirped a great deal and looked very busy, as if he were showing her things. Everything was strange and silent, and she seemed to be hundreds of miles from anyone. Somehow she did not feel lonely at all. The only thing that troubled her was wanting to know whether all the roses were dead. Perhaps some had lived, and would put out leaves and buds as the weather got warmer. She did not want it to be a completely dead garden. If it were truly alive, how wonderful it would be, and what thousands of roses would grow on every side!

Her skipping rope had been hanging over her arm when she came in. After she had walked about for a while, she decided to skip all the way around the garden, stopping whenever she wanted to look at something. There seemed to have been grass paths here and there. In one or two corners there were alcoves of evergreen with stone seats, or tall flower urns covered in moss.

Near the second of these alcoves she stopped skipping. A flowerbed had once been planted there, and she thought she could see something poking up out of the black soil—sharp little points, pale green in color. Ben Weatherstaff’s words came back to her, and she dropped to her knees to examine them.
“Yes, they’re tiny growing things. They _could_ be crocuses, or snowdrops, or daffodils,” she whispered.
Leaning in close, she breathed in the fresh smell of the damp soil. It pleased her very much.
“Maybe there are others coming up in other places,” she said. “I’ll go all over the garden and look.”

She did not skip. She walked. She went slowly and kept her eyes on the ground. She looked in the old flower beds and among the grass. After she had gone all the way around, trying not to miss anything, she had found ever so many more sharp, pale green points. She had become quite excited again.
“It’s not a completely dead garden!” she cried softly to herself. “Even if the roses are dead, other things are alive.”

She did not know anything about gardening. But in some of the places where the green points were pushing through, the grass was so thick that they didn’t seem to have room to grow. She searched around until she found a fairly sharp piece of wood. Then she knelt down and dug, and pulled out the weeds and grass until she had made nice little clear spaces around them.

“Now they look as if they can breathe,” she said when she had finished the first ones. “I’m going to do ever so many more. I’ll do every one I can see. If I don’t have time today, I can come back tomorrow.”

She went from place to place, digging and weeding. She enjoyed herself so much that she was led on from bed to bed and into the grass under the trees. The work made her so warm that she took off her coat first, and then her hat. All the while, without knowing it, she was smiling down at the grass and the pale green points.

The robin was tremendously busy. He was very pleased to see gardening begun on his own land. He had often wondered about Ben Weatherstaff. Where there is gardening, all sorts of delicious things to eat get turned up with the soil. Now here was a new kind of creature, not half Ben’s size, who had been clever enough to come into his garden and start right away.

Mistress Mary kept working in her garden until it was time for her midday dinner. She was actually a little late remembering it. As she put on her coat and hat and picked up her skipping rope, she could hardly believe two or three hours had gone by. All that time she had been truly happy. Dozens and dozens of tiny pale green points now showed in the cleared spots, and they looked twice as cheerful as they had when grass and weeds were smothering them.
“I’ll come back this afternoon,” she said, looking all around at her new kingdom and speaking to the trees and rosebushes as if they could hear her.

Then she ran lightly across the grass, pushed open the slow old door, and slipped through it under the ivy. Her cheeks were so red, her eyes so bright, and she ate such a dinner that Martha was delighted.
“Two pieces o’ meat and two helpings o’ rice pudding!” she said. “Eh! Mother will be pleased when I tell her what the skipping rope’s done for you.”

While she was digging with her pointed stick, Mistress Mary had come across a sort of white root, rather like an onion. She had put it back in its place and patted the earth carefully down over it. Now she wondered if Martha could tell her what it was.
“Martha,” she said, “what are those white roots that look like onions?”

“They’re bulbs,” answered Martha. “Lots o’ spring flowers grow from ’em. The very little ones are snowdrops and crocuses, and the big ones are narcissuses and jonquils and daffydowndillys. The biggest of all are lilies and purple flags. Eh! They’re lovely. Dickon’s got a whole lot of ’em planted in our bit o’ garden.”
“Does Dickon know all about them?” Mary asked, struck by a new idea.
“Our Dickon could make a flower sprout from a brick path. Mother says he simply whispers things up out o’ the ground.”
“Do bulbs last a long time? If nobody looked after them, would they live for years and years?” Mary asked anxiously.

“They look after themselves,” said Martha. “That’s why poor folk can afford ’em. Leave ’em alone, and most of ’em’ll work away underground their whole lives, spreading out and having little ’uns. There’s a spot in the park woods here with snowdrops by the thousands. When spring comes, it’s the prettiest sight in Yorkshire. Nobody knows when they were first planted.”
“I wish it were spring right now,” said Mary. “I want to see everything that grows in England.”
She had finished her dinner and gone to her favorite seat on the hearth rug.
“I wish—I wish I had a little spade,” she said.
“Whatever do you want a spade for?” asked Martha, laughing. “Are you going to take up digging? I’ll have to tell Mother that, too.”

Mary watched the fire and thought it over. If she meant to keep her secret kingdom, she had to be careful. She wasn’t doing any harm. But if Mr. Craven discovered the open door, he would be terribly angry. He would get a new key and lock the garden up for good, and she simply could not bear that.

“It’s such a big, lonely place,” she said slowly, as though she were working things out as she spoke. “The house is lonely, and so are the park and the gardens. So many places are shut up. I never did much in India, but there was more to look at—natives, and soldiers marching past, and sometimes a band playing—and my Ayah told me stories. Here there’s nobody to talk to except you and Ben Weatherstaff. You have your work to do, and Ben Weatherstaff hardly ever speaks to me. I was thinking that with a little spade I could dig somewhere, the way he does. Maybe I could make a little garden, if he’d give me some seeds.”
Martha’s face lit up.

“There now!” she exclaimed. “If that isn’t one o’ the things Mother said! She says, ‘There’s such a lot o’ room in that big place. Why don’t they give her a bit for herself, even if she plants nothing but parsley and radishes? She’d dig and rake and be right down happy over it.’ Those were the very words she said.”
“Did she?” said Mary. “She knows so many things, doesn’t she?”
“Eh!” said Martha. “It’s like she says: ‘A woman who brings up twelve children learns something besides her A B C. Children are as good as arithmetic for setting you finding things out.’”
“How much would a spade cost—a little one?” Mary asked.

“Well,” Martha answered thoughtfully, “there’s a shop or two in Thwaite village, and I saw little garden sets there. A spade, a rake and a fork, all tied together, for two shillings. And they looked sturdy enough for real work.”
“I have more than that in my purse,” said Mary. “Mrs. Morrison gave me five shillings, and Mrs. Medlock passed on some money from Mr. Craven.”
“Did he remember you that much?” exclaimed Martha.
“Mrs. Medlock told me I could have a shilling a week for spending. She hands me one every Saturday. Until now I couldn’t think what to spend it on.”

“My word! That’s riches,” said Martha. “You can buy anything in the world you want. The rent on our cottage is only one and threepence, and it’s like pulling teeth to get it. Now I’ve just thought of something,” she said, putting her hands on her hips.
“What?” said Mary eagerly.

“The shop at Thwaite sells packets o’ flower seeds, a penny each, and our Dickon knows which ones are prettiest and how to get ’em growing. Many a day he walks over to Thwaite just for the fun of it. Can you print letters?” she asked suddenly.
“I know how to write,” Mary answered.
Martha shook her head.
“Our Dickon can only read printing. If you could print, we could write him a letter and ask him to go and buy the garden tools and the seeds at the same time.”
“Oh, you’re a good one!” Mary cried. “You really are! I never knew you were so kind. I’m sure I can print if I try hard. Let’s ask Mrs. Medlock if we can borrow pen, ink and paper.”
“I’ve some o’ my own,” said Martha. “I bought it so I could print a little letter to Mother on Sundays. I’ll run and fetch it.”
Martha hurried out of the room. Mary stood by the fire, twisting her thin little hands together in pure delight.
“With a spade,” she whispered, “I could make the ground soft and nice and dig out the weeds. And if I have seeds and can get flowers growing, the garden won’t be dead at all—it will come to life.”

She did not go out again that afternoon. When Martha came back with her pen and ink and paper, she had to clear the table and carry the plates and dishes downstairs. When she got to the kitchen, Mrs. Medlock was there and told her to do something. So Mary waited what seemed to her a very long time before Martha returned. Then writing to Dickon turned out to be a serious piece of work. Mary had been taught very little, because her governesses had disliked her too much to stay with her. She couldn’t spell especially well, but she found that she could print letters when she tried. This was the letter Martha dictated to her:
“_My Dear Dickon:_

I hope this letter finds you well, as it leaves me at present. Miss Mary has plenty of money. Would you go to Thwaite and buy her some flower seeds, and a set of garden tools for making a flower bed? Choose the prettiest seeds, and ones that are easy to grow, since she has never done this before and comes from India, which is a different sort of place. Give my love to Mother and all of you. Miss Mary is going to tell me a lot more, so on my next day out you can hear about elephants and camels, and gentlemen who go hunting lions and tigers.
“Your loving sister,
“Martha Phœbe Sowerby.”
“We’ll slip the money into the envelope, and I’ll have the butcher boy carry it in his cart. He’s a great friend o’ Dickon’s,” Martha said.
“How will I get the things when Dickon buys them?”
“He’ll bring ’em to you himself. He’ll like to walk over this way.”
“Oh!” exclaimed Mary. “Then I’ll see him! I never thought I would see Dickon.”
“Do you want to see him?” asked Martha suddenly, because Mary looked so pleased.
“Yes, I do. I’ve never met a boy that foxes and crows love. I want very much to meet him.”
Martha gave a little start, as if she had remembered something.
“Now, to think,” she broke out, “to think o’ me forgetting that! And I thought I was going to tell you first thing this morning. I asked Mother—and she said she’d ask Mrs. Medlock her own self.”
“Do you mean—” Mary began.
“What I told you on Tuesday. Ask if you could be driven over to our cottage one day, to have a bit o’ Mother’s hot oat cake with butter, and a glass o’ milk.”
All the interesting things seemed to be happening in a single day. Imagine going across the moor in broad daylight, with a blue sky overhead! Imagine stepping into a cottage full of twelve children!
“Does she think Mrs. Medlock would let me go?” she asked, quite anxiously.
“Aye, she reckons so. She knows Mother’s a tidy woman, and how spotless she keeps our cottage.”
“If I went, I’d meet your mother as well as Dickon,” said Mary. She turned the idea over and liked it very much. “She doesn’t sound like the mothers in India.”

Mary’s work in the garden and the excitement of the afternoon left her feeling calm and thoughtful. Martha stayed until teatime, and the two of them sat in easy quiet, hardly talking at all. But just as Martha was about to go downstairs for the tea tray, Mary asked her a question.
“Martha,” she said, “has the scullery maid had the toothache again today?”
Martha certainly started a little.
“What makes you ask that?” she said.

“I waited a long time for you to come back, so I opened the door and walked down the corridor to see if you were coming. And I heard that faraway crying again, just like the other night. There isn’t any wind today, so you can see it couldn’t have been the wind.”
“Eh!” said Martha, fidgeting. “You mustn’t go walking about in corridors and listening. Mr. Craven would be so angry there’s no telling what he’d do.”
“I wasn’t listening,” said Mary. “I was only waiting for you, and I heard it. That’s three times now.”
“My word! That’s Mrs. Medlock’s bell,” said Martha, and she nearly ran out of the room.

“It’s the strangest house anyone ever lived in,” said Mary sleepily, as she let her head sink onto the cushioned seat of the armchair beside her. The fresh air, the digging and the skipping-rope had made her so pleasantly tired that she fell asleep.

chapters.title: Dickon
paragraphs: For nearly a week the sun shone down on the secret garden. The Secret Garden was what Mary called it whenever she thought about it. She liked the name. She liked even more the feeling that, once its beautiful old walls closed around her, no one in the world knew where she was. It felt almost like being shut out of the world and tucked away in some fairy place. The few books she had read and enjoyed had been fairy tales, and in some of them she had come across secret gardens. Sometimes people fell asleep in them for a hundred years, which she had thought rather silly. She had no plans to fall asleep. In fact, she was growing more wide awake with every day that passed at Misselthwaite. She was beginning to like being outdoors. She no longer hated the wind but enjoyed it. She could run faster and farther, and she could skip up to a hundred. The bulbs in the secret garden must have been very surprised. Such nice clear spaces had been made around them that they had all the room to breathe they wanted. Really, if Mistress Mary had known it, they were starting to cheer up beneath the dark earth and to work hard. The sun could reach them and warm them, and when rain fell it soaked straight down to them, so they began to feel very much alive.

Mary was an odd, determined little person, and now that she had something interesting to be determined about, she was completely absorbed. She worked and dug and pulled up weeds steadily, and instead of growing tired of it, she grew more pleased with her work every hour. To her it felt like a fascinating kind of game. She found many more of the pale green sprouting points than she had ever hoped for. They seemed to be pushing up everywhere, and every day she felt sure she found new ones, some so tiny they barely peeped above the soil. There were so many that she remembered what Martha had said about “snowdrops by the thousands,” and about bulbs spreading and making new bulbs. These had been left alone for ten years, and perhaps they had spread, like the snowdrops, into thousands. She wondered how long it would be before they showed that they were flowers. Sometimes she stopped digging to look around the garden and try to picture how it would look covered with thousands of lovely blooms.

During that week of sunshine, she grew friendlier with Ben Weatherstaff. Several times she startled him by turning up beside him as though she had sprung out of the ground. The truth was that she was afraid he would pick up his tools and leave if he saw her coming, so she always walked toward him as quietly as she could. But in fact he did not mind her as much as he had at first. Perhaps he was secretly a little flattered that she so plainly wanted the company of an old man like him. Also, she was more polite than she had been. He did not know that when she first met him she had spoken to him the way she would have spoken to a native servant. She had not understood that a sturdy, cross old Yorkshireman was not used to bowing to his betters and simply being ordered about by them.
“You’re like the robin,” he said to her one morning, when he lifted his head and saw her standing next to him. “I never know when I’ll see you or which side you’ll come from.”
“He’s my friend now,” Mary said.

“That’s just like him,” Ben Weatherstaff snapped. “Sweet-talking the womenfolk out of vanity and silliness. There’s nothing he won’t do to show off and flirt with his tail feathers. He’s as full of pride as an egg is full of meat.”

Ben rarely said much. Often he answered Mary’s questions with nothing but a grunt. This morning, though, he was more talkative than usual. He straightened up, set one hobnailed boot on the blade of his spade and looked her up and down.
“How long have you been here?” he jerked out.
“About a month, I think,” she answered.

“You’re starting to do Misselthwaite some credit,” he said. “You’re a bit fatter than you were, and you’re not so yellow. You looked like a plucked young crow when you first came into this garden. I thought to myself, I never laid eyes on an uglier, sourer-faced youngster.”
Mary was not vain, and since she had never thought much about her looks, she was not very bothered.
“I know I’m fatter,” she said. “My stockings are getting tighter. They used to wrinkle. Look, there’s the robin, Ben Weatherstaff.”

There he was, sure enough, and she thought he looked handsomer than ever. His red waistcoat was as glossy as satin. He fluttered his wings and tail, tilted his head and hopped about with all sorts of lively charm. He seemed determined to make Ben Weatherstaff admire him. But Ben was sarcastic.

“Aye, there you are!” he said. “You’ll put up with me for a bit sometimes, when you’ve got no one better. You’ve been brightening up your waistcoat and polishing your feathers these two weeks. I know what you’re up to. You’re courting some bold young madam somewhere, telling her lies about being the finest cock robin on Missel Moor and ready to fight all the rest.”
“Oh! Look at him!” Mary exclaimed.

The robin was plainly in a charming, bold mood. He hopped closer and closer and looked at Ben Weatherstaff more and more winningly. He flew onto the nearest currant bush, tilted his head and sang a little song straight at him.

“You think you’ll win me over by doing that,” said Ben, wrinkling up his face in a way that made Mary sure he was trying not to look pleased. “You think no one can hold out against you. That’s what you think.”

The robin spread his wings, and Mary could hardly believe her eyes. He flew right up to the handle of Ben Weatherstaff’s spade and landed on top of it. Then the old man’s face slowly creased into a new expression. He stood perfectly still, as if he were afraid to breathe, as if he would not have moved for anything in the world in case his robin flew away. He spoke in a whisper.
“Well, I’ll be danged!” he said, as softly as if he were saying something quite different. “You do know how to get around a fellow, you do! You’re downright uncanny, you’re so clever.”

And he stood without moving, hardly even breathing, until the robin gave his wings another flick and flew away. Then he stood looking at the spade handle as if there might be magic in it. After that he began to dig again and said nothing for several minutes.
But he kept breaking into a slow grin every now and then, so Mary was not afraid to talk to him.
“Do you have a garden of your own?” she asked.
“No. I’m a bachelor, and I lodge with Martin at the gate.”
“If you had one,” said Mary, “what would you plant?”
“Cabbages and potatoes and onions.”
“But if you wanted to make a flower garden,” Mary pressed on, “what would you plant?”
“Bulbs and sweet-smelling things, but mostly roses.”
Mary’s face lit up.
“Do you like roses?” she asked.
Ben Weatherstaff pulled up a weed and tossed it aside before he answered.

“Well, yes, I do. I was taught that by a young lady I worked for as gardener. She had a lot of them in a place she was fond of, and she loved them as if they were children, or robins. I’ve seen her bend over and kiss them.” He dragged out another weed and scowled at it. “That was ten years ago, easily.”
“Where is she now?” asked Mary, very interested.
“Heaven,” he answered, and drove his spade deep into the soil, “according to what the parson says.”
“What happened to the roses?” Mary asked again, more interested than ever.
“They were left to themselves.”
Mary was getting quite excited.
“Did they die completely? Do roses die completely when they’re left to themselves?” she ventured.

“Well, I’d grown fond of them, and I was fond of her, and she was fond of them,” Ben Weatherstaff admitted reluctantly. “Once or twice a year I’d go and work on them a bit, pruning them and digging around the roots. They ran wild, but they were in rich soil, so some of them lived.”
“When they have no leaves and look gray and brown and dry, how can you tell if they’re dead or alive?” Mary asked.
“Wait till spring gets to them. Wait till the sun shines on the rain and the rain falls on the sunshine, and then you’ll find out.”
“How? How?” cried Mary, forgetting to be careful.

“Look along the twigs and branches, and if you see a bit of a brown lump swelling here and there, watch it after a warm rain and see what happens.” He stopped suddenly and looked curiously at her eager face. “Why do you care so much about roses and such, all of a sudden?” he demanded.
Mistress Mary felt her face turn red. She was almost afraid to answer.
“I—I want to pretend that—that I have a garden of my own,” she stammered. “I—there’s nothing for me to do. I have nothing—and no one.”
“Well,” said Ben Weatherstaff slowly, watching her, “that’s true. You don’t.”

The odd way he said it made Mary wonder whether he actually felt a little sorry for her. She had never pitied herself. She had only ever felt tired and cross, since she disliked so many people and things. Now, though, the world seemed to be changing for the better. As long as nobody discovered the secret garden, she would always be able to enjoy herself.

She stayed with him another ten or fifteen minutes and asked as many questions as she dared. He answered every one of them in his strange grunting way. He did not seem truly cross, and he did not pick up his spade and leave her. Just as she was going away, he said something about roses, and it reminded her of the ones he had said he was fond of.
“Do you go and see those other roses now?” she asked.
“Haven’t been this year. My rheumatism has made my joints too stiff.”
He said it in his grumbling voice, and then quite suddenly he seemed to get angry with her, though she could not see why he should.
“Now look here!” he said sharply. “Don’t ask so many questions. You’re the worst girl for asking questions I’ve ever come across. Off with you and go play. I’m done talking for today.”

And he said it so crossly that she knew there was no use staying another minute. She went skipping slowly down the outside path, thinking him over. Odd as it was, she told herself, here was another person she liked in spite of his crossness. She liked old Ben Weatherstaff. Yes, she really did. She always wanted to try to get him talking to her. She was also starting to believe that he knew everything in the world about flowers.

A laurel-hedged path curved around the secret garden and ended at a gate that opened into a wood in the park. She decided to slip along this path and look into the wood to see if any rabbits were hopping about. She enjoyed the skipping very much. When she reached the little gate she opened it and went through, because she had heard a low, strange whistling sound and wanted to find out what it was.

It was a very strange sight indeed. She caught her breath and stopped to look. A boy was sitting under a tree with his back against it, playing on a rough wooden pipe. He was a funny-looking boy of about twelve. He looked very clean, his nose turned up, and his cheeks were as red as poppies. Mistress Mary had never seen such round, blue eyes in any boy’s face. On the trunk of the tree he leaned against clung a brown squirrel, watching him. From behind a bush nearby a cock pheasant was delicately stretching out his neck to peek. Quite close to him two rabbits sat up, sniffing with trembling noses. It actually looked as if they were all creeping closer to watch him and listen to the strange, low little call of his pipe.
When he saw Mary he held up his hand and spoke to her in a voice almost as low as his piping, and rather like it.
“Don’t move,” he said. “You’ll scare them off.”

Mary stayed perfectly still. He stopped playing his pipe and began to rise from the ground. He moved so slowly that it hardly seemed as if he were moving at all, but at last he stood on his feet. Then the squirrel scampered back up into the branches of his tree, the pheasant pulled in his head, and the rabbits dropped down on all fours and began to hop away, though not at all as if they were frightened.
“I’m Dickon,” the boy said. “I know you’re Miss Mary.”

Then Mary realized that somehow she had known from the start that he was Dickon. Who else could be charming rabbits and pheasants the way the natives charm snakes in India? He had a wide, red, curving mouth, and his smile spread all over his face.
“I got up slow,” he explained, “because if you make a quick move, it startles them. You’ve got to move gently and speak low when wild things are about.”
He talked to her not like a stranger but as though he had known her for a long time. Mary knew nothing about boys, and she felt rather shy, so her own words came out a bit stiffly.
“Did you get Martha’s letter?” she asked.
He nodded his curly, rust-colored head.
“That’s why I came.”
He stooped to pick up something that had been lying on the ground beside him while he piped.

“I’ve brought the garden tools. There’s a little spade and a rake and a fork and a hoe. Eh! They’re good ones. There’s a trowel, too. And the woman in the shop threw in a packet of white poppy and one of blue larkspur when I bought the other seeds.”
“Will you show me the seeds?” Mary said.

She wished she could talk the way he did. His speech was so quick and easy. It sounded as if he liked her and was not the least bit afraid she wouldn’t like him, though he was only a common moor boy in patched clothes, with a funny face and a rough, rusty-red head of hair. As she came closer to him she noticed a clean, fresh scent of heather and grass and leaves about him, almost as if he were made of them. She liked it very much, and when she looked into his funny face with its red cheeks and round blue eyes, she forgot that she had felt shy.
“Let’s sit down on this log and look at them,” she said.

They sat down, and he took a clumsy little brown paper package out of his coat pocket. He untied the string, and inside were ever so many smaller, neater packets, each with a picture of a flower on it.

“There’s plenty of mignonette and poppies,” he said. “Mignonette’s the sweetest-smelling thing that grows, and it’ll grow wherever you scatter it, same as poppies will. The ones that’ll come up and bloom if you just whistle to them, those are the nicest of all.”
He stopped and quickly turned his head, his poppy-cheeked face lighting up.
“Where’s that robin that’s calling us?” he said.
The chirp came from a thick holly bush bright with scarlet berries, and Mary thought she knew whose it was.
“Is he really calling us?” she asked.

“Aye,” said Dickon, as though nothing could be more natural, “he’s calling to somebody he’s friends with. It’s like him saying, ‘Here I am. Look at me. I’d like a bit of a chat.’ There he is, in the bush. Whose robin is he?”
“He’s Ben Weatherstaff’s, but I think he knows me a little,” Mary answered.
“Aye, he knows you,” said Dickon, in his low voice again. “And he likes you. He’s taken to you. He’ll tell me all about you in a minute.”

He moved quite close to the bush, with the same slow movement Mary had noticed before. Then he made a sound almost like the robin’s own twitter. The robin listened intently for a few seconds and then answered, just as if he were replying to a question.
“Aye, he’s a friend of yours,” Dickon chuckled.
“Do you think so?” Mary cried eagerly. She wanted so much to know. “Do you think he really likes me?”

“He wouldn’t come near you if he didn’t,” Dickon answered. “Birds are very choosy, and a robin can snub a body worse than a man can. See, he’s making up to you now. ‘Can’t you see me, friend?’ he’s saying.”
And it really seemed as if it must be true. He sidled and twittered and tilted so much as he hopped about on his bush.
“Do you understand everything birds say?” Mary asked.
Dickon’s grin spread wider and wider until his face seemed to be nothing but a broad, red, curving mouth. He rubbed his rough head.

“I think I do, and they think I do,” he said. “I’ve lived on the moor with them so long. I’ve watched them break out of the shell and fledge and learn to fly and start to sing, till I feel like one of them. Sometimes I think maybe I’m a bird, or a fox, or a rabbit, or a squirrel, or even a beetle, and I just don’t know it.”

He laughed, went back to the log, and began talking about the flower seeds again. He told her what they would look like when they were in bloom. He told her how to plant them, how to watch over them, and how to feed and water them.
“Look here,” he said suddenly, turning to face her. “I’ll plant them for you myself. Where is your garden?”

Mary’s thin hands gripped each other in her lap. She did not know what to say, so for a whole minute she said nothing. She had never thought of this. She felt miserable. She could feel herself going red and then pale.
“You’ve got a bit of garden, haven’t you?” Dickon said.
It was true that she had turned red and then pale. Dickon saw it happen, and since she still said nothing, he began to be puzzled.
“Wouldn’t they give you a bit?” he asked. “Haven’t you got any yet?”
She gripped her hands even tighter and turned her eyes up to him.

“I know nothing about boys,” she said slowly. “If I told you a secret, could you keep it? It’s a huge secret. If anyone found out, I can’t think what I’d do. I truly believe I’d die!” She said that last bit quite fiercely.
Dickon looked more puzzled than ever and even rubbed his rough head again, but he answered in a good-natured way.

“I’m keeping secrets all the time,” he said. “If I couldn’t keep secrets from the other lads, secrets about fox cubs and birds’ nests and the holes of wild things, nothing on the moor would be safe. Aye, I can keep secrets.”
Mistress Mary had not meant to reach out and clutch his sleeve, but she did.

“I’ve stolen a garden,” she said, very fast. “It doesn’t belong to me. It doesn’t belong to anybody. No one wants it, no one looks after it, and no one ever goes inside. Maybe everything in there is dead already. I can’t tell.”
She began to feel hot, and as contrary as she had ever felt in her life.

“I don’t care, I don’t care! No one has the right to take it away from me, when I care about it and they don’t. They’re just letting it die, shut away all alone,” she finished passionately. Then she flung her arms over her face and burst into tears—poor little Mistress Mary.
Dickon’s curious blue eyes grew rounder and rounder.
“Eh-h-h!” he said, drawing the word out slowly, and the way he said it meant both wonder and sympathy.
“There’s nothing else for me to do,” said Mary. “Nothing is mine. I found the garden myself, and I got in by myself. I was just like the robin, and no one would take the garden from the robin.”
“Where is it?” asked Dickon in a hushed voice.
Mistress Mary stood up from the log at once. She knew she was feeling contrary again, and stubborn, and she did not care at all. She was bossy and Indian, and at the same time hot and sorrowful.
“Come with me and I’ll show you,” she said.

She led him around the laurel path to the walk where the ivy grew so thickly. Dickon followed her with a strange, almost pitying look on his face. He felt as if he were being led to see some rare bird’s nest and must move softly. When she stepped up to the wall and lifted the hanging ivy, he gave a start. There was a door. Mary pushed it slowly open and they went in together. Then Mary stood and swept her hand around defiantly.
“This is it,” she said. “It’s a secret garden, and I’m the only one in the world who wants it to be alive.”
Dickon looked all around it, and then around again.
“Eh!” he almost whispered, “it is a strange, pretty place! It’s as if a body were in a dream.”

chapters.title: The Nest of the Missel Thrush
paragraphs: Dickon stood for two or three minutes, looking all around him while Mary watched. Then he began to walk about quietly, even more lightly than Mary had the first time she found herself inside the four walls. His eyes seemed to be drinking in everything: the gray trees with gray creepers climbing over them and hanging from their branches, the tangle along the walls and through the grass, and the evergreen alcoves with their stone seats and tall flower urns.
“I never thought I’d see this place,” he said at last, in a whisper.
“Did you know about it?” Mary asked.
She had spoken out loud, and he signaled to her to be quiet.
“We have to talk low,” he said, “or someone will hear us and wonder what’s going on in here.”
“Oh! I forgot!” said Mary. She was frightened, and she pressed her hand quickly over her mouth. When she had calmed down, she asked again, “Did you know about the garden?”
Dickon nodded.
“Martha told me there was a garden no one ever went into,” he answered. “We used to wonder what it was like.”
He stopped and looked around at the lovely gray tangle, and his round eyes had a strange, happy look.

“Eh! Just think of the nests there’ll be here come springtime,” he said. “It’d be the safest nesting place in England. No one ever comes near, and there are tangles of trees and roses to build in. I wonder that all the birds on the moor don’t nest here.”
Mistress Mary put her hand on his arm again without even knowing she did it.
“Will there be roses?” she whispered. “Can you tell? I thought maybe they were all dead.”
“Eh! No! Not them, not all of them!” he answered. “Look here!”

He stepped over to the nearest tree. It was a very old one, with gray lichen all over its bark, yet it held up a curtain of tangled sprays and branches. He took a thick knife out of his pocket and opened one of its blades.

“There’s plenty of dead wood that ought to be cut out,” he said. “And there’s a lot of old wood, but it grew some new last year. This is a new bit,” and he touched a shoot that looked brownish green instead of hard, dry gray.
Mary touched it herself, eagerly and with great care.
“This one?” she said. “Is it really alive? Quite alive?”
Dickon curved his wide, smiling mouth.
“It’s as wick as you or me,” he said. Mary remembered that Martha had told her “wick” meant “alive” or “lively.”
“Oh, I’m so glad it’s wick!” she cried in her whisper. “I want every one of them to be wick. Let’s walk around the whole garden and count the wick ones.”

She was nearly breathless with eagerness, and Dickon was just as eager. They went from tree to tree and from bush to bush. Dickon held his knife in his hand and showed her things that she thought were wonderful.

“They’ve run wild,” he said, “but the strongest ones have done well on it. The most delicate ones have died out, but the others have grown and grown, and spread and spread, till they’re a marvel. See here!” He pulled down a thick gray branch that looked dry. “A person might think this was dead wood, but I don’t believe it is, not all the way down to the root. I’ll cut it low down and see.”
He knelt and cut through the lifeless-looking branch with his knife, not far above the ground.
“There!” he said triumphantly. “I told you so. There’s still green in that wood. Look at it.”
Mary was down on her knees before he even spoke, staring with all her might.

“When it looks a bit green and juicy like that, it’s wick,” he explained. “When the inside is dry and snaps easily, like this piece I’ve cut off, it’s finished. There’s a big root here that all this live wood grew out of. If the old wood is cut away, and the soil is dug around it and looked after, there’ll be—” He stopped and lifted his face to look up at the climbing, hanging sprays above him. “There’ll be a fountain of roses here this summer.”

They went from bush to bush and from tree to tree. He was very strong and clever with his knife. He knew how to cut away the dry, dead wood, and he could tell when a poor-looking bough or twig still had green life in it. After half an hour Mary thought she could tell too. When he cut through a lifeless-looking branch, she would cry out with joy, under her breath, whenever she spotted the faintest shade of moist green. The spade, the hoe, and the fork were very useful. He showed her how to use the fork while he dug around the roots with the spade, stirring the earth and letting the air in.
They were hard at work around one of the biggest standard roses when he noticed something that made him gasp in surprise.
“Why!” he cried, pointing to the grass a few feet away. “Who did that?”
It was one of Mary’s own little clearings around the pale green points.
“I did it,” said Mary.
“Why, I thought you didn’t know anything about gardening,” he exclaimed.

“I don’t,” she answered. “But they were tiny, and the grass around them was thick and strong, and they seemed to have no room to breathe. So I cleared a space for them. I don’t even know what they are.”
Dickon went and knelt beside them, with his wide smile.

“You were right,” he said. “A gardener couldn’t have told you better. They’ll grow now like Jack’s beanstalk. These are crocuses and snowdrops, and these here are narcissuses,” he said, turning to another patch, “and here’s daffydowndillys. Eh! They’ll be a sight to see.”
He ran from one clearing to the next.
“You’ve done a lot of work for such a little lass,” he said, looking her over.
“I’m getting fatter,” said Mary, “and I’m getting stronger. I used to be tired all the time. When I dig, I’m not tired at all. I like the smell of the earth when it’s turned up.”

“It’s wonderful good for you,” he said, nodding wisely. “There’s nothing as nice as the smell of good clean earth, except the smell of fresh growing things when the rain falls on them. Many a day I go out on the moor when it’s raining, and I lie under a bush and listen to the soft swish of the drops on the heather, and I just sniff and sniff. The end of my nose twitches like a rabbit’s, Mother says.”
“Don’t you ever catch cold?” Mary asked, gazing at him in wonder. She had never seen such a funny boy, or such a nice one.

“Not me,” he said, grinning. “I’ve never caught a cold since I was born. I wasn’t brought up soft enough. I’ve run about the moor in all weathers, same as the rabbits do. Mother says I’ve sniffed up too much fresh air in twelve years ever to get a sniffle. I’m as tough as a hawthorn walking stick.”
He kept working the whole time he talked, and Mary followed him, helping with her fork or the trowel.
“There’s a lot of work to do here!” he said once, looking around with delight.
“Will you come back and help me with it?” Mary begged. “I’m sure I can be useful, too. I can dig and pull weeds and do anything you tell me. Oh! Please come, Dickon!”
“I’ll come every day if you want me, rain or shine,” he answered firmly. “It’s the best fun I’ve ever had in my life, shut in here and waking up a garden.”
“If you’ll come,” said Mary, “if you’ll help me make it alive, I’ll—I don’t know what I’ll do,” she ended helplessly. What could anyone do for a boy like that?

“I’ll tell you what you’ll do,” said Dickon, with his happy grin. “You’ll get fat, and you’ll get as hungry as a young fox, and you’ll learn to talk to the robin the way I do. Eh! We’ll have a lot of fun.”
He began to walk about, looking up into the trees and at the walls and bushes with a thoughtful face.

“I wouldn’t want to make it look like a gardener’s garden, all clipped and neat and tidy, would you?” he said. “It’s nicer like this, with things running wild and swinging and catching hold of each other.”
“Let’s not make it tidy,” said Mary anxiously. “It wouldn’t feel like a secret garden if it was tidy.”
Dickon stood rubbing his rusty-red head, looking rather puzzled.
“It’s a secret garden, sure enough,” he said, “but it seems to me someone besides the robin must have been in it since it was shut up ten years ago.”
“But the door was locked and the key was buried,” said Mary. “No one could get in.”
“That’s true,” he answered. “It’s a strange place. It seems to me as if there’s been a bit of pruning done here and there, later than ten years ago.”
“But how could that have happened?” said Mary.
He was looking closely at a branch of a standard rose, and he shook his head.
“Aye! How could it?” he murmured. “With the door locked and the key buried.”

Mistress Mary always felt that no matter how many years she lived, she would never forget that first morning when her garden began to grow. Of course, it did seem to begin to grow for her that morning. When Dickon started to clear places to plant seeds, she remembered what Basil had sung at her when he wanted to tease her.
“Are there any flowers that look like bells?” she asked.
“Lilies of the valley do,” he answered, digging away with the trowel, “and there’s Canterbury bells, and campanulas.”
“Let’s plant some,” said Mary.

“There’s lilies of the valley here already. I saw them. They’ll have grown too close together and we’ll have to separate them, but there’s plenty. The other kinds take two years to bloom from seed, but I can bring you some bits of plants from our cottage garden. Why do you want them?”
Then Mary told him about Basil and his brothers and sisters in India, and how she had hated them, and how they had called her “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary.”
“They used to dance around me and sing at me. They sang—

‘Mistress Mary, quite contrary,
How does your garden grow?
With silver bells, and cockle shells,
And marigolds all in a row.’
I just remembered it, and it made me wonder if there really were flowers like silver bells.”
She frowned a little and gave her trowel a rather spiteful jab into the earth.
“I wasn’t as contrary as they were.”
But Dickon laughed.

“Eh!” he said. As he crumbled the rich black soil, she saw that he was breathing in its scent. “There doesn’t seem to be any need for anyone to be contrary when there are flowers and such, and so many friendly wild things running about making homes for themselves, or building nests and singing and whistling, does there?”
Mary was kneeling beside him, holding the seeds. She looked at him and stopped frowning.
“Dickon,” she said, “you’re every bit as nice as Martha said. I like you, and that makes five people I like. I never thought I could like five people.”
Dickon sat back on his heels, the way Martha did when she was polishing the grate. He looked funny and delightful, Mary thought, with his round blue eyes and red cheeks and happy, turned-up nose.
“Only five folk you like?” he said. “Who are the other four?”
“Your mother and Martha,” Mary counted them off on her fingers, “and the robin and Ben Weatherstaff.”
Dickon laughed so hard that he had to muffle the sound by putting his arm over his mouth.
“I know you think I’m a queer lad,” he said, “but I think you’re the queerest little lass I ever saw.”

Then Mary did something strange. She leaned toward him and asked him a question she had never dreamed of asking anyone. She tried to say it in Yorkshire, because that was his own language, and in India a native was always pleased when you knew how he spoke.
“Do you like me?” she said, in Yorkshire.
“Eh!” he answered heartily, “that I do. I like you wonderful well, and so does the robin, I do believe!”
“That’s two, then,” said Mary. “That’s two for me.”
After that they worked harder than ever, and with more joy. Mary was startled and sorry when the big clock in the courtyard struck the hour for her midday dinner.
“I’ll have to go,” she said sadly. “And you’ll have to go too, won’t you?”
Dickon grinned.
“My dinner’s easy to carry around with me,” he said. “Mother always lets me put a bit of something in my pocket.”

He picked his coat up off the grass and pulled from its pocket a lumpy little bundle knotted in a coarse blue and white handkerchief, which was quite clean. Inside were two thick pieces of bread with a slice of something laid between them.
“It’s most often nothing but bread,” he said, “but today I’ve got a fine slice of fat bacon with it.”
Mary thought it looked like a queer dinner, but he seemed ready to enjoy it.
“Run along and get your dinner,” he said. “I’ll be finished with mine first. I’ll get some more work done before I start back home.”
He sat down with his back against a tree.
“I’ll call the robin up,” he said, “and give him the rind of the bacon to peck at. They like a bit of fat wonderfully well.”

Mary could hardly stand to leave him. All at once she felt he might be a kind of wood fairy, who would vanish before she came back into the garden. He seemed too good to be true. She walked slowly halfway to the door in the wall, then stopped and turned back.
“Whatever happens, you—you would never tell?” she said.
His poppy-colored cheeks were puffed out with his first big bite of bread and bacon, but he managed to smile encouragingly.
“If you were a missel thrush and showed me where your nest was, do you think I’d tell anyone? Not me,” he said. “You’re as safe as a missel thrush.”
And she was quite sure she was.

chapters.title: “Might I Have a Bit of Earth?”
paragraphs: Mary ran so fast that she was almost out of breath by the time she reached her room. Her hair was tousled across her forehead, and her cheeks were bright pink. Her dinner was waiting on the table, and Martha stood close by.
“You’re a bit late,” she said. “Where have you been?”
“I’ve seen Dickon!” said Mary. “I’ve seen Dickon!”
“I knew he’d come,” said Martha happily. “How do you like him?”
“I think—I think he’s beautiful!” said Mary in a determined voice.
Martha looked a little taken aback, but she looked pleased, too.
“Well,” she said, “he’s the best lad that was ever born, but we never thought him handsome. His nose turns up too much.”
“I like it turned up,” said Mary.
“And his eyes are so round,” said Martha, sounding a little unsure. “Though they are a nice color.”
“I like them round,” said Mary. “And they’re exactly the color of the sky over the moor.”
Martha glowed with satisfaction.
“Mother says he got them that color from always looking up at the birds and the clouds. But he has got a big mouth, hasn’t he, now?”
“I love his big mouth,” said Mary stubbornly. “I wish mine were just like it.”
Martha laughed with delight.
“It’d look very odd and funny in that little face of yours,” she said. “But I knew you’d feel this way when you saw him. How did you like the seeds and the garden tools?”
“How did you know he brought them?” asked Mary.
“Eh! It never crossed my mind that he wouldn’t bring them. He’d be sure to bring them if they were anywhere in Yorkshire. He’s such a dependable lad.”

Mary was afraid Martha might start asking hard questions, but she didn’t. She was far too interested in the seeds and the tools. There was only one moment when Mary felt frightened. That was when Martha asked where the flowers were going to be planted.
“Who did you ask about it?” she wanted to know.
“I haven’t asked anybody yet,” said Mary, hesitating.
“Well, I wouldn’t ask the head gardener. He’s too grand, is Mr. Roach.”
“I’ve never seen him,” said Mary. “I’ve only seen the undergardeners and Ben Weatherstaff.”

“If I were you, I’d ask Ben Weatherstaff,” Martha advised. “He’s not half as bad as he looks, even if he is so crabby. Mr. Craven lets him do as he likes, because he was here when Mrs. Craven was alive, and he used to make her laugh. She liked him. Maybe he’d find you a corner somewhere out of the way.”
“If it was out of the way and nobody wanted it, then nobody _could_ mind my having it, could they?” Mary asked anxiously.
“There’d be no reason to,” answered Martha. “You wouldn’t be doing any harm.”
Mary ate her dinner as fast as she could. When she got up from the table she meant to run to her room and put on her hat again, but Martha stopped her.
“There’s something I have to tell you,” she said. “I figured I’d wait until you’d finished eating. Mr. Craven got home this morning, and I believe he wants to see you.”
Mary went quite pale.
“Oh!” she said. “Why! Why! He didn’t want to see me when I came. I heard Pitcher say so.”

“Well,” Martha explained, “Mrs. Medlock says it’s because of Mother. She was walking to Thwaite village and she met him. She’d never spoken to him before, but Mrs. Craven had been to our cottage two or three times. He’d forgotten that, but Mother hadn’t, and she was bold enough to stop him. I don’t know what she said to him about you, but it put it in his mind to see you before he goes away again tomorrow.”
“Oh!” cried Mary. “Is he going away tomorrow? I’m so glad!”
“He’s going for a long time. He might not come back until autumn or winter. He’s going to travel in foreign places. He’s always doing it.”
“Oh! I’m so glad—so glad!” said Mary thankfully.
