If he stayed away until winter, or even autumn, there would be plenty of time to watch the secret garden wake up. And if he found out later and took it from her, at least she would have had these months.
“When do you think he will want to see—”

She never finished the sentence, because the door opened and Mrs. Medlock walked in. She was wearing her best black dress and cap, and her collar was fastened with a large brooch with a man’s face pictured on it. It was a colored photograph of Mr. Medlock, who had died years ago, and she always wore it when she dressed up. She looked nervous and excited.
“Your hair’s a mess,” she said sharply. “Go brush it. Martha, help her into her best dress. Mr. Craven has told me to take her to his study.”

All the pink drained from Mary’s cheeks. Her heart began to thump, and she felt herself turning back into a stiff, plain, silent child. She did not even answer Mrs. Medlock. She just turned and walked into her bedroom, with Martha behind her. She said nothing while her dress was changed and her hair was brushed. When she was perfectly tidy, she followed Mrs. Medlock down the corridors in silence. What was there for her to say? She had to go and see Mr. Craven, and he would not like her, and she would not like him. She knew what he would think of her.

They went through a part of the house Mary had never seen. At last Mrs. Medlock knocked on a door. Someone called, “Come in,” and the two of them stepped inside together. A man sat in an armchair by the fire, and Mrs. Medlock spoke to him.
“This is Miss Mary, sir,” she said.
“You can go and leave her here. I will ring for you when I want you to take her away,” said Mr. Craven.

Mrs. Medlock left and shut the door. Mary could do nothing but stand and wait, a plain little girl wringing her thin hands. She could see now that the man in the chair was not really a hunchback. His shoulders were simply high and a little crooked, and his black hair had white streaks in it. He turned his head over those high shoulders and spoke to her.
“Come here!” he said.
Mary went to him.

He was not ugly. His face would have been handsome if it had not been so miserable. He looked as though the sight of her worried and upset him, and as though he had no idea what in the world to do with her.
“Are you well?” he asked.
“Yes,” answered Mary.
“Do they take good care of you?”
“Yes.”
He rubbed his forehead restlessly as he looked her over.
“You are very thin,” he said.
“I’m getting fatter,” Mary answered, in what she knew was her stiffest way.
What an unhappy face he had! His black eyes hardly seemed to see her. They seemed to be looking at something else, and he could barely keep his thoughts on her.
“I forgot you,” he said. “How could I remember you? I meant to send you a governess or a nurse, or someone of that sort, but I forgot.”
“Please,” Mary began. “Please—” and then the lump in her throat choked her.
“What do you want to say?” he asked.
“I’m—I’m too big for a nurse,” said Mary. “And please—please don’t make me have a governess yet.”
He rubbed his forehead again and stared at her.
“That’s just what the Sowerby woman said,” he muttered absent-mindedly.
Then Mary found a scrap of courage.
“Is she—is she Martha’s mother?” she stammered.
“Yes, I think so,” he replied.
“She knows about children,” said Mary. “She has twelve. She knows.”
He seemed to wake himself up.
“What do you want to do?”
“I want to play outdoors,” Mary answered, hoping her voice didn’t shake. “I never liked it in India. Here it makes me hungry, and I’m getting fatter.”
He was watching her.
“Mrs. Sowerby said it would do you good. Perhaps it will,” he said. “She thought you should get stronger before you had a governess.”
“It makes me feel strong when I play and the wind comes over the moor,” Mary argued.
“Where do you play?” he asked next.
“Everywhere,” Mary gasped. “Martha’s mother sent me a skipping rope. I skip and run—and I look around to see if things are starting to poke up out of the earth. I don’t do any harm.”
“Don’t look so frightened,” he said in a worried voice. “You couldn’t do any harm, a child like you! You may do what you like.”
Mary put her hand up to her throat, afraid he might see the excited lump that had jumped into it. She came a step closer to him.
“May I?” she said, trembling.
Her anxious little face seemed to trouble him more than ever.

“Don’t look so frightened,” he exclaimed. “Of course you may. I’m your guardian, though a poor one for any child. I have no time or attention to give you. I’m too sick, too unhappy, too distracted. But I do want you to be happy and comfortable. I know nothing about children, but Mrs. Medlock will make sure you have whatever you need. I sent for you today because Mrs. Sowerby told me I should see you. Her daughter had spoken of you. Mrs. Sowerby thinks you need fresh air, freedom and plenty of running around.”
“She knows all about children,” Mary said again, in spite of herself.

“She should,” said Mr. Craven. “I thought it quite bold of her to stop me on the moor. But she said—Mrs. Craven had been kind to her.” It was clearly hard for him to speak his dead wife’s name. “She is a respectable woman. Now that I’ve seen you, I think what she told me was sensible. Play outside as much as you please. The place is big, and you may go anywhere and amuse yourself however you like. Is there anything you want?” he asked, as though the thought had just come to him. “Would you like toys, books, dolls?”
“Might I,” Mary quavered, “might I have a bit of earth?”
She was so eager that she didn’t notice how strange her words would sound. They weren’t what she had planned to say at all. Mr. Craven looked startled.
“Earth!” he repeated. “What do you mean?”
“To plant seeds in—to make things grow—to see them come alive,” Mary faltered.
He gazed at her for a moment and then quickly passed his hand over his eyes.
“Do you—care so much about gardens?” he said slowly.
“I didn’t know about them in India,” said Mary. “I was always sick and tired, and it was too hot. Sometimes I made little flower beds in the sand and stuck flowers in them. But here it’s different.”
Mr. Craven got up and began to walk slowly across the room.
“A bit of earth,” he murmured to himself. Mary thought she must have reminded him of something. When he stopped and turned to her, his dark eyes had grown almost gentle and kind.

“You may have all the earth you want,” he said. “You remind me of someone else who loved the soil and everything that grows in it. Whenever you see a bit of earth you’d like,” and he almost smiled, “take it, child, and make it live.”
“May I take it from anywhere—if nobody wants it?”
“Anywhere,” he said. “Now, you must go. I’m tired.” He rang the bell for Mrs. Medlock. “Good-bye. I will be away the whole summer.”
Mrs. Medlock came so quickly that Mary thought she must have been waiting in the corridor.

“Mrs. Medlock,” Mr. Craven told her, “having seen the child, I understand what Mrs. Sowerby meant. She has to be stronger before she starts lessons. Feed her simple, wholesome food. Let her run wild in the garden. Don’t hover over her. She needs freedom, fresh air and romping. Mrs. Sowerby will come to see her from time to time, and she may visit the cottage now and then.”

Mrs. Medlock looked pleased. She was relieved to hear that she need not “look after” Mary too much. She had found her a tiresome burden, and had indeed seen as little of her as she dared. On top of that, she was fond of Martha’s mother.

“Thank you, sir,” she said. “Susan Sowerby and I were in school together. She’s as sensible and kindhearted a woman as you’d meet in a day’s walk. I never had children of my own, but she’s had twelve, and there never were healthier or finer ones. Miss Mary can’t be harmed by them. I’d always take Susan Sowerby’s advice on children, myself. She’s what you might call healthy-minded—if you take my meaning.”
“I understand,” Mr. Craven answered. “Take Miss Mary away now and send Pitcher to me.”

When Mrs. Medlock left her at the end of her own corridor, Mary flew back to her room. She found Martha waiting there. Martha had, in fact, hurried back as soon as she had cleared away the dinner dishes.

“I’m going to have my garden!” cried Mary. “I can have it wherever I choose! And no governess for a long time! Your mother is coming to visit me, and I can go to your cottage! He says a little girl like me couldn’t do any harm, and I can do whatever I like—anywhere!”
“Eh!” said Martha delightedly. “That was nice of him, wasn’t it?”
“Martha,” said Mary solemnly, “he really is a nice man. It’s only that his face is so miserable and his forehead is all pinched together.”

She ran to the garden as fast as she could. She had been away much longer than she had expected, and she knew Dickon would have to start early on his five-mile walk. When she slipped through the door under the ivy, she saw that he was not working where she had left him. The gardening tools were laid together under a tree. She ran to them, looking all around the place, but there was no Dickon to be seen. He had gone away, and the secret garden was empty—except for the robin, who had just flown across the wall and was sitting on a standard rose-bush, watching her.
“He’s gone,” she said sadly. “Oh! was he—was he—was he only a wood fairy?”

Something white, tied to the standard rose-bush, caught her eye. It was a scrap of paper. Actually, it was a piece of the letter she had printed for Martha to send to Dickon. A long thorn held it to the bush, and she knew at once that Dickon had left it. It had some roughly printed letters on it and a kind of picture. At first she couldn’t make out what it showed. Then she saw it was a nest with a bird sitting on it. Below it were the printed words, which said:
“I will cum bak.”

chapters.title: “I Am Colin”
paragraphs: When Mary went down to her supper, she carried the picture back to the house and showed it to Martha.
“Eh!” said Martha, bursting with pride. “I never knew our Dickon was so clever. That’s a picture of a missel thrush on her nest, big as life an’ twice as natural.”

Then Mary understood that Dickon had meant the picture as a message. He was telling her she could trust him to keep her secret. Her garden was her nest, and she was like the missel thrush. Oh, how she liked that odd, plain-spoken boy!
She hoped he would come back the very next day. She fell asleep looking forward to the morning.

But you can never tell what the weather will do in Yorkshire, especially in springtime. In the night Mary was woken by heavy raindrops beating against her window. The rain was coming down in torrents, and the wind was “wuthering” around the corners and through the chimneys of the huge old house. Mary sat up in bed, feeling miserable and angry.
“The rain is as contrary as I ever was,” she said. “It came because it knew I didn’t want it.”

She threw herself back on her pillow and buried her face in it. She did not cry, but she lay there hating the sound of the pounding rain, and she hated the wind and its “wuthering.” She could not get back to sleep. The mournful sound kept her awake because she felt mournful herself. If she had been happy, it would probably have lulled her to sleep. How it “wuthered,” and how the big raindrops poured down and beat against the windowpane!
“It sounds just like someone lost on the moor, wandering on and on and crying,” she said.
She had been lying awake for about an hour, tossing from side to side, when suddenly something made her sit up in bed and turn her head toward the door. She listened and listened.
“That isn’t the wind now,” she said in a loud whisper. “It’s different. It’s that crying I heard before.”

Her bedroom door was open a crack, and the sound came down the corridor, a faint, far-off sound of fretful crying. She listened for a few minutes, and with each minute she grew more certain. She felt she had to find out what it was. It seemed even stranger than the secret garden and the buried key. Perhaps being in a rebellious mood made her bold. She put one foot out of bed and stood on the floor.
“I am going to find out what it is,” she said. “Everyone is in bed, and I don’t care about Mrs. Medlock—I don’t care!”

A candle stood by her bedside. She picked it up and went quietly out of the room. The corridor looked very long and dark, but she was too excited to mind. She thought she remembered which corners to turn to reach the short corridor with the tapestry-covered door—the one Mrs. Medlock had come through the day Mary got lost. The sound had come up that passage. So she went on with her dim light, almost feeling her way, her heart beating so loudly that she imagined she could hear it. The faint, far-off crying went on and led her forward. Sometimes it stopped for a moment and then began again. Was this the right corner? She stopped and thought. Yes, it was. Down this passage, then left, then up two broad steps, then right again. Yes, there was the tapestry door.

She pushed it open very gently and closed it behind her. Standing in the corridor, she could hear the crying quite plainly, though it was not loud. It came from the other side of the wall on her left, and a few yards farther on there was a door. A glimmer of light showed beneath it. Someone was crying in that room, and it was quite a young Someone.
So she walked to the door and pushed it open, and there she was, standing in the room!

It was a big room with old, handsome furniture. A low fire glowed faintly on the hearth, and a night light burned beside a carved four-poster bed hung with brocade. On the bed lay a boy, crying fretfully.
Mary wondered whether she was in a real place, or whether she had fallen asleep again and was dreaming without knowing it.

The boy had a sharp, delicate face the color of ivory, and his eyes seemed too big for it. He also had a lot of hair, which tumbled over his forehead in heavy locks and made his thin face look smaller. He looked like a boy who had been ill, but he was crying more like someone tired and cross than like someone in pain.

Mary stood near the door with her candle in her hand, holding her breath. Then she crept across the room. As she came closer, the light caught the boy’s attention. He turned his head on his pillow and stared at her, his gray eyes opening so wide that they looked immense.
“Who are you?” he said at last, in a half-frightened whisper. “Are you a ghost?”
“No, I’m not,” Mary answered, her own whisper sounding half frightened. “Are you?”

He stared and stared and stared. Mary couldn’t help noticing what strange eyes he had. They were agate gray, and they looked too big for his face because they were ringed all around with black lashes.
“No,” he replied, after waiting a moment. “I’m Colin.”
“Who is Colin?” she asked shakily.
“I’m Colin Craven. Who are you?”
“I’m Mary Lennox. Mr. Craven is my uncle.”
“He’s my father,” said the boy.
“Your father!” gasped Mary. “Nobody ever told me he had a son! Why not?”
“Come here,” he said, still keeping his strange eyes fixed on her with an anxious look.
She came close to the bed, and he put out his hand and touched her.
“You’re real, aren’t you?” he said. “I often have dreams that feel very real. You could be one of them.”
Mary had pulled on a woolen wrapper before leaving her room, and now she put a corner of it between his fingers.
“Feel this and you’ll know how thick and warm it is,” she said. “If you like, I’ll pinch you a bit, to prove I’m real. For a moment I wondered if you were a dream as well.”
“Where did you come from?” he asked.
“From my own room. The wind was wuthering so loudly that I couldn’t sleep, and I heard someone crying and wanted to find out who it was. Why were you crying?”
“Because I couldn’t sleep either, and my head ached. Tell me your name again.”
“Mary Lennox. Didn’t anyone ever tell you I’d come to live here?”
He was still fingering the fold of her wrapper, but he was beginning to look a little more as if he believed she was real.
“No,” he answered. “They wouldn’t dare.”
“Why?” asked Mary.
“Because I would have been afraid you’d see me. I won’t let people see me and talk about me.”
“Why?” Mary asked again, feeling more puzzled every moment.

“Because I’m like this all the time, ill and having to lie down. My father won’t let people talk about me either. The servants aren’t allowed to speak of me. If I live, I might turn into a hunchback, but I won’t live. My father hates the thought that I might be like him.”
“Oh, this is such a strange house!” Mary said. “So strange! Everything here is a kind of secret. Rooms are shut away, gardens are shut away—and you! Have they shut you away too?”
“No. I stay in this room because I don’t want to be moved out of it. It tires me too much.”
“Does your father come to see you?” Mary ventured.
“Sometimes. Usually when I’m asleep. He doesn’t want to see me.”
“Why?” Mary couldn’t help asking again.
A kind of angry shadow crossed the boy’s face.
“My mother died the day I was born, and he can’t look at me without feeling wretched. He thinks I don’t know, but I’ve heard people talk. He nearly hates me.”
“He hates the garden because she died,” said Mary, half to herself.
“What garden?” the boy asked.
“Oh! Just—just a garden she used to like,” Mary stammered. “Have you always been here?”

“Almost always. Now and then I’ve been taken to the seaside, but I never stay, because people stare at me. I used to wear an iron brace to hold my back straight. Then a famous doctor came from London to examine me and said the brace was silly. He ordered them to take it off and keep me outdoors in the fresh air. I hate fresh air, and I don’t want to go outside.”
“I didn’t either, when I first came here,” said Mary. “Why do you keep looking at me like that?”
“Because of the dreams that feel so real,” he answered, rather fretfully. “Sometimes when I open my eyes, I don’t believe I’m awake.”

“We’re both awake,” said Mary. She glanced around the room with its high ceiling, shadowy corners and dim firelight. “It looks quite like a dream, and it’s the middle of the night, and everyone in the house is asleep—everyone but us. We’re wide awake.”
“I don’t want it to be a dream,” the boy said restlessly.
Mary suddenly thought of something.
“If you don’t like people to see you,” she began, “do you want me to go away?”
He was still holding the fold of her wrapper, and he gave it a little tug.
“No,” he said. “If you went, I’d be sure you were a dream. If you’re real, sit down on that big footstool and talk. I want to hear about you.”

Mary set her candle on the table near the bed and sat down on the cushioned stool. She didn’t want to go away at all. She wanted to stay in that mysterious, hidden-away room and talk to the mysterious boy.
“What do you want me to tell you?” she said.

He wanted to know how long she had been at Misselthwaite. He wanted to know which corridor her room was on. He wanted to know what she had been doing, whether she disliked the moor the way he did, and where she had lived before she came to Yorkshire. She answered all these questions and many more, and he lay back on his pillow and listened. He made her tell him a great deal about India and about her voyage across the ocean. She found out that, because he had been an invalid, he had not learned things the way other children had. One of his nurses had taught him to read when he was quite little, and he was always reading and looking at the pictures in splendid books.

His father rarely saw him when he was awake, but he was given all sorts of wonderful things to amuse himself with. Still, he never seemed to have been amused. He could have anything he asked for, and he was never made to do anything he didn’t want to do.
“Everyone has to do what pleases me,” he said, without interest. “Getting angry makes me ill. No one believes I’ll live to grow up.”

He said it as if he was so used to the idea that it had stopped mattering to him at all. He seemed to like the sound of Mary’s voice. As she went on talking, he listened in a drowsy, interested way. Once or twice she wondered whether he was slowly drifting off to sleep. But at last he asked a question that opened up a new subject.
“How old are you?” he asked.
“I’m ten,” answered Mary, forgetting herself for a moment, “and so are you.”
“How do you know that?” he demanded, sounding surprised.
“Because the garden door was locked and the key was buried when you were born. And it has been locked for ten years.”
Colin half sat up, turning toward her and leaning on his elbows.
“What garden door was locked? Who did it? Where was the key buried?” he exclaimed, as if he had suddenly become very interested.
“It—it was the garden Mr. Craven hates,” said Mary nervously. “He locked the door. No one—no one knew where he buried the key.”
“What sort of garden is it?” Colin pressed eagerly.
“No one has been allowed to go into it for ten years,” was Mary’s careful answer.

But it was too late to be careful. He was too much like her. He had never had anything to think about either, and a hidden garden pulled at him just as it had pulled at her. He fired off question after question. Where was it? Had she never searched for the door? Had she never asked the gardeners?
“They won’t talk about it,” said Mary. “I think they’ve been told not to answer questions.”
“I’d make them,” said Colin.
“Could you?” Mary faltered, beginning to feel frightened. If he could make people answer questions, who knew what might happen!
“Everyone has to please me. I told you that,” he said. “If I lived, this place would belong to me someday. They all know that. I’d make them tell me.”

Mary had never realized that she herself had been spoiled, but she could plainly see that this mysterious boy was. He believed the whole world was his. How odd he was, and how calmly he talked about not living.
“Do you think you won’t live?” she asked, partly because she was curious and partly in the hope of making him forget the garden.

“I don’t suppose I will,” he answered, as indifferently as before. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve heard people say I won’t. At first they thought I was too little to understand, and now they think I can’t hear. But I can. My doctor is my father’s cousin. He is quite poor, and if I die, he will get all of Misselthwaite when my father is dead. I’d think he wouldn’t want me to live.”
“Do you want to live?” Mary asked.
“No,” he answered, in a cross, tired way. “But I don’t want to die. When I feel ill, I lie here and think about it until I cry and cry.”
“I’ve heard you crying three times,” Mary said, “but I didn’t know who it was. Were you crying about that?” She wanted so badly for him to forget the garden.
“I dare say,” he answered. “Let’s talk about something else. Talk about that garden. Don’t you want to see it?”
“Yes,” answered Mary, in quite a low voice.

“Well, I do,” he went on stubbornly. “I don’t think I ever truly wanted to see anything before, but I want to see that garden. Have the key dug up. Have the door unlocked. They can carry me there in my chair. That would count as fresh air. I’ll make them open the door.”
He had become quite excited, and his strange eyes began to shine like stars and looked more immense than ever.
“They have to please me,” he said. “I’ll make them take me there, and I’ll let you come too.”
Mary wrung her hands together. Everything would be ruined—everything! Dickon would never come back. She would never again feel like a missel thrush with a safe, hidden nest.
“Oh, don’t—don’t—don’t—don’t do that!” she cried out.
He stared as if he thought she had gone crazy!
“Why?” he exclaimed. “You said you wanted to see it.”
“I do,” she answered, a sob almost catching in her throat, “but if you force them to open the door and carry you in that way, it can never be a secret again.”
He leaned still farther forward.
“A secret,” he said. “What do you mean? Tell me.”
Mary’s words almost tumbled over one another.

“You see—you see,” she panted, “suppose no one knew except us—suppose there was a door, hidden somewhere under the ivy—suppose there was—and we could find it; and suppose we could slip through it together and shut it behind us, so that no one knew anyone was inside. Suppose we called it our garden and pretended that—that we were missel thrushes and it was our nest. And suppose we played there almost every day and dug and planted seeds and made it all come alive—”
“Is it dead?” he interrupted her.
“It soon will be if no one takes care of it,” she went on. “The bulbs will live, but the roses—”
He stopped her again, as excited as she was herself.
“What are bulbs?” he put in quickly.
“They’re daffodils and lilies and snowdrops. They’re working in the earth now—pushing up pale green points because spring is coming.”
“Is spring coming?” he said. “What is it like? You can’t see it in a room if you’re ill.”

“Think of the sun shining on the rain and the rain falling through the sunshine, and of everything pushing up and working away under the earth,” said Mary. “If the garden were a secret and we found a way in, we could watch things grow a little bigger each day and count how many roses are still alive. Don’t you see? Oh, don’t you see how much nicer it would be as a secret?”
He dropped back onto his pillow and lay there with a strange look on his face.
“I never had a secret,” he said, “except the one about not living to grow up. They don’t know that I know about it, so it’s a sort of secret. But I like this kind better.”

“If you won’t make them take you to the garden,” Mary pleaded, “then maybe—I feel almost sure I can find out how to get in sometime. And then—if the doctor wants you to go out in your chair, and if you can always do what you want—maybe we could find some boy who would push you, and we could go there alone, and it would always be a secret garden.”
“I would—like—that,” he said very slowly, his eyes growing dreamy. “I would like that. I wouldn’t mind fresh air in a secret garden.”

Mary began to catch her breath and feel safer, because the idea of keeping the secret seemed to please him. She felt almost sure that if she kept talking, and could make him see the garden in his mind the way she had seen it, he would like it so much that he couldn’t stand the thought of everybody tramping in whenever they pleased.
“I’ll tell you what I _think_ it would be like, if we could go into it,” she said. “It has been shut up for so long that perhaps everything has grown into a tangle.”

He lay perfectly still and listened as she went on talking about the roses that _might_ have climbed from tree to tree and hung down, and about the many birds that _might_ have built their nests there because it was so safe. Then she told him about the robin and Ben Weatherstaff. There was so much to tell about the robin, and it was so easy and safe to talk about, that she stopped feeling afraid. The robin pleased him so much that he smiled until he looked almost beautiful. At first Mary had thought he was even plainer than she was, with his big eyes and his heavy locks of hair.
“I didn’t know birds could be like that,” he said. “But if you stay in a room, you never see things. You know so many things! I feel as if you had been inside that garden.”
She didn’t know what to say, so she said nothing. He plainly didn’t expect an answer, and a moment later he surprised her.
“I’m going to let you look at something,” he said. “Do you see that rose-colored silk curtain hanging on the wall over the mantelpiece?”
Mary hadn’t noticed it before, but now she looked up and saw it. It was a curtain of soft silk, hanging over what seemed to be a picture.
“Yes,” she answered.
“There’s a cord hanging from it,” said Colin. “Go and pull it.”

Mary got up, very puzzled, and found the cord. When she pulled it, the silk curtain slid back on its rings and uncovered a picture. It was a picture of a girl with a laughing face. Her bright hair was tied up with a blue ribbon, and her happy, lovely eyes were exactly like Colin’s unhappy ones—agate gray, and looking twice as big as they really were because of the black lashes all around them.
“She’s my mother,” said Colin, in a complaining voice. “I don’t see why she had to die. Sometimes I hate her for doing it.”
“How strange!” said Mary.

“If she had lived, I believe I wouldn’t have been sick all the time,” he grumbled. “I suppose I would have lived, too. And my father wouldn’t have hated to look at me. I suppose I would have had a strong back. Draw the curtain again.”
Mary did as she was told and went back to her footstool.
“She’s much prettier than you are,” she said, “but her eyes are just like yours. They’re the same shape and color, at least. Why did you have the curtain pulled over her?”
He shifted uncomfortably.
“I made them do it,” he said. “Sometimes I don’t like to see her looking at me. She smiles too much when I’m sick and miserable. Besides, she’s mine, and I don’t want everyone to see her.”
There were a few moments of silence, and then Mary spoke.
“What would Mrs. Medlock do if she found out I had been here?” she asked.
“She would obey me,” he answered. “I would tell her I want you to come and talk to me every day. I’m glad you came.”
“So am I,” said Mary. “I’ll come as often as I can, but”—she hesitated—“I’ll have to look every day for the garden door.”
“Yes, you must,” said Colin, “and afterward you can tell me about it.”
He lay thinking for a few minutes, as he had done before, and then he spoke again.
“I think you should be a secret, too,” he said. “I won’t say anything until they find out on their own. I can always send the nurse from the room and tell her I want to be alone. Do you know Martha?”
“Yes, I know her very well,” said Mary. “She waits on me.”
He nodded toward the outer corridor.

“She’s the one who is asleep in the other room. The nurse went away yesterday to spend the night with her sister, and whenever she wants to go out, she always makes Martha look after me. Martha will tell you when to come here.”
Then Mary understood why Martha had looked so troubled when she had asked questions about the crying.
“Martha knew about you all the time?” she said.
“Yes. She often looks after me. The nurse likes to get away from me, and then Martha comes.”
“I’ve been here a long time,” said Mary. “Should I go now? Your eyes look sleepy.”
“I wish I could fall asleep before you leave me,” he said, rather shyly.
“Shut your eyes,” said Mary, drawing her footstool closer, “and I’ll do what my Ayah used to do in India. I’ll pat your hand and stroke it and sing something very softly.”
“I think I might like that,” he said drowsily.

For some reason she felt sorry for him and didn’t want him to lie awake. So she leaned against the bed and began to stroke and pat his hand, and she sang a very quiet little chanting song in Hindustani.

“That’s nice,” he said, even more drowsily. She went on chanting and stroking, but when she looked at him again, his black lashes were lying close against his cheeks, for his eyes were shut and he was fast asleep. So she got up softly, took her candle, and crept away without making a sound.

chapters.title: A Young Rajah
paragraphs: The moor was hidden in mist when morning came, and the rain was still pouring down. No one could go outside. Martha was so busy that Mary had no chance to talk to her. But in the afternoon Mary asked her to come and sit with her in the nursery. Martha came with the stocking she always knitted whenever she had nothing else to do.
“What’s the matter with you?” she asked as soon as they sat down. “You look like you’ve got something to say.”
“I do. I’ve found out what the crying was,” said Mary.
Martha let her knitting fall into her lap and stared at Mary with startled eyes.
“You haven’t!” she cried. “Never!”
“I heard it in the night,” Mary went on. “I got up and went to find where it came from. It was Colin. I found him.”
Martha’s face turned red with fright.

“Eh! Miss Mary!” she said, almost crying. “You shouldn’t have done it—you shouldn’t! You’ll get me in trouble. I never told you a thing about him—but you’ll get me in trouble all the same. I’ll lose my place, and what will Mother do!”
“You won’t lose your place,” said Mary. “He was glad I came. We talked and talked, and he said he was glad I came.”

“Was he?” cried Martha. “Are you sure? You don’t know what he’s like when something upsets him. He’s a big lad to cry like a baby, but when he’s in a rage he’ll scream on purpose to frighten us. He knows we daren’t call our souls our own.”

“He wasn’t upset,” said Mary. “I asked him if I should go away, and he made me stay. He asked me questions, and I sat on a big footstool and told him about India and the robin and gardens. He wouldn’t let me go. He showed me his mother’s picture. And before I left, I sang him to sleep.”
Martha gasped with amazement.

“I can hardly believe you!” she protested. “It’s as if you’d walked straight into a lion’s den. If he’d been the way he is most times, he’d have thrown one of his tantrums and woken the whole house. He won’t let strangers look at him.”
“He let me look at him. I looked at him the whole time, and he looked at me. We stared!” said Mary.
“I don’t know what to do!” cried Martha, all in a flutter. “If Mrs. Medlock finds out, she’ll think I broke orders and told you, and I’ll be packed back home to Mother.”
“He isn’t going to tell Mrs. Medlock anything about it yet. It’s going to be a sort of secret, just at first,” said Mary firmly. “And he says everyone has to do as he wishes.”
“Aye, that’s true enough—the bad lad!” sighed Martha, wiping her forehead with her apron.
“He says Mrs. Medlock has to, too. And he wants me to come and talk to him every day. And you’re to tell me when he wants me.”
“Me!” said Martha. “I’ll lose my place—I will, for sure!”
“You can’t, if you’re doing what he wants and everyone has been ordered to obey him,” Mary argued.
“Do you mean to say,” cried Martha, her eyes wide open, “that he was nice to you!”
“I think he almost liked me,” Mary answered.
“Then you must have bewitched him!” Martha decided, drawing a long breath.

“Do you mean Magic?” asked Mary. “I’ve heard about Magic in India, but I can’t do it. I just went into his room, and I was so surprised to see him that I stood and stared. Then he turned around and stared at me. He thought I was a ghost or a dream, and I thought maybe he was. It was so strange, being there alone together in the middle of the night, not knowing anything about each other. So we began to ask each other questions. And when I asked him if I should go away, he said I mustn’t.”
“The world’s coming to an end!” gasped Martha.
“What is the matter with him?” asked Mary.

“Nobody knows for sure,” said Martha. “Mr. Craven went half out of his mind the day Colin was born. The doctors thought he’d have to be put in an asylum. It was because Mrs. Craven died, like I told you. He wouldn’t even look at the baby. He just raved and said it would be another hunchback like him, and it would be better off dead.”
“Is Colin a hunchback?” Mary asked. “He didn’t look like one.”

“Not yet,” said Martha. “But he got off to a bad start. Mother said there was enough trouble and raging in that house to set any child wrong. They were afraid his back was weak, and they’ve always been looking after it—keeping him lying down and not letting him walk. Once they made him wear a brace, but he fretted so much it made him really ill. Then a big doctor came to see him and made them take it off. He spoke quite roughly to the other doctor—though in a polite way. He said there’d been too much medicine and too much letting him have his own way.”
“I think he’s a very spoiled boy,” said Mary.

“He’s the worst young rascal that ever lived!” said Martha. “I won’t say he hasn’t been ill a good deal. He’s had coughs and colds that nearly killed him two or three times. Once he had rheumatic fever, and once he had typhoid. Eh! Mrs. Medlock got a fright then. He’d been out of his head, and she was talking to the nurse, thinking he didn’t know anything, and she said, ‘He’ll die this time for sure, and it’s the best thing for him and for everybody.’ Then she looked at him, and there he was with his big eyes open, staring at her as sensibly as she could be herself. She didn’t know what would happen, but he just stared at her and said, ‘Give me some water and stop talking.’”
“Do you think he will die?” asked Mary.

“Mother says there’s no reason a child should live if he gets no fresh air and does nothing but lie on his back reading picture-books and taking medicine. He’s weak, and he hates the bother of being taken outdoors, and he catches cold so easily that he says it makes him ill.”
Mary sat and looked at the fire.
“I wonder,” she said slowly, “if it wouldn’t do him good to go out into a garden and watch things grow. It did me good.”

“One of the worst fits he ever had,” said Martha, “was the time they took him out where the roses are by the fountain. He’d been reading in a newspaper about people getting something called ‘rose cold,’ and he began to sneeze and said he had it. Then a new gardener who didn’t know the rules walked by and looked at him with curiosity. Colin flew into a rage and said the man had looked at him because he was going to be a hunchback. He cried himself into a fever and was ill all night.”
“If he ever gets angry at me, I’ll never go and see him again,” said Mary.
“He’ll send for you if he wants you,” said Martha. “You may as well know that from the start.”
Very soon afterward a bell rang, and Martha rolled up her knitting.
“I expect the nurse wants me to stay with him a bit,” she said. “I hope he’s in a good mood.”
She was out of the room about ten minutes, and then she came back looking puzzled.

“Well, you have bewitched him,” she said. “He’s up on his sofa with his picture-books. He’s told the nurse to stay away until six o’clock. I’m to wait in the next room. The minute she was gone he called me over and said, ‘I want Mary Lennox to come and talk to me, and remember, you’re not to tell anyone.’ You’d better go as fast as you can.”
Mary was quite willing to hurry. She did not want to see Colin as much as she wanted to see Dickon. But she did want to see him very much.

A bright fire was burning on the hearth when she came into his room, and in the daylight she saw that it was a very beautiful room indeed. The rugs, the hangings, the pictures on the walls and the books had rich colors that made the room look warm and comfortable, even with the gray sky and the falling rain outside. Colin looked rather like a picture himself. He was wrapped in a velvet dressing gown and propped against a big brocaded cushion. He had a red spot on each cheek.
“Come in,” he said. “I’ve been thinking about you all morning.”
“I’ve been thinking about you as well,” Mary answered. “You can’t imagine how scared Martha is. She says Mrs. Medlock will decide she told me about you, and then Martha will be sent away.”
He frowned.
“Go and tell her to come here,” he said. “She’s in the next room.”
Mary went and brought her back. Poor Martha was shaking in her shoes. Colin was still frowning.
“Do you have to do what I wish, or don’t you?” he demanded.
“I have to do what you wish, sir,” Martha stammered, turning quite red.
“Does Medlock have to do what I wish?”
“Everybody does, sir,” said Martha.
“Well, then, if I order you to bring Miss Mary to me, how can Medlock send you away if she finds out?”
“Please don’t let her, sir,” pleaded Martha.
“I’ll send _her_ away if she dares to say a word about such a thing,” said Master Craven grandly. “She wouldn’t like that, I can tell you.”
“Thank you, sir,” said Martha, bobbing a curtsy. “I want to do my duty, sir.”
“What I want is for you to do your duty to me,” said Colin, even more grandly. “I’ll take care of you. Now go away.”
When the door closed behind Martha, Colin saw that Mistress Mary was gazing at him as if he had made her wonder about something.
“Why are you looking at me like that?” he asked. “What are you thinking about?”
“I’m thinking about two things.”
“What are they? Sit down and tell me.”

“Here’s the first one,” said Mary, sitting down on the big stool. “Once in India I saw a boy who was a Rajah. He had rubies and emeralds and diamonds stuck all over him. He spoke to his people just the way you spoke to Martha. Everyone had to do whatever he told them—that very minute. I think they’d have been killed if they hadn’t.”
“I’ll make you tell me about Rajahs soon,” he said, “but first tell me what the second thing was.”
“I was thinking,” said Mary, “how different you are from Dickon.”
“Who is Dickon?” he said. “What a strange name!”

She decided she might as well tell him. She thought she could talk about Dickon without mentioning the secret garden. She had liked hearing Martha talk about him. Besides, she longed to talk about him herself. It would seem to bring him closer.

“He’s Martha’s brother. He’s twelve years old,” she explained. “He isn’t like anyone else in the world. He can charm foxes and squirrels and birds, just the way the natives in India charm snakes. He plays a very soft tune on a pipe, and they come and listen.”
There were some big books on a table beside him, and he suddenly dragged one toward him.
“There’s a picture of a snake-charmer in this one,” he exclaimed. “Come and look at it.”
It was a beautiful book with splendid colored illustrations, and he turned to one of them.
“Can he do that?” he asked eagerly.

“He plays his pipe and they listen,” Mary explained. “But he doesn’t call it Magic. He says it’s only that he spends so much time on the moor that he knows how they live. Sometimes, he says, he feels like a bird or a rabbit himself, because he’s so fond of them. I think he asked the robin questions. They seemed to talk to each other in soft little chirps.”
Colin lay back on his cushion. His eyes grew larger and larger, and the spots on his cheeks burned.
“Tell me more about him,” he said.

“Dickon knows everything about eggs and nests,” Mary went on. “He knows where the foxes, badgers and otters have their homes, too, and he keeps those places secret so no other boys will find the holes and scare the animals. Whatever grows or lives on the moor, he knows it.”
“Does he like the moor?” said Colin. “How can he, when it’s such a great, bare, gloomy place?”

“It’s the most beautiful place,” Mary protested. “Thousands of lovely things grow on it, and thousands of little creatures are busy building nests and digging holes and burrows, chirping or singing or squeaking to each other. They’re so busy and having such fun under the earth or in the trees or the heather. It’s their world.”
“How do you know all that?” said Colin, turning on his elbow to look at her.

“I’ve never really been there at all,” said Mary, suddenly remembering. “I only drove across it in the dark. I thought it was hideous. Martha told me about it first, and then Dickon did. When Dickon talks about it, you feel as if you can see and hear everything, as if you’re standing in the heather with the sun shining and the gorse smelling like honey—and everything full of bees and butterflies.”
“You never see anything if you’re ill,” said Colin restlessly. He looked like someone listening to a new sound far away and wondering what it was.
“You can’t, if you stay in a room,” said Mary.
“I couldn’t go out on the moor,” he said in a bitter tone.
Mary was silent for a minute, and then she said something bold.
“You might—sometime.”
He moved as if he had been startled.
“Go out on the moor! How could I? I’m going to die.”
“How do you know?” said Mary, with no sympathy at all. She didn’t like the way he talked about dying. She didn’t feel very sorry for him. She felt, in fact, as if he almost boasted about it.
“Oh, I’ve heard it ever since I can remember,” he answered crossly. “They’re always whispering about it, thinking I don’t notice. They wish I would die, too.”
Mistress Mary felt very contrary. She pressed her lips together.
“If they wished it,” she said, “I wouldn’t. Who wishes you would?”

“The servants do—and Dr. Craven, of course, since he would inherit Misselthwaite and be rich instead of poor. He wouldn’t dare say it, but he always looks cheerful when I’m worse. While I had typhoid fever, his face grew quite plump. I think my father wishes it, too.”
“I don’t believe he does,” said Mary, quite stubbornly.
That made Colin turn and look at her again.
“Don’t you?” he said.
Then he lay back on his cushion and was still, as if he were thinking. There was quite a long silence. Perhaps they were both thinking strange things that children don’t usually think about.
“I like the grand doctor from London, because he made them take the iron brace off,” said Mary at last. “Did he say you were going to die?”
“No.”
“What did he say?”

“He didn’t whisper,” Colin answered. “Maybe he could tell I hate whispering. There was one thing I heard him say out loud: ‘The lad might live if he would make up his mind to it. Put him in the right frame of mind.’ He sounded as if he were angry.”

“I’ll tell you who might put you in the right frame of mind,” said Mary, thinking it over. She felt she would like this question settled one way or the other. “I believe Dickon could. He’s always talking about living things. He never talks about dead things or sick things. He’s always looking up at the sky to watch birds flying—or looking down at the earth to see something growing. He has round blue eyes, and they’re wide open from looking at everything. And he has such a big laugh with his wide mouth—and his cheeks are as red—as red as cherries.”
She pulled her stool nearer to the sofa, and her whole expression changed as she remembered his wide, curving mouth and wide-open eyes.
“Look,” she said. “Let’s not talk about dying. I don’t like it. Let’s talk about living. Let’s talk and talk about Dickon. And then we’ll look at your pictures.”

It was the best thing she could have said. Talking about Dickon meant talking about the moor and the cottage, and the fourteen people who lived in it on sixteen shillings a week—and the children who grew fat on the moor grass, like the wild ponies. It meant talking about Dickon’s mother—and the skipping-rope—and the moor with the sun on it—and the pale green points sticking up out of the black soil. It was all so full of life that Mary talked more than she ever had before—and Colin both talked and listened as he never had before. Soon they both began to laugh over nothing, the way children do when they are happy together. They laughed until they were making as much noise as two ordinary, healthy, natural ten-year-olds—instead of a hard, unloving little girl and a sickly boy who believed he was going to die.

They were having such a good time that they forgot all about the pictures and what time it was. They had been laughing out loud over Ben Weatherstaff and his robin, and Colin was sitting straight up, as though he had forgotten his weak back. Then he suddenly remembered something.
“Do you know, there’s one thing we never once thought of,” he said. “We’re cousins.”

It seemed so strange that they had talked for so long and never remembered such a simple fact that they laughed harder than ever. They were in such a mood that anything could set them off. And right in the middle of the fun, the door opened and in walked Dr. Craven and Mrs. Medlock.
Dr. Craven jumped in real alarm, and Mrs. Medlock nearly stumbled backward, because he had accidentally bumped into her.
“Good Lord!” cried poor Mrs. Medlock, her eyes almost popping out of her head. “Good Lord!”
“What is this?” said Dr. Craven, stepping forward. “What does it mean?”

Mary thought of the boy Rajah again. Colin answered as if the doctor’s alarm and Mrs. Medlock’s terror did not matter in the least. He was no more bothered or frightened than if an old cat and an old dog had wandered into the room.
“This is Mary Lennox, my cousin,” he said. “I invited her to come and talk with me. I like her. She has to come and talk with me any time I send for her.”
Dr. Craven turned to Mrs. Medlock with a look of reproach.
“Oh, sir,” she gasped. “I don’t know how it happened. There isn’t a servant on the place who would dare to talk—they all have their orders.”
“Nobody told her anything,” said Colin. “She heard me crying and found me on her own. I’m glad she came. Don’t be silly, Medlock.”
Mary saw that Dr. Craven did not look pleased, but it was quite clear that he did not dare to go against his patient. He sat down beside Colin and felt his pulse.
“I’m afraid there has been too much excitement. Excitement is not good for you, my boy,” he said.

“I would be excited if she stayed away,” answered Colin, his eyes starting to sparkle in a dangerous way. “I’m better. She makes me better. The nurse must bring her tea up with mine. We will have tea together.”
Mrs. Medlock and Dr. Craven glanced at each other, troubled, but there was clearly nothing they could do.
“He does look a little better, sir,” Mrs. Medlock ventured. “But”—thinking it over—“he looked better this morning, before she came into the room.”

“She came into my room last night and stayed a long while. She sang me a Hindustani song, and it sent me to sleep,” said Colin. “When I woke up I felt better. I was hungry for breakfast. Now I want my tea. Go and tell the nurse, Medlock.”

Dr. Craven did not stay very long. When the nurse came in, he talked to her for a few minutes, and he said a few words of warning to Colin. Colin must not talk too much. He must not forget that he was ill. He must not forget that he got tired very easily. Mary thought there seemed to be a great many unpleasant things he was never supposed to forget.
Colin looked cross and kept his strange, black-lashed eyes fixed on Dr. Craven’s face.
“I _want_ to forget it,” he said at last. “She makes me forget it. That is why I want her.”

Dr. Craven did not look happy as he left the room. He gave a puzzled glance at the little girl sitting on the large stool. She had turned into a stiff, silent child again the moment he came in, and he could not see what the attraction was. Still, the boy really did look brighter—and the doctor sighed rather heavily as he went down the corridor.

“People are always trying to make me eat when I don’t feel like it,” said Colin, as the nurse carried in the tea and put it down on the table beside the sofa. “Now, I’ll eat if you will. Those muffins look so warm and good. Tell me about Rajahs.”

chapters.title: Nest Building
paragraphs: Another week of rain went by, and then the high blue arch of the sky came back, and the sun poured down hot and bright. Mistress Mary had not been able to visit either the secret garden or Dickon, but she had enjoyed herself very much anyway. The week had not felt long. Every day she spent hours with Colin in his room, talking about Rajahs, or gardens, or Dickon and the cottage on the moor. They looked through his splendid books and pictures. Sometimes Mary read aloud to Colin, and sometimes he read a little to her. When he was amused and interested, she thought he hardly looked like an invalid at all. Only his colorless face and the way he was always on the sofa gave it away.

“You were a sly one, listening in the night and climbing out of bed to go hunting for whatever was crying,” Mrs. Medlock said once. “But I can’t say it hasn’t turned out to be a blessing for all of us. He hasn’t had a single tantrum or whining fit since you two became friends. The nurse was ready to give up the case because she was so sick of him, but she says she doesn’t mind staying now that you’ve joined her on duty,” and she laughed a little.

While she talked with Colin, Mary tried hard to be careful about the secret garden. There were things she wanted to find out from him, but she felt she had to learn them without asking direct questions. First, now that she was beginning to like being with him, she wanted to know whether he was the kind of boy who could keep a secret. He was nothing like Dickon, but he was so delighted by the idea of a garden that nobody knew about that she thought he might be trusted. Still, she hadn’t known him long enough to be sure. The second thing she wanted to learn was this. If he could be trusted—if he truly could—might it be possible to take him to the garden without anyone finding out? The grand doctor had said Colin needed fresh air, and Colin had said he wouldn’t mind fresh air in a secret garden. Perhaps if he had plenty of fresh air, and met Dickon and the robin, and saw things growing, he would stop thinking so much about dying. Lately Mary had caught sight of herself in the mirror and realized she looked like a very different creature from the child who had arrived from India. This child looked nicer. Even Martha had noticed the change.

“The air from the moor has done you good already,” Martha had said. “You’re not nearly so yellow, and not nearly so scrawny. Even your hair doesn’t lie flat and slimy on your head. It’s got some life in it now, so it sticks out a bit.”
“It’s like me,” said Mary. “It’s growing stronger and fatter. I’m sure there’s more of it.”
“It looks that way, for sure,” said Martha, ruffling it up around her face. “You’re not half so ugly when it’s like that, and with a bit of red in your cheeks.”
If gardens and fresh air had been good for Mary, perhaps they would be good for Colin too. But then, if he hated people looking at him, maybe he wouldn’t want to see Dickon.
“Why does it make you angry when people look at you?” she asked one day.

“I’ve always hated it,” he answered, “even when I was very little. Then they took me to the seaside, and I would lie in my carriage, and everyone would stare. Ladies would stop and talk to my nurse, and then they would start whispering, and I knew they were saying I wouldn’t live to grow up. Sometimes the ladies would pat my cheeks and say ‘Poor child!’ Once, when a lady did that, I screamed out loud and bit her hand. She was so frightened that she ran away.”
“She thought you had gone mad, like a dog,” said Mary, not sounding admiring at all.
“I don’t care what she thought,” said Colin, frowning.
“I wonder why you didn’t scream and bite me when I came into your room,” said Mary. Then she slowly began to smile.
“I thought you were a ghost or a dream,” he said. “You can’t bite a ghost or a dream, and if you scream at them, they don’t care.”
“Would you hate it if—if a boy looked at you?” Mary asked, not sure how he would take it.
He lay back on his cushion and thought for a moment.
“There’s one boy,” he said very slowly, as if he were weighing every word, “there’s one boy I don’t think I would mind. It’s the boy who knows where the foxes live—Dickon.”
“I’m sure you wouldn’t mind him,” said Mary.
“The birds don’t mind him, and neither do other animals,” he said, still thinking it over. “Maybe that’s why I wouldn’t. He’s a sort of animal charmer, and I’m a boy animal.”
Then he laughed, and she laughed too. In fact they ended up laughing a great deal, because the idea of a boy animal hiding in his hole struck them as very funny indeed.
Afterward, what Mary felt was that she didn’t need to worry about Dickon.

On the first morning that the sky was blue again, Mary woke very early. The sun was pouring in through the blinds in slanting rays, and it looked so joyful that she jumped out of bed and ran to the window. She pulled up the blinds and opened the window itself, and a great wave of fresh, sweet-smelling air blew in on her. The moor was blue, and the whole world looked as if something Magic had happened to it. Tender little fluting sounds came from here and there and everywhere, as if dozens of birds were beginning to tune up for a concert. Mary put her hand out of the window and held it in the sun.
“It’s warm—so warm!” she said. “It will coax the green points to push up and up and up. The bulbs and roots under the ground will work and struggle with all their might.”

She knelt and leaned as far out of the window as she could, breathing deep and sniffing the air. She sniffed until she began to laugh, remembering how Dickon’s mother had said the tip of his nose quivered like a rabbit’s.
“It has to be very early,” she said. “The little clouds are all pink, and the sky has never looked like this before. Nobody is awake. I can’t even hear the stable boys moving about.”
A sudden thought made her scramble to her feet.
“I can’t wait! I’m going to see the garden!”

By now she had learned to dress herself, and she was ready in five minutes. She knew of a small side door that she could unbolt on her own. She flew downstairs in her stocking feet and put her shoes on in the hall. She took off the chain, drew the bolts and turned the lock. When the door was open, she sprang over the step in one bound, and there she stood on the grass, which seemed to have turned green. The sun poured down on her, sweet warm breezes drifted around her, and fluting and twittering and singing came from every bush and tree. She clasped her hands for pure joy and looked up at the sky. It was so blue and pink and pearly and white, and so flooded with springtime light, that she felt she had to flute and sing aloud herself. She knew that thrushes and robins and skylarks could not possibly help it either. She ran around the shrubs and along the paths toward the secret garden.

“It’s all different already,” she said. “The grass is greener, and things are sticking up everywhere. Things are uncurling, and green buds of leaves are showing. I’m sure Dickon will come this afternoon.”

The long warm rain had done strange things to the flower beds that bordered the walk by the lower wall. Shoots were sprouting and pushing out from the roots of the plant clumps. Here and there, among the stems of the crocuses, there were even glimpses of royal purple and yellow unfurling. Six months earlier, Mistress Mary would not have noticed how the world was waking up, but now she missed nothing.

She reached the place where the door hid itself under the ivy, and a strange loud sound startled her. It was the caw—caw of a crow. It came from the top of the wall, and when she looked up, there sat a big, glossy blue-black bird, looking down at her very wisely indeed. She had never seen a crow so close before, and he made her a little nervous. But in the next moment he spread his wings and flapped away across the garden. She hoped he wasn’t going to stay inside, and she pushed the door open, wondering if he would. When she had gone well into the garden, she saw that he probably did mean to stay. He had landed on a dwarf apple tree, and under the apple tree lay a little reddish animal with a Bushy tail. Both of them were watching the stooping body and rust-red head of Dickon, who was kneeling on the grass, working hard.
Mary flew across the grass to him.
“Oh, Dickon! Dickon!” she cried out. “How did you get here so early! How could you! The sun has only just come up!”
He got to his feet, laughing and glowing and tousled, his eyes like a bit of the sky.

“Eh!” he said. “I was up long before him. How could I have stayed in bed! The world’s all begun again this morning, it has. It’s working and humming and scratching and piping and nest-building and breathing out scents, till you’ve got to be out in it instead of lying on your back. When the sun jumped up, the moor went mad for joy. I was right in the middle of the heather, and I ran like mad myself, shouting and singing. And I came straight here. I couldn’t have stayed away. Why, the garden was lying here, waiting!”
Mary put her hands on her chest and panted, as if she had been running herself.
“Oh, Dickon! Dickon!” she said. “I’m so happy I can hardly breathe!”

Seeing him talking to a stranger, the little bushy-tailed animal got up from its place under the tree and came to him. The rook cawed once, flew down from its branch and settled quietly on his shoulder.

“This is the little fox cub,” he said, rubbing the little reddish animal’s head. “His name’s Captain. And this here’s Soot. Soot flew across the moor with me, and Captain ran as if the hounds were after him. They both felt just the same as I did.”
Neither creature looked the least bit afraid of Mary. When Dickon began to walk around, Soot stayed on his shoulder, and Captain trotted quietly close to his side.
“Look here!” said Dickon. “See how these have pushed up, and these, and these! And Eh! Look at these here!”

He threw himself down on his knees, and Mary dropped beside him. They had come upon a whole clump of crocuses that had burst into purple and orange and gold. Mary bent her face down and kissed them again and again.
“You never kiss a person like that,” she said when she lifted her head. “Flowers are so different.”
He looked puzzled, but he smiled.
“Eh!” he said. “I’ve kissed Mother that way many a time, when I come in from the moor after a day of roaming, and she’s standing at the door in the sun, looking so glad and comfortable.”

They ran from one part of the garden to another and found so many wonders that they had to remind themselves to whisper or speak low. He showed her swelling leaf buds on rose branches that had looked dead. He showed her ten thousand new green points pushing up through the soil. They put their eager young noses close to the earth and sniffed its warm springtime breath. They dug and pulled and laughed low with delight, until Mistress Mary’s hair was as tumbled as Dickon’s and her cheeks were almost as poppy-red as his.

There was every joy on earth in the secret garden that morning. In the midst of them came a delight more delightful than all the rest, because it was more wonderful. Something swiftly flew across the wall and darted through the trees to a thickly grown corner. It was a little flare of a red-breasted bird with something hanging from its beak. Dickon stood quite still and put his hand on Mary, almost as if they had suddenly found themselves laughing in a church.

“We mustn’t stir,” he whispered in broad Yorkshire. “We mustn’t hardly breathe. I knew he was hunting for a mate when I saw him last. It’s Ben Weatherstaff’s robin. He’s building his nest. He’ll stay here if we don’t frighten him.”
They settled down softly on the grass and sat there without moving.

“We mustn’t seem to be watching him too close,” said Dickon. “He’d be cross with us for good if he got the notion we were interfering now. He’ll be a good bit different till all this is over. He’s setting up housekeeping. He’ll be shyer and quicker to take things badly. He’s got no time for visiting and gossiping. We must keep still a bit and try to look like grass and trees and bushes. Then, when he’s got used to seeing us, I’ll chirp a bit, and he’ll know we won’t be in his way.”

Mistress Mary was not at all sure she knew how to look like grass and trees and bushes, the way Dickon seemed to. But he had said the odd thing as if it were the simplest and most natural thing in the world. She felt it must be quite easy for him. In fact, she watched him carefully for a few minutes, wondering whether he could quietly turn green and put out branches and leaves. But he only sat wonderfully still. When he spoke, he dropped his voice so softly that it was strange she could hear him, but she could.

“It’s part of the springtime, this nest-building is,” he said. “I’d wager it’s gone on the same way every year since the world began. They’ve got their own way of thinking and doing things, and a body had better not meddle. You can lose a friend in springtime easier than in any other season, if you’re too curious.”
“If we talk about him, I can’t help looking at him,” Mary said, as softly as she could. “We must talk about something else. There’s something I want to tell you.”
“He’ll like it better if we talk of something else,” said Dickon. “What is it you’ve got to tell me?”
“Well—do you know about Colin?” she whispered.
He turned his head to look at her.
“What do you know about him?” he asked.
“I’ve seen him. I’ve gone to talk with him every day this week. He wants me to visit. He says I’m helping him forget he’s ill and dying,” answered Mary.
As soon as the surprise faded from his round face, Dickon looked truly relieved.
“I’m glad of that,” he exclaimed. “I’m right down glad. It makes me easier. I knew I mustn’t say anything about him, and I don’t like having to hide things.”
“Don’t you like hiding the garden?” said Mary.

“I’ll never tell about it,” he answered. “But I said to Mother, ‘Mother,’ I said, ‘I’ve got a secret to keep. It’s not a bad one, you know that. It’s no worse than hiding where a bird’s nest is. You don’t mind it, do you?’”
Mary always wanted to hear about his mother.
“What did she say?” she asked, not at all afraid to hear.
Dickon grinned good-naturedly.
“It was just like her, what she said,” he answered. “She gave my head a bit of a rub and laughed, and she said, ‘Eh, lad, you can have all the secrets you like. I’ve known you twelve years.’”
“How did you know about Colin?” asked Mary.

“Everybody who knew about Mr. Craven knew there was a little lad who was likely to be a cripple, and they knew Mr. Craven didn’t like him talked about. Folks are sorry for Mr. Craven because Mrs. Craven was such a pretty young lady and they were so fond of each other. Mrs. Medlock stops at our cottage whenever she goes to Thwaite, and she doesn’t mind talking to Mother in front of us children, because she knows we’ve been brought up to be trustworthy. How did you find out about him? Martha was in fine trouble the last time she came home. She said you’d heard him fretting and you were asking questions, and she didn’t know what to say.”

Mary told him her story. She told about the wind wuthering at midnight, which had woken her, and the faint, far-off sounds of the complaining voice, which had led her down the dark corridors with her candle. She told how it had ended with her opening the door of the dimly lit room, with the carved four-posted bed in the corner. When she described the small ivory-white face and the strange black-rimmed eyes, Dickon shook his head.

“They’re just like his mother’s eyes, only hers were always laughing, so they say,” he said. “They say Mr. Craven can’t bear to look at him when he’s awake. It’s because his eyes are so like his mother’s, and yet they look so different in his miserable little face.”
“Do you think he wants to die?” Mary whispered.

“No, but he wishes he’d never been born. Mother says that’s the worst thing on earth for a child. Those who aren’t wanted hardly ever thrive. Mr. Craven would buy anything money could buy for the poor lad, but he’d like to forget he’s even alive. For one thing, he’s afraid he’ll look at him some day and find he’s grown a hunchback.”
“Colin is so afraid of it himself that he won’t sit up,” said Mary. “He says he’s always thinking that if he felt a lump coming, he’d go crazy and scream himself to death.”
“Eh! He shouldn’t lie there thinking things like that,” said Dickon. “No lad could get well while he thinks that sort of thing.”

The fox was lying on the grass close beside him, looking up now and then to ask for a pat. Dickon bent down and rubbed its neck gently, and he thought for a few minutes in silence. Then he lifted his head and looked around the garden.
“When we first got in here,” he said, “everything seemed gray. Look around now and tell me if you don’t see a difference.”
Mary looked, and her breath caught a little.
“Why!” she cried. “The gray wall is changing. It’s as if a green mist were creeping over it. It’s almost like a green gauze veil.”
“Aye,” said Dickon. “And it’ll get greener and greener until the gray is all gone. Can you guess what I was thinking?”
“I know it was something nice,” said Mary eagerly. “I think it was something about Colin.”

“I was thinking that if he was out here, he wouldn’t be watching for lumps to grow on his back. He’d be watching for buds to break on the rose-bushes, and he’d likely be healthier,” Dickon explained. “I was wondering if we could ever get him in the mood to come out here and lie under the trees in his carriage.”

“I’ve been wondering about that too. It crosses my mind almost every time I talk with him,” said Mary. “Could he keep a secret? Could we bring him here without anyone seeing? I thought maybe you could push his carriage. The doctor ordered fresh air for him, so if he asks us to take him outside, nobody will dare say no. He won’t go out with other people, and they may even be glad if he goes with us. He could tell the gardeners to stay away, and then they’d never find out.”
Dickon was thinking very hard as he scratched Captain’s back.

“It’d be good for him, I’ll warrant,” he said. “We’d not be thinking he’d be better off never born. We’d be just two children watching a garden grow, and he’d be another. Two lads and a little lass just looking on at the springtime. I warrant it’d be better than doctor’s medicine.”

“He’s spent so long lying in his room, always terrified about his back, that it’s made him odd,” said Mary. “He’s learned plenty from books, but nothing else. He says he’s been too sick to notice anything around him. He hates going outside, and he hates gardens and gardeners. Still, he likes hearing about this garden, because it’s a secret. I didn’t dare tell him much, but he told me he wanted to see it.”

“We’ll have him out here sometime, for sure,” said Dickon. “I could push his carriage well enough. Have you noticed how the robin and his mate have been working while we’ve been sitting here? Look at him perched on that branch, wondering where it’d be best to put the twig in his beak.”

He whistled one of his low calls. The robin turned his head and gave him a questioning look, his twig still in his beak. Dickon talked to him much as Ben Weatherstaff did, but his tone was friendly advice.
“Wherever you put it,” he said, “it’ll be all right. You knew how to build your nest before you came out of the egg. Get on with it, lad. You’ve got no time to lose.”

“Oh, I do like to hear you talk to him!” Mary said, laughing with delight. “Ben Weatherstaff scolds him and teases him, and he hops about and looks as if he understands every word, and I know he likes it. Ben Weatherstaff says he’s so conceited that he’d rather have stones thrown at him than not be noticed.”
Dickon laughed too and kept on talking.
“You know we won’t trouble you,” he said to the robin. “We’re nearly wild things ourselves. We’re building a nest too, bless you. Mind you don’t tell on us.”

The robin did not answer, because his beak was full. But when he flew off with his twig to his own corner of the garden, Mary knew that the darkness of his dew-bright eye meant he would not tell their secret for the world.

chapters.title: “I Won’t!” Said Mary
paragraphs: There was so much to do in the garden that morning that Mary got back to the house late. She was in such a rush to return to her work that she forgot all about Colin until the very last minute.
“Tell Colin I can’t come to see him yet,” she said to Martha. “I’m very busy in the garden.”
Martha looked rather scared.
“Eh! Miss Mary,” she said, “it might put him in a terrible mood when I tell him that.”
But Mary was not as afraid of him as other people were, and she was not the kind of person who gave things up for others.
“I can’t stay,” she answered. “Dickon’s waiting for me.” And she ran off.

The afternoon was even lovelier and busier than the morning. Almost all the weeds were already cleared out of the garden, and most of the roses and trees had been trimmed or had the soil loosened around them. Dickon had brought a spade of his own and had taught Mary how to use all her tools. By now it was clear that the lovely, wild place would never become a neat “gardener’s garden,” but that it would be a wilderness full of growing things before spring was over.

“There’ll be apple blossoms and cherry blossoms overhead,” Dickon said, working away with all his strength. “And there’ll be peach and plum trees in bloom against the walls, and the grass’ll be a carpet of flowers.”

The little fox and the rook were as happy and busy as the children were, and the robin and his mate darted back and forth like tiny streaks of lightning. Sometimes the rook spread his black wings and sailed off over the treetops in the park. Each time he came back, he settled near Dickon and cawed a few times, as if he were telling about his adventures, and Dickon talked to him just as he had talked to the robin. Once, when Dickon was so busy that he did not answer right away, Soot flew onto his shoulder and gently pinched his ear with his big beak. When Mary wanted to rest for a while, Dickon sat down with her under a tree. Once he pulled his pipe out of his pocket and played its soft, strange little notes, and two squirrels appeared on the wall to look and listen.
“You’re a good bit stronger than you were,” Dickon said, watching her dig. “You’re starting to look different, for sure.”
Mary was glowing from the exercise and in high spirits.
“I’m getting fatter every day,” she said, quite triumphantly. “Mrs. Medlock will have to get me some bigger dresses. Martha says my hair is growing thicker. It isn’t so flat and stringy anymore.”
The sun was starting to set, sending deep golden rays slanting in under the trees, when they said goodbye.
“It’ll be fine tomorrow,” said Dickon. “I’ll be working by sunrise.”
“So will I,” said Mary.

She ran back to the house as fast as her feet could carry her. She wanted to tell Colin about Dickon’s fox cub and the rook, and about everything spring had been doing. She felt sure he would like to hear it. So it was not very pleasant, when she opened the door of her room, to find Martha standing there waiting for her with a gloomy face.
“What is the matter?” she asked. “What did Colin say when you told him I couldn’t come?”
“Eh!” said Martha, “I wish you’d gone. He nearly threw one of his tantrums. There’s been a fine fuss all afternoon just to keep him quiet. He kept watching the clock the whole time.”

Mary’s lips pressed tightly together. She was no more used to thinking about other people than Colin was, and she saw no reason why a bad-tempered boy should get in the way of the thing she liked best. She knew nothing about how sad it is for people who have been sick and nervous, and who don’t realize they can control their tempers and need not make everyone else sick and nervous too. When she had had a headache in India, she had done her best to make sure everybody else had a headache, or something just as bad. She felt she had been perfectly right to do so, but of course now she felt that Colin was completely wrong.

His sofa was empty when she walked into his room. He lay flat on his back in bed and kept his face turned away as she entered. That was a poor beginning, and Mary stalked over to his bedside, stiff and cold.
“Why didn’t you get up?” she said.

“I did get up this morning, when I thought you were coming,” he answered, without looking at her. “This afternoon I made them put me back in bed. My back hurt and my head hurt and I was tired. Why didn’t you come?”
“I was working in the garden with Dickon,” said Mary.
Colin frowned, then graciously agreed to look at her.
“I won’t let that boy come here if you go off and stay with him instead of coming to talk to me,” he said.
Mary flew into a terrible rage. She could get angry without making any noise at all. She just turned sour and stubborn and stopped caring what happened.
“If you send Dickon away, I’ll never come into this room again!” she shot back.
“You’ll have to, if I want you,” said Colin.
“I won’t!” said Mary.
“I’ll make you,” said Colin. “They’ll drag you in.”

“Will they, Mr. Rajah!” said Mary fiercely. “They can drag me in, but they can’t make me talk once they get me here. I’ll sit with my teeth clenched and never tell you one thing. I won’t even look at you. I’ll stare at the floor!”

What a lovely, agreeable pair they made as they glared at each other. If they had been two little boys from the street, they would have leaped at each other and had a rough-and-tumble fight. As it was, they did the next best thing.
“You are a selfish thing!” cried Colin.
“And what are you?” said Mary. “Selfish people always say that. To them, anyone who won’t do what they want is selfish. You’re worse than I am. You’re the most selfish boy I’ve ever seen.”
“I am not!” snapped Colin. “I’m not as selfish as your precious Dickon is! He keeps you playing in the dirt when he knows I’m all alone. He’s selfish, if you ask me!”
Mary’s eyes flashed with fury.
“He’s the nicest boy who ever lived!” she said. “He’s—he’s like an angel!” That might sound rather silly, but she did not care one bit.
“Some angel!” Colin sneered savagely. “He’s a common cottage boy from the moor!”
“He’s better than a common Rajah!” Mary shot back. “He’s a thousand times better!”

Because she was the stronger of the two, she was starting to get the better of him. The truth was that he had never had a fight with anyone like himself in his whole life. On the whole, it was rather good for him, though neither he nor Mary knew it. He turned his head on his pillow and shut his eyes, and a big tear squeezed out and rolled down his cheek. He was starting to feel pitiful and sorry for himself—and for no one else.
“I’m not as selfish as you, because I’m always sick, and I’m sure there’s a lump coming on my back,” he said. “And I’m going to die, besides.”
“You are not!” Mary contradicted him, without a bit of sympathy.
He opened his eyes wide with outrage. He had never heard anyone say such a thing before. He was furious and a little bit pleased all at once, if a person can be both at the same time.
“I’m not?” he cried. “I am! You know I am! Everybody says so.”

“Well, I don’t believe it!” said Mary bitterly. “You only say so to make people feel sorry for you. I think you’re proud of it. I just don’t believe it! Maybe it would be true if you were a nice boy—but you’re far too nasty!”
Despite his sickly back, Colin sat straight up in bed in a perfectly healthy rage.

“Get out of this room!” he shouted, and he grabbed his pillow and threw it at her. He was not strong enough to throw it far, and it only dropped at her feet, but Mary’s face looked as tight and sharp as a nutcracker.
“I’m going,” she said. “And I won’t come back!”
She walked to the door, and when she got there she turned around and spoke again.
“I had so many nice things to tell you,” she said. “Dickon brought along his fox and his rook, and I meant to tell you everything about them. Well, now you won’t hear a single word!”

She marched out the door and shut it behind her. There, to her great surprise, she found the trained nurse standing as if she had been listening, and, even more amazing, she was laughing. She was a big, handsome young woman who should never have been a trained nurse at all, since she could not stand sick people. She was always finding excuses to leave Colin to Martha or to anyone else who would take her place. Mary had never liked her. She just stood and stared up at her as the nurse stood giggling into her handkerchief.
“What are you laughing at?” she asked her.

“At you two youngsters,” said the nurse. “It’s the best thing that could happen to that sickly, pampered boy, to have someone stand up to him who’s as spoiled as he is.” And she laughed into her handkerchief again. “If he’d had a spitfire of a little sister to fight with, it would have been the saving of him.”
“Is he going to die?”
“I don’t know and I don’t care,” said the nurse. “Hysterics and temper are half of what ails him.”
“What are hysterics?” asked Mary.
“You’ll find out if you work him into another tantrum after this. But anyway, you’ve given him something to have hysterics about, and I’m glad of it.”

Mary went back to her room feeling nothing like the way she had felt when she came in from the garden. She was cross and disappointed, but not the least bit sorry for Colin.
