She had been looking forward to telling him many things, and she had meant to try to decide whether it would be safe to trust him with the great secret. She had been starting to think it would be, but now she had changed her mind completely. She would never tell him, and he could stay in his room and never get any fresh air and die if he liked! It would serve him right! She felt so sour and unforgiving that for a few minutes she almost forgot about Dickon, and the green veil creeping over the world, and the soft wind blowing down from the moor.

Martha was waiting for her, and the trouble on her face had been replaced, for the moment, by interest and curiosity. A wooden box sat on the table. Its lid had been taken off, and inside it was full of neat packages.
“Mr. Craven sent it to you,” said Martha. “It looks like it has picture books in it.”

Mary remembered what he had asked her the day she went to his room. “Do you want anything—dolls—toys—books?” She opened a package, wondering whether he had sent a doll, and wondering what she would do with it if he had. But he had not sent one. There were several beautiful books like the ones Colin had, and two of them were about gardens and full of pictures. There were two or three games, and there was a beautiful little writing case with a gold monogram on it, along with a gold pen and an inkstand.
The gifts were all so lovely that her delight began to crowd the anger out of her head. She had never expected him to remember her at all, and her stubborn little heart warmed up.
“I can write better than I can print,” she said, “and the first thing I’ll write with that pen will be a letter to tell him I’m very grateful.”

If she had been friends with Colin, she would have run straight to show him her presents. They would have looked at the pictures, read some of the gardening books, and maybe tried the games. He would have enjoyed himself so much that he would never once have thought about dying, or put his hand on his spine to feel for a lump. He had a habit of doing that, and she could not stand it. It gave her an uncomfortable, frightened feeling, because he always looked so frightened himself. He said that if he ever felt even a small lump, he would know his hunch had begun to grow. He had gotten the idea from something he had heard Mrs. Medlock whispering to the nurse, and he had thought about it in secret until it was firmly fixed in his mind. Mrs. Medlock had said that his father’s back had started to show its crookedness that way when he was a child. Colin had never told anyone but Mary that most of his “tantrums,” as people called them, grew out of this hidden, hysterical fear. Mary had felt sorry for him when he told her.
“He always starts thinking about it when he’s cross or tired,” she said to herself. “And he’s been cross today. Maybe—maybe he’s been thinking about it all afternoon.”
She stood still, looking down at the carpet and thinking.

“I said I would never go back again—” she hesitated, knitting her brows—“but maybe, just maybe, I’ll go and see him—if he wants me—in the morning. Maybe he’ll try to throw his pillow at me again, but—I think—I’ll go.”

chapters.title: A Tantrum
paragraphs: She had gotten up very early that morning and worked hard in the garden, so she was tired and sleepy. As soon as Martha had brought her supper and she had eaten it, she was glad to go to bed. As she laid her head on the pillow, she murmured to herself:
“I’ll go out before breakfast and work with Dickon, and then afterward—I think—I’ll go and see him.”

She thought it was the middle of the night when she was woken by such dreadful sounds that she leaped out of bed at once. What was it? What was it? A moment later she felt sure she knew. Doors were opening and slamming, feet were hurrying along the corridors, and someone was crying and screaming at the same time, in a horrible way.
“It’s Colin,” she said. “He’s having one of those tantrums the nurse called hysterics. It sounds awful.”

As she listened to the sobbing screams, she was not surprised that people were so frightened they would give him his own way in everything rather than hear them. She clapped her hands over her ears and felt sick and shaky.
“I don’t know what to do. I don’t know what to do,” she kept saying. “I can’t stand it.”

For a moment she wondered whether he would stop if she dared to go to him. Then she remembered how he had thrown her out of the room, and thought that seeing her might only make him worse. She pressed her hands even harder over her ears, but she could not shut out the awful sounds. She hated them so much, and they frightened her so badly, that suddenly they started to make her angry. She felt she would like to throw a tantrum herself and frighten him the way he was frightening her. She was not used to anyone’s temper but her own. She took her hands from her ears, sprang up, and stamped her foot.
“Somebody ought to stop him! Somebody ought to make him stop! Somebody ought to give him a good beating!” she cried out.
Just then she heard footsteps almost running down the corridor, and her door opened and the nurse came in. She was certainly not laughing now. She even looked rather pale.
“He’s worked himself into hysterics,” she said in a great hurry. “He’ll make himself ill. No one can do anything with him. Come and try, there’s a good girl. He likes you.”
“He threw me out of his room this morning,” said Mary, stamping her foot in her excitement.
That stamp pleased the nurse quite a bit. She had been afraid of finding Mary in tears, hiding under the blankets with her head covered.
“That’s the spirit,” she said. “You’re in just the right mood. Go and scold him. Give him something new to think about. Please go, child, as fast as you can.”

Only afterward did Mary realize that the whole thing had been funny as well as dreadful. It was funny that all the grown-ups were so frightened that they came to a little girl, just because they guessed she was almost as bad as Colin himself.

She flew along the corridor, and the closer she got to the screams, the angrier she became. By the time she reached the door she felt downright wicked. She slapped the door open with her hand and ran across the room to the four-poster bed.

“Stop it!” she almost shouted. “Stop it! I hate you! Everybody hates you! I wish everybody would run out of the house and leave you to scream yourself to death! You _will_ scream yourself to death in a minute, and I wish you would!”

A nice, kind child could never have thought of such things, let alone said them. But it happened that the shock of hearing them was the best possible thing for this hysterical boy, whom no one had ever dared to hold back or contradict.

He had been lying on his face, beating his pillow with his hands. At the sound of that furious little voice he turned so fast that he almost jumped around. His face looked dreadful, white and red and swollen, and he was gasping and choking. But fierce little Mary did not care one bit.
“If you scream one more scream,” she said, “I’ll scream too—and I can scream louder than you can, and I’ll frighten you. I’ll frighten you!”
He had actually stopped screaming, because she had startled him so much. The scream that had been rising in him almost choked him. Tears streamed down his face, and he shook all over.
“I can’t stop!” he gasped and sobbed. “I can’t—I can’t!”
“You can!” shouted Mary. “Half of what’s wrong with you is hysterics and temper—just hysterics—hysterics—hysterics!” And she stamped her foot each time she said it.

“I felt the lump—I felt it,” Colin choked out. “I knew I would. I’ll get a hunch on my back and then I’ll die.” He began to writhe again, turned over onto his face, and sobbed and wailed, but he did not scream.

“You did not!” Mary shot back fiercely. “If you felt anything, it was only a hysterical lump, because hysterics makes lumps. Your horrid back is perfectly fine. The only thing wrong is hysterics! Now turn over and let me look at it!”
She liked the word “hysterics” and somehow felt that it had an effect on him. He had probably never heard it before, just as she hadn’t.
“Nurse,” she ordered, “come here and show me his back this minute!”

Near the door stood the nurse, Mrs. Medlock and Martha, huddled close together and staring at Mary with their mouths hanging half open. More than once, all three had gasped in fear. Now the nurse stepped forward as though she were nervous. Colin was shaking with great, breathless sobs.
“Perhaps he—he won’t let me,” she said hesitantly, in a low voice.
Colin heard her, though, and gasped out between two sobs:
“Sh-show her! She-she’ll see then!”

It was a poor, thin back to look at once it was bared. Every rib could be counted, and every joint of the spine. Mistress Mary did not count them, though, as she bent over and studied them with a solemn, fierce little face. She looked so sour and so oddly grown-up that the nurse turned her head aside to hide the twitching of her mouth. There was a full minute of silence. Even Colin tried to hold his breath while Mary looked up and down his spine, and down and up again, as carefully as if she were the great doctor from London.

“There’s not a single lump there!” she said at last. “There’s not a lump as big as a pin—except backbone lumps, and you can only feel those because you’re thin. I have backbone lumps myself. They used to stick out just as much as yours do, until I started to get fatter, and I’m still not fat enough to hide them. There’s not a lump as big as a pin! If you ever say there is again, I’ll laugh!”

No one but Colin himself knew what effect those crossly spoken, childish words had on him. Suppose he had ever had anyone to talk to about his secret terrors. Suppose he had ever dared to let himself ask questions. Suppose he had had friends his own age, instead of lying on his back in the huge, closed-up house, breathing air heavy with the fears of people who were mostly ignorant and tired of him. Then he would have found out that most of his fright and illness was made by himself. But he had lain there thinking about himself and his aches and weariness for hours and days and months and years. And now an angry, unsympathetic little girl stubbornly insisted that he was not as sick as he thought he was, and he actually felt as if she might be telling the truth.

“I had no idea,” the nurse ventured, “that he believed there was a lump on his spine. His back is weak only because he refuses to try sitting up. I could have told him there was nothing there.” Colin gulped and turned his face a little to look at her.
“C-could you?” he said pitifully.
“Yes, sir.”
“There!” said Mary, and she gulped too.

Colin turned onto his face again. His long, broken breaths were the last of his storm of sobbing, and he lay still for a minute, though great tears streamed down his face and wet the pillow. Those tears actually meant that a strange, great relief had come over him. After a while he turned and looked at the nurse again, and oddly enough, he did not sound at all like a Rajah as he spoke to her.
“Do you think—I could—live to grow up?” he said.
The nurse was neither clever nor soft-hearted, but she could repeat some of what the London doctor had said.
“You probably will, if you do what you’re told, don’t give in to your temper, and spend a great deal of time out in the fresh air.”

Colin’s tantrum had passed, and he was weak and worn out from crying, which perhaps made him feel gentle. He held out his hand a little toward Mary. I am glad to say that her own tantrum had passed too, and she was softened as well. She met him halfway with her hand, so that it was a kind of making up.

“I’ll—I’ll go outside with you, Mary,” he said. “Fresh air won’t be so bad if we can find—” He remembered just in time and stopped himself before saying “if we can find the secret garden.” Instead he finished, “I’d like to go out with you, as long as Dickon comes to push my chair. I want so much to see Dickon and the fox and the crow.”

The nurse remade the tumbled bed and shook out and straightened the pillows. Then she made Colin a cup of beef tea and gave a cup to Mary, who was truly glad to have it after all her excitement. Mrs. Medlock and Martha were happy to slip away. Once everything was neat and calm and in order, the nurse looked as if she would be very happy to slip away too. She was a healthy young woman who resented being robbed of her sleep. She yawned quite openly as she looked at Mary, who had pushed her big footstool close to the four-poster bed and was holding Colin’s hand.
“You must go back to bed and get some sleep,” she said. “He’ll doze off soon, as long as he doesn’t get upset again. I’ll go and lie down in the next room.”
“Would you like me to sing you the song I learned from my Ayah?” Mary whispered to Colin.
His hand gently tugged hers, and he turned his tired eyes on her, pleading.
“Oh, yes!” he answered. “It’s such a soft song. I’ll be asleep in a minute.”
“I’ll put him to sleep,” Mary said to the yawning nurse. “You can go if you like.”
“Well,” said the nurse, pretending to be reluctant. “If he isn’t asleep in half an hour, you must call me.”
“Very well,” answered Mary.
The nurse was out of the room in a minute, and as soon as she had gone, Colin pulled on Mary’s hand again.

“I nearly told,” he said, “but I caught myself in time. I won’t talk, and I’ll go to sleep. But you said you had lots of nice things to tell me. Have you—do you think you’ve found out anything at all about the way into the secret garden?”
Mary looked at his poor little tired face and swollen eyes, and her heart softened.
“Ye-es,” she answered, “I think I have. And if you go to sleep, I’ll tell you tomorrow.” His hand actually trembled.

“Oh, Mary!” he said. “Oh, Mary! If I could get into it, I think I would live to grow up! Do you think that instead of singing the Ayah song, you could just tell me softly, as you did that first day, what you imagine it looks like inside? I’m sure it will make me go to sleep.”
“Yes,” answered Mary. “Shut your eyes.”
He closed his eyes and lay perfectly still. She held his hand and began to speak, very slowly and in a very low voice.

“I think it has been left alone for so long that it has all grown into a lovely tangle. I think the roses have climbed and climbed until they hang down from the branches and walls and trail across the ground—almost like a strange gray mist. Some have died, but many are alive, and when summer comes there will be curtains and fountains of roses. I think the ground is full of daffodils and snowdrops and lilies and irises, pushing their way up out of the dark. Now that spring has begun—perhaps—perhaps—”
The soft drone of her voice was making him stiller and stiller, and she saw it and went on.

“Perhaps they are pushing up through the grass—perhaps there are clumps of purple crocuses and golden ones—even now. Perhaps the leaves are starting to burst open and unfurl—and perhaps—the gray is turning, and a green gauze veil is creeping—and creeping across—everything. And the birds are coming to look at it—because it is—so safe and quiet. And perhaps—perhaps—perhaps—” very softly and slowly indeed, “the robin has found a mate—and is building a nest.”
And Colin was asleep.

chapters.title: “Tha’ Munnot Waste No Time”
paragraphs: Naturally, Mary did not wake early the next morning. She slept late because she was tired. When Martha brought her breakfast, she said that Colin was quiet now, but he was sick and feverish, as he always was after wearing himself out with a fit of crying. Mary ate her breakfast slowly and listened.

“He says he wishes you would please go and see him as soon as you can,” Martha said. “It’s strange what a fancy he’s taken to you. You gave it to him good last night, for sure, didn’t you? Nobody else would have dared. Eh! Poor lad! He’s been spoiled past all saving. Mother says the two worst things that can happen to a child are never getting his own way, or always getting it. She can’t say which is worse. You were in a fine temper yourself, too. But when I went into his room, he said to me, ‘Please ask Miss Mary if she’ll please come and talk to me?’ Think of him saying please! Will you go, Miss?”
“I’ll run and find Dickon first,” said Mary. “No, wait. I’ll see Colin first and tell him—yes, I know just what I’ll tell him!” she added, struck by a sudden idea.
She still had her hat on when she came into Colin’s room, and for a second he looked disappointed. He was in bed. His face was pitifully white, and there were dark circles around his eyes.
“I’m glad you came,” he said. “My head aches and I ache all over, because I’m so tired. Are you going somewhere?”
Mary went over and leaned against his bed.
“I won’t be long,” she said. “I’m going to Dickon, but I’ll come back. Colin, it’s—it’s something about the garden.”
His whole face brightened, and a little color came into it.

“Oh! Is it?” he cried. “I dreamed about it the whole night long. I heard you say something about gray turning to green. Then I dreamed I stood in a place crowded with shivering little green leaves, with birds sitting on nests all around, looking so soft and quiet. I’ll lie here and think about it until you’re back.”
Five minutes later Mary was with Dickon in their garden. The fox and the crow were with him again, and this time he had brought two tame squirrels too.
“I came over on the pony this morning,” he said. “Eh! He’s a good little fellow—Jump is! I brought these two in my pockets. This one here is called Nut, and this other one is called Shell.”
When he said “Nut,” one squirrel leaped onto his right shoulder, and when he said “Shell,” the other leaped onto his left shoulder.

They sat down on the grass with Captain curled up at their feet, Soot listening solemnly from a tree, and Nut and Shell nosing around close by. To Mary it seemed almost too hard to leave such delight. But when she began to tell her story, the look on Dickon’s funny face slowly changed her mind. She could see he felt sorrier for Colin than she did. He looked up at the sky and all around him.

“Just listen to those birds—the world seems full of them—all whistling and piping,” he said. “Look at them darting about, and hark at them calling to each other. When springtime comes, it seems as if the whole world’s calling. The leaves are uncurling so you can see them—and, my word, the nice smells there are!” he said, sniffing with his happy turned-up nose. “And that poor lad lying shut up and seeing so little that he gets to thinking of things that set him screaming. Eh! My! We must get him out here—we must get him watching and listening and sniffing the air, and get him just soaked through with sunshine. And we must not lose any time about it.”

When he was very interested, he often spoke in a broad Yorkshire accent, though at other times he tried to soften his speech so that Mary could understand him better. But she loved his broad Yorkshire. In fact, she had been trying to learn to speak it herself. So she tried a little now.

“Aye, that we must,” she said (which meant “Yes, indeed, we must”). “I’ll tell you what we’ll do first,” she went on. Dickon grinned, because it amused him very much when the little lass tried to twist her tongue around Yorkshire. “He’s taken a grand fancy to you. He wants to see you, and he wants to see Soot and Captain. When I go back to the house to talk to him, I’ll ask him if you can come and see him tomorrow morning, and bring your creatures with you. Then, in a bit, when there are more leaves out, and maybe a bud or two, we’ll get him to come outside. You shall push him in his chair, and we’ll bring him here and show him everything.”
When she stopped, she was quite proud of herself. She had never made a long speech in Yorkshire before, and she had remembered it very well.

“You must talk a bit of Yorkshire like that to Master Colin,” Dickon chuckled. “You’ll make him laugh, and there’s nothing as good for sick folk as laughing. Mother says she believes half an hour of a good laugh every morning would cure a fellow who was getting ready to come down with typhus fever.”
“I’m going to talk Yorkshire to him this very day,” said Mary, chuckling herself.

The garden had reached the time when it seemed that every day and every night, Magicians passed through it with wands, drawing loveliness out of the earth and the branches. It was hard to go away and leave it all, especially since Nut had actually crept onto her dress. Shell had scrambled down the trunk of the apple tree they sat under and stayed there, looking at her with curious eyes. But she went back to the house, and when she sat down close to Colin’s bed, he began to sniff the way Dickon did, though not so skillfully.
“You smell like flowers and—and fresh things,” he cried, quite delighted. “What is it that you smell of? Somehow it’s cool and warm and sweet, all at once.”

“It’s the wind from the moor,” said Mary. “It comes from sitting on the grass under a tree with Dickon and Captain and Soot and Nut and Shell. It’s the springtime and the outdoors and the sunshine that smell so grand.”
She said it as broadly as she could. You don’t know how broad Yorkshire sounds until you have heard someone speak it. Colin began to laugh.
“What are you doing?” he said. “I never heard you talk like that before. How funny it sounds.”

“I’m giving you a bit of Yorkshire,” Mary answered triumphantly. “I can’t talk as grandly as Dickon and Martha can, but you see I can manage a bit. Don’t you understand a bit of Yorkshire when you hear it? And you a Yorkshire lad yourself, born and bred! Eh! I wonder you’re not ashamed of your face.”

And then she began to laugh too, and they both laughed until they couldn’t stop. They laughed until the room echoed, and Mrs. Medlock, who was opening the door to come in, drew back into the corridor and stood there listening, amazed.

“Well, upon my word!” she said. Because no one was there to hear her, and she was so astonished, she spoke rather broad Yorkshire herself. “Whoever heard the like! Whoever on earth would have thought it!”

There was so much to talk about. Colin seemed unable to hear enough about Dickon and Captain and Soot and Nut and Shell and the pony named Jump. Mary had run around into the wood with Dickon to see Jump. He was a tiny, shaggy moor pony with thick locks hanging over his eyes, a pretty face, and a soft velvet nose that nuzzled. He was rather thin from living on moor grass, but he was as tough and wiry as if the muscles in his little legs were made of steel springs. The moment he saw Dickon, he had lifted his head and whinnied softly. Then he had trotted up and laid his head across Dickon’s shoulder, and Dickon had talked into his ear, and Jump had talked back in odd little whinnies and puffs and snorts. Dickon had made him give Mary his small front hoof and kiss her on the cheek with his velvet muzzle.
“Does he really understand everything Dickon says?” Colin asked.
“It does seem so,” Mary answered. “Dickon says any creature will understand you if you’re truly friends with it. But you have to be truly friends.”
Colin lay quiet for a little while, and his strange gray eyes seemed to be staring at the wall, but Mary could see he was thinking.
“I wish I were friends with things,” he said at last, “but I’m not. I never had anything to be friends with, and I can’t stand people.”
“Can’t you stand me?” asked Mary.
“Yes, I can,” he answered. “It’s funny, but I even like you.”

“Ben Weatherstaff said I was like him,” said Mary. “He said he’d bet we both had the same nasty tempers. I think you’re like him too. We’re all three alike—you and I and Ben Weatherstaff. He said neither of us was much to look at, and we were as sour as we looked. But I don’t feel as sour as I used to, before I knew the robin and Dickon.”
“Did you feel as if you hated people?”
“Yes,” answered Mary, without any pretending. “I would have hated you if I had seen you before I met the robin and Dickon.”
Colin put out his thin hand and touched her.
“Mary,” he said, “I’m sorry for what I said about sending Dickon away. I hated you when you called him an angel, and I laughed at you. But—but maybe he is one.”

“Well, it was rather funny to say it,” she admitted frankly, “because his nose does turn up, and he has a big mouth, and his clothes have patches all over them, and he talks broad Yorkshire. But—but if an angel did come to Yorkshire and live on the moor—if there were a Yorkshire angel—I believe he’d understand the green things and know how to make them grow. He’d know how to talk to the wild creatures the way Dickon does, and they’d know he was their friend for sure.”
“I wouldn’t mind Dickon looking at me,” said Colin. “I want to see him.”
“I’m glad you said that,” answered Mary, “because—because—”
Quite suddenly it came to her that this was the moment to tell him. Colin knew something new was coming.
“Because what?” he cried eagerly.
Mary was so anxious that she got up from her stool, came over to him, and took hold of both his hands.
“Can I trust you? I trusted Dickon because the birds trusted him. Can I trust you—for sure—_for sure?_” she begged.
Her face was so solemn that he almost whispered his answer.
“Yes—yes!”
“Well, Dickon will come to see you tomorrow morning, and he’ll bring his creatures with him.”
“Oh! Oh!” Colin cried out in delight.
“But that’s not everything,” Mary went on, nearly pale with solemn excitement. “The rest is even better. There’s a door into the garden. I found it. It’s hidden under the ivy on the wall.”
If he had been a strong, healthy boy, Colin would probably have shouted “Hooray! Hooray! Hooray!” But he was weak and rather hysterical. His eyes grew bigger and bigger, and he gasped for breath.
“Oh! Mary!” he cried, half sobbing. “Will I see it? Will I get inside? Will I _live_ long enough to get inside?” He clutched her hands and pulled her close.
“Of course you’ll see it!” snapped Mary indignantly. “Of course you’ll live to get into it! Don’t be silly!”

And she was so calm and natural and childish that she brought him back to his senses. He began to laugh at himself, and a few minutes later she was sitting on her stool again, telling him not what she imagined the secret garden to be like, but what it really was. Colin’s aches and tiredness were forgotten, and he listened, enraptured.
“It’s just what you thought it would be,” he said at last. “It sounds just as if you had really seen it. You know I said so when you first told me.”
Mary hesitated for about two minutes, and then she boldly told the truth.
“I had seen it—and I had been inside,” she said. “I found the key and got in weeks ago. But I didn’t dare tell you. I was too afraid I couldn’t trust you—_for sure!_”

chapters.title: “It Has Come!”
paragraphs: Of course Dr. Craven was sent for the morning after Colin’s tantrum. He was always called at once when something like that happened. And when he arrived, he always found the same thing: a pale, shaken boy lying on his bed, sulky and still so hysterical that the slightest word could set him sobbing again. Dr. Craven honestly dreaded and hated these visits, because they were so difficult. This time he was away from Misselthwaite Manor until the afternoon.

“How is he?” he asked Mrs. Medlock rather irritably when he got there. “One of these days he will burst a blood vessel in one of those fits. The boy is half out of his mind with hysteria and from being spoiled.”

“Well, sir,” answered Mrs. Medlock, “you’ll hardly believe your eyes when you see him. That plain, sour-faced child, who is almost as bad as he is, has simply bewitched him. There’s no telling how she did it. Heaven knows she’s nothing to look at, and you hardly ever hear her speak. But she did what none of us dared to do. Last night she flew at him like a little cat. She stamped her feet and ordered him to stop screaming, and somehow she gave him such a start that he actually did stop. And this afternoon—well, just come up and see, sir. You won’t be able to believe it.”

The scene Dr. Craven saw when he entered his patient’s room really did astonish him. As Mrs. Medlock opened the door, he heard laughing and chattering. Colin was on his sofa in his dressing gown, sitting up quite straight. He was looking at a picture in one of the garden books and talking to the plain child. At that moment she could hardly be called plain at all, because her face was glowing with happiness.
“Those long spires of blue ones—we’ll have lots of those,” Colin was announcing. “They’re called Del-phin-iums.”
“Dickon says they’re larkspurs, only bigger and grander,” cried Mistress Mary. “There are clumps of them there already.”
Then they saw Dr. Craven and stopped. Mary went quite still, and Colin looked fretful.
“I’m sorry to hear you were ill last night, my boy,” Dr. Craven said, a little nervously. He was rather a nervous man.
“I feel better now—much better,” Colin replied, sounding rather like a Rajah. “If the weather is fine, I’ll go out in my chair in a day or two. I want some fresh air.”
Dr. Craven sat down beside him, felt his pulse, and studied him with curiosity.
“It will have to be a very fine day,” he said, “and you must be very careful not to tire yourself.”
“Fresh air won’t tire me,” said the young Rajah.
There had been times when this same young gentleman had shrieked with rage and insisted that fresh air would give him a cold and kill him. So it is no wonder that his doctor felt rather startled.
“I thought you didn’t like fresh air,” he said.
“I don’t, when I’m by myself,” replied the Rajah. “But my cousin is going out with me.”
“And the nurse, of course?” suggested Dr. Craven.

“No, I will not have the nurse,” he said, so grandly that Mary could not help remembering the young native Prince. He had been covered all over with diamonds and emeralds and pearls, and he had waved his small dark hand, heavy with great rubies, to call his servants forward to bow low and receive their orders.
“My cousin knows how to look after me. I always feel better when she’s near me. She made me feel better last night. A very strong boy I know will push my carriage.”

Dr. Craven felt rather alarmed. If this troublesome, hysterical boy happened to get well, he himself would lose any chance of inheriting Misselthwaite. But he was not an unscrupulous man, though he was a weak one, and he did not mean to let the boy run into real danger.
“He must be a strong boy and a steady one,” he said. “And I must know something about him. Who is he? What is his name?”
“It’s Dickon,” Mary spoke up suddenly. Somehow she felt that everybody who knew the moor must know Dickon. And she was right. She saw Dr. Craven’s serious face relax at once into a relieved smile.
“Oh, Dickon,” he said. “If it’s Dickon, you’ll be safe enough. He’s as strong as a moor pony, is Dickon.”
“And he’s trusty,” said Mary. “He’s the trustiest lad in Yorkshire.” She had been talking Yorkshire to Colin, and she forgot herself.
“Did Dickon teach you that?” asked Dr. Craven, laughing out loud.
“I’m learning it the way you’d learn French,” said Mary rather coldly. “It’s like a native language in India. Very clever people try to learn those. I like it, and so does Colin.”
“Well, well,” he said. “If it amuses you, perhaps it won’t do you any harm. Did you take your bromide last night, Colin?”
“No,” Colin answered. “At first I wouldn’t take it. Then, after Mary calmed me down, she talked me to sleep—in a low voice—about spring creeping into a garden.”

“That sounds soothing,” said Dr. Craven, more puzzled than ever. He glanced sideways at Mistress Mary, who sat on her stool looking silently down at the carpet. “You are clearly better, but you must remember—”

“I don’t want to remember,” interrupted the Rajah, appearing again. “When I lie by myself and remember, I begin to have pains everywhere. I think of things that make me scream, because I hate them so much. If there were a doctor anywhere who could make you forget you were ill, instead of reminding you of it, I would have him brought here.” And he waved a thin hand, which really ought to have been covered with royal signet rings set with rubies. “It’s because my cousin makes me forget that she makes me better.”

Dr. Craven had never made such a short visit after a “tantrum.” Usually he had to stay a very long time and do a great many things. This afternoon he gave no medicine and left no new orders, and he was spared any unpleasant scenes. When he went downstairs he looked very thoughtful, and when he talked to Mrs. Medlock in the library, she could tell he was a deeply puzzled man.
“Well, sir,” she ventured, “could you have believed it?”
“It is certainly a new state of affairs,” said the doctor. “And there’s no denying it is better than the old one.”

“I believe Susan Sowerby’s right—I really do,” said Mrs. Medlock. “I stopped at her cottage on my way to Thwaite yesterday and had a bit of a talk with her. And she says to me, ‘Well, Sarah Ann, she may not be a good child, and she may not be a pretty one, but she’s a child, and children need children.’ We went to school together, Susan Sowerby and I.”
“She’s the best sick nurse I know,” said Dr. Craven. “When I find her in a cottage, I know there’s a good chance I’ll save my patient.”
Mrs. Medlock smiled. She was fond of Susan Sowerby.

“She has a way about her, does Susan,” she went on, quite chattily. “I’ve been thinking all morning about something she said yesterday. She says, ‘Once I was giving the children a bit of a sermon after they’d been fighting, and I said to them all, “When I was at school, my geography book said the world was shaped like an orange. And I found out before I was ten that nobody owns the whole orange. No one owns more than his bit of a quarter, and sometimes it seems there aren’t enough quarters to go round. But don’t any of you think you own the whole orange, or you’ll find out you’re mistaken, and you won’t find it out without hard knocks.” ‘What children learn from children,’ she says, ‘is that there’s no sense in grabbing at the whole orange—peel and all. If you do, you’ll likely not even get the pips, and they’re too bitter to eat.’”
“She’s a shrewd woman,” said Dr. Craven, putting on his coat.

“Well, she has a way of saying things,” ended Mrs. Medlock, much pleased. “Sometimes I’ve said to her, ‘Eh! Susan, if you were a different woman and didn’t talk such broad Yorkshire, there have been times I’d have said you were clever.’”

Colin slept all that night without waking once. In the morning he opened his eyes and lay quietly, smiling without even knowing it, because he felt so strangely comfortable. Being awake was actually pleasant. He rolled over and stretched his arms and legs, enjoying every bit of it. He felt as if tight strings that had held him had loosened themselves and let him go. He did not know that Dr. Craven would have said his nerves had relaxed and rested. Instead of lying there staring at the wall and wishing he had not woken up, his mind was full of the plans he and Mary had made the day before. It was full of pictures of the garden and of Dickon and his wild creatures. It was so nice to have things to think about. He had not been awake more than ten minutes when he heard feet running along the corridor, and Mary was at the door. The next minute she was in the room and had run across to his bed, bringing with her a rush of fresh air full of the scent of the morning.
“You’ve been out! You’ve been out! I can smell the leaves!” he cried.
She had been running, and her hair was loose and windblown. She was bright from the air, and her cheeks were pink, though he could not see that.

“It’s so beautiful!” she said, a little breathless from running. “You’ve never seen anything so beautiful! It has _come!_ I thought it had come that other morning, but it was only coming. It’s here now! It has come, the Spring! Dickon says so!”
“Has it?” cried Colin. He really knew nothing about it, but he felt his heart beat faster. He actually sat up in bed.
“Open the window!” he added, laughing, half with joyful excitement and half at his own fancy. “Maybe we’ll hear golden trumpets!”
And though he laughed, Mary was at the window in a moment. A moment later it was opened wide, and freshness and softness and scents and birdsong were pouring in.

“That’s fresh air,” she said. “Lie on your back and breathe it in, in long breaths. That’s what Dickon does when he lies on the moor. He says he feels it in his veins and it makes him strong, and he feels as if he could live forever and ever. Breathe it and breathe it.”
She was only repeating what Dickon had told her, but it caught Colin’s imagination.

“‘Forever and ever’! Does it make him feel like that?” he said. And he did as she told him, drawing long, deep breaths again and again, until he felt that something quite new and delightful was happening to him.
Mary was at his bedside again.

“Things are crowding up out of the earth,” she ran on, in a hurry. “There are flowers uncurling and buds on everything. The green veil has covered nearly all the gray. The birds are in such a hurry to build their nests, for fear they’ll be too late, that some of them are even fighting for places in the secret garden. The rosebushes look as alive as alive can be. There are primroses in the lanes and woods, and the seeds we planted are up. And Dickon has brought the fox and the crow and the squirrels and a newborn lamb.”

And then she stopped for breath. Dickon had found the newborn lamb three days before, lying beside its dead mother among the gorse bushes on the moor. It was not the first motherless lamb he had found, and he knew what to do with it. He had carried it to the cottage wrapped in his jacket, let it lie near the fire, and fed it warm milk. It was a soft little thing with a darling, silly baby face and legs rather long for its body. Dickon had carried it over the moor in his arms, with its feeding bottle in his pocket, along with a squirrel. When Mary sat under a tree with its limp warmth huddled in her lap, she had felt too full of strange joy to speak. A lamb—a lamb! A living lamb, lying on your lap like a baby!

She was describing it with great joy, and Colin was listening and breathing in long breaths of air, when the nurse came in. She gave a little start at the sight of the open window. She had sat stifling in that room on many a warm day because her patient was sure that open windows gave people colds.
“Are you sure you’re not chilly, Master Colin?” she asked.
“No,” was the answer. “I’m taking long breaths of fresh air. It makes you strong. I’m going to get up onto the sofa for breakfast. My cousin will have breakfast with me.”

Hiding a smile, the nurse went off to order two breakfasts. The servants’ hall was a far more entertaining place than the invalid’s room, and right now everyone there was eager for news from upstairs. There was a great deal of joking about the unpopular young recluse who, as the cook said, “had met his match, and good for him.” The servants’ hall had grown very tired of the tantrums. The butler, a man with a family, had more than once given his opinion that the invalid would be all the better “for a good hiding.”
When Colin was on his sofa and the breakfast for two had been set on the table, he made an announcement to the nurse in his most Rajah-like manner.

“This morning a boy, a fox, a crow, two squirrels and a newborn lamb are coming to visit me,” he said. “Bring them upstairs the moment they get here. You are not to start playing with the animals in the servants’ hall and keep them down there. I want them here with me.”
The nurse gave a slight gasp and tried to cover it with a cough.
“Yes, sir,” she answered.
“Here is what you can do,” Colin went on, with a wave of his hand. “Tell Martha to bring them up. The boy is her brother. His name is Dickon, and he charms animals.”
“I hope the animals won’t bite, Master Colin,” said the nurse.
“I told you he was a charmer,” said Colin sternly. “A charmer’s animals never bite.”
“There are snake charmers in India,” said Mary. “And they can put their snakes’ heads in their mouths.”
“Goodness!” shuddered the nurse.
The two of them ate with the morning air streaming in around them. Colin made a very good breakfast, and Mary watched him closely, with real interest.
“You’ll start getting fatter, just as I did,” she said. “I never wanted my breakfast when I was in India, and now I always want it.”
“I wanted mine this morning,” said Colin. “Maybe it was the fresh air. When do you think Dickon will come?”
He was not long in coming. In about ten minutes Mary held up her hand.
“Listen!” she said. “Did you hear a caw?”
Colin listened and heard it—the oddest sound in the world to hear inside a house, a hoarse “caw-caw.”
“Yes,” he answered.
“That’s Soot,” said Mary. “Listen again. Do you hear a bleat—a tiny one?”
“Oh, yes!” cried Colin, quite flushed.
“That’s the newborn lamb,” said Mary. “He’s coming.”

Dickon’s moorland boots were thick and clumsy, and though he tried to walk quietly, they made a clumping sound as he came through the long corridors. Mary and Colin heard him marching and marching, until he passed through the tapestry door onto the soft carpet of Colin’s own passage.
“If you please, sir,” announced Martha, opening the door, “if you please, sir, here’s Dickon and his creatures.”

Dickon walked in with his friendliest, widest smile. He carried the newborn lamb in his arms, and the little red fox trotted beside him. Nut perched on his left shoulder, Soot on his right, and Shell’s head and paws poked out of his coat pocket.

Colin slowly sat up and stared and stared—just as he had stared when he first saw Mary. But this was a stare of wonder and delight. The truth was that, in spite of all he had heard, he had not in the least understood what this boy would be like. He had not understood that the fox and the crow and the squirrels and the lamb would be so close to him and to his kindness. They seemed almost part of him. Colin had never talked to a boy in his life. He was so overwhelmed by his own pleasure and curiosity that he did not even think of speaking.

But Dickon did not feel the least bit shy or awkward. He had not been embarrassed when the crow only stared at him and said nothing, because the crow did not know his language. Creatures were always like that until they found out who you were. He walked over to Colin’s sofa and quietly set the newborn lamb on his lap. At once the little creature turned toward the warm velvet dressing gown. It began to nuzzle deep into the folds and push its tight-curled head against Colin’s side with soft impatience. After that, of course, no boy could have kept from speaking.
“What is it doing?” cried Colin. “What does it want?”
“It wants its mother,” said Dickon, smiling more and more. “I brought it to you a bit hungry, because I knew you’d like to see it feed.”
He knelt down beside the sofa and took a feeding bottle out of his pocket.

“Come on, little one,” he said, gently turning the small woolly white head with his brown hand. “This is what you’re after. You’ll get more good out of this than out of any silk velvet coat. There now,” and he pushed the rubber tip of the bottle into the nuzzling mouth, and the lamb began to suck it with greedy delight.

After that, nobody had to wonder what to say. By the time the lamb fell asleep, the questions were pouring out, and Dickon answered every one. He told them how he had found the lamb three mornings ago, just as the sun was rising. He had been standing on the moor, listening to a skylark. He watched it swing higher and higher into the sky, until it was only a speck in the blue heights.

“I’d almost lost sight of him, but I could still hear his song. I was wondering how a chap could hear it when he looked ready to leave the world altogether. And just then I heard something else, far off among the gorse bushes. It was a weak bleating, and I knew it was a new lamb that was hungry. I knew it wouldn’t be hungry unless it had lost its mother somehow, so I set off searching. Eh! I did have a hunt for it. I went in and out among the gorse bushes and round and round, and I always seemed to take the wrong turn. But at last I saw a bit of white by a rock on top of the moor. I climbed up and found the little one half dead with cold and hunger.”

While he talked, Soot flew solemnly in and out of the open window and cawed his remarks about the scenery. Nut and Shell made trips into the big trees outside, running up and down the trunks and exploring the branches. Captain curled up near Dickon, who sat on the hearth rug because he liked it best.
Together they studied the pictures in the gardening books. Dickon could name every flower the way country people did, and he could tell exactly which ones were already growing in the secret garden.

“I couldn’t tell you that long name,” he said, pointing to one with “Aquilegia” written under it. “But we call that a columbine, and that one there is a snapdragon. They both grow wild in the hedges, but these are garden ones, and they’re bigger and grander. There are some big clumps of columbine in the garden. When they’re out, they’ll look like a bed of blue and white butterflies fluttering.”
“I’m going to see them,” cried Colin. “I am going to see them!”
“Aye, you must,” said Mary, quite seriously. “And you mustn’t waste any time about it.”

chapters.title: “I Shall Live Forever—And Ever—And Ever!”
paragraphs: They had to wait more than a week, though. First came several very windy days, and then Colin seemed to be catching a cold. Either of those, let alone both in a row, would surely have sent him into a rage. But there was so much careful, secret planning to do that he hardly noticed. Almost every day Dickon came in, even if only for a few minutes. He told them what was happening on the moor, in the lanes and hedges, and along the banks of streams. He told about the homes of otters, badgers and water-rats, not to mention birds’ nests and field-mice and their burrows. Hearing all these little details from a boy who could charm animals was enough to make you tremble with excitement. You realized how eagerly and anxiously the whole busy underground world was working.
“They’re just the same as us,” said Dickon. “Only they have to build their homes new every year. And it keeps them so busy they can hardly hurry fast enough to get them done.”

The most absorbing task, though, was getting ready to bring Colin to the garden in secret. No one must see the chair and Dickon and Mary once they turned a certain corner of the shrubbery and started along the path outside the ivy-covered walls. As the days passed, Colin grew more and more sure that the mystery around the garden was one of its greatest charms. Nothing must spoil it. No one must ever guess that they had a secret. People should think he was simply going out with Mary and Dickon because he liked them and did not mind them looking at him. They had long, thoroughly enjoyable talks about their route. They would go up this path, down that one, and across another, and wander around the fountain flower-beds as if they were looking at the “bedding-out plants” that the head gardener, Mr. Roach, had been having set out. That would seem such a sensible thing to do that no one would think it mysterious at all. Then they would turn into the shrubbery walks and lose themselves until they reached the long walls. It was planned almost as seriously and carefully as the marches that great generals map out in wartime.

Of course, rumors about the strange new things going on in the invalid’s rooms had already seeped down through the servants’ hall into the stable yards and out among the gardeners. Even so, Mr. Roach was startled one day when an order came from Master Colin’s room. He was to report to the apartment that no outsider had ever seen, because the invalid himself wanted to speak with him.
“Well, well,” he said to himself as he hurried to change his coat, “what’s all this about? His Royal Highness, who was never to be looked at, sending for a man he’s never laid eyes on.”

Mr. Roach felt curious. He had never caught so much as a glimpse of the boy. He had heard dozens of wild stories about his eerie looks and habits and his furious tempers. What he had heard most often was that the boy might die at any moment. Many people who had never seen him had made up detailed descriptions of a humped back and helpless limbs.
“Things are changing in this house, Mr. Roach,” said Mrs. Medlock, as she led him up the back staircase to the corridor where the long-mysterious room opened.
“Let’s hope they’re changing for the better, Mrs. Medlock,” he answered.

“They couldn’t very well change for the worse,” she went on. “And strange as it all is, there are some who find their work a lot easier to bear. Don’t be surprised, Mr. Roach, if you find yourself in the middle of a menagerie, with Martha Sowerby’s Dickon more at home there than you or I could ever be.”
There really was a sort of Magic about Dickon, as Mary had always privately believed. When Mr. Roach heard his name, he smiled quite kindly.
“He’d be at home in Buckingham Palace or at the bottom of a coal mine,” he said. “And yet it isn’t cheek, either. He’s simply a fine lad.”

It was just as well that he had been warned, or he might have jumped. When the bedroom door opened, a large crow was perched on the high back of a carved chair, looking perfectly at home. It announced the visitor by saying “Caw—Caw” quite loudly. Even with Mrs. Medlock’s warning, Mr. Roach barely stopped himself from doing something very undignified and leaping backward.

The young Rajah was neither in bed nor on his sofa. He was sitting in an armchair. A young lamb stood beside him, wagging its tail the way lambs do when they are being fed, while Dickon knelt and gave it milk from a bottle. A squirrel sat on Dickon’s bent back, nibbling a nut with great attention. The little girl from India sat on a big footstool, watching.
“Here is Mr. Roach, Master Colin,” said Mrs. Medlock.
The young Rajah turned and looked his servant up and down. At least, that was how it felt to the head gardener.
“Oh, so you are Roach, are you?” he said. “I sent for you because I have some very important orders for you.”
“Very good, sir,” answered Roach. He wondered whether he was about to be told to cut down every oak in the park or turn the orchards into water-gardens.

“I’m going out in my chair this afternoon,” said Colin. “If the fresh air does me good, I may go out every day. While I’m out, no gardener is to come anywhere near the Long Walk beside the garden walls. Not one of them. I’ll go at about two o’clock, and they must all keep away until I send word that they can return to their work.”
“Very good, sir,” replied Mr. Roach, greatly relieved to learn that the oaks could stay and the orchards were safe.
“Mary,” said Colin, turning to her, “what is it you say in India when you have finished talking and want people to leave?”
“You say, ‘You have my permission to go,’” answered Mary.
The Rajah waved his hand.
“You have my permission to go, Roach,” he said. “But remember, this is very important.”
“Caw—Caw!” remarked the crow, hoarsely but not rudely.
“Very good, sir. Thank you, sir,” said Mr. Roach, and Mrs. Medlock led him out of the room.
Out in the corridor, being a good-natured man, he smiled until he nearly laughed.
“My word!” he said. “He has a fine lordly way about him, hasn’t he? You’d think he was a whole Royal Family rolled into one, Prince Consort and all.”
“Eh!” protested Mrs. Medlock. “We’ve had to let him trample all over every one of us since the day he first had feet, and he thinks that’s what folks were born for.”
“Perhaps he’ll grow out of it, if he lives,” suggested Mr. Roach.

“Well, one thing is pretty certain,” said Mrs. Medlock. “If he does live, and that Indian child stays here, I’ll bet she teaches him that the whole orange doesn’t belong to him, as Susan Sowerby says. And he’ll likely find out how big his own quarter is.”
Inside the room, Colin was leaning back against his cushions.
“It’s all safe now,” he said. “And this afternoon I will see it. This afternoon I will be in it!”

Dickon went back to the garden with his creatures, and Mary stayed with Colin. She did not think he looked tired, but he was very quiet before their lunch came, and he stayed quiet while they ate. She wondered why and asked him about it.
“What big eyes you have, Colin,” she said. “When you are thinking, they get as big as saucers. What are you thinking about now?”
“I can’t stop thinking about what it will look like,” he answered.
“The garden?” asked Mary.
“The springtime,” he said. “I was thinking that I have never really seen it before. I hardly ever went outside, and when I did, I never looked at it. I didn’t even think about it.”
“I never saw it in India, because there wasn’t any,” said Mary.
Colin’s life had been shut in and gloomy, but he had more imagination than she did. At least he had spent a great deal of time looking at wonderful books and pictures.

“That morning when you ran in and said, ‘It’s come! It’s come!’ it made me feel quite strange. It sounded as if things were arriving in a great procession, with big bursts and drifting waves of music. I have a picture like it in one of my books. There are crowds of lovely people and children with garlands and branches covered in blossoms, all laughing and dancing and crowding along and playing on pipes. That was why I said, ‘Perhaps we shall hear golden trumpets,’ and told you to throw open the window.”

“How funny!” said Mary. “That’s exactly what it feels like. And if all the flowers and leaves and green things and birds and wild creatures danced past at once, what a crowd it would be! I’m sure they would dance and sing and play their flutes, and that would be your waves of music.”
They both laughed. It was not because the idea was silly but because they both liked it so much.

A little later the nurse got Colin ready. She noticed that instead of lying like a log while his clothes were put on, he sat up and tried to help himself. He talked and laughed with Mary the whole time.
“It’s one of his good days, sir,” she told Dr. Craven, who had stopped by to look him over. “His spirits are so high that they’re making him stronger.”
“I’ll come again later this afternoon, after he is back,” said Dr. Craven. “I must see how going out agrees with him. I wish,” he added in a very low voice, “that he would let you go with him.”
“I would rather give up the case this very moment, sir, than even stay here while that’s suggested,” answered the nurse, with sudden firmness.
“I hadn’t really decided to suggest it,” said the doctor, with his usual slight nervousness. “We’ll try the experiment. Dickon is a lad I would trust with a newborn child.”

The strongest footman in the house carried Colin downstairs and put him in his wheeled chair, where Dickon was waiting outside. After the footman had arranged the rugs and cushions, the Rajah waved his hand at him and at the nurse.
“You have my permission to go,” he said. They both vanished quickly, and, it must be admitted, giggled once they were safely inside the house.

Dickon began to push the wheeled chair slowly and steadily. Mistress Mary walked beside it, and Colin leaned back and lifted his face to the sky. The great arch of it looked very high, and the small snowy clouds seemed like white birds floating on outspread wings beneath its crystal blue. The wind swept down from the moor in soft, big breaths, carrying a wild, clear, scented sweetness. Colin kept lifting his thin chest to breathe it in. His big eyes looked as if they were the ones doing the listening, instead of his ears.
“There are so many sounds of singing and humming and calling,” he said. “What is that scent the puffs of wind bring?”
“It’s the gorse on the moor, opening out,” answered Dickon. “Eh! The bees are working it wonderfully today.”

Not a single human being could be seen on the paths they took. Every gardener and gardener’s lad had been spirited away. But they wound in and out among the shrubbery and around the fountain beds, following their carefully planned route just for the mysterious fun of it. At last they turned into the Long Walk by the ivy-covered walls. The thrill of what was coming was so strong that, for some odd reason they could not have explained, they began to speak in whispers.
“This is it,” breathed Mary. “This is where I used to walk up and down and wonder and wonder.”
“Is it?” cried Colin, and his eyes began to search the ivy eagerly. “But I can’t see anything,” he whispered. “There is no door.”
“That’s what I thought,” said Mary.
Then there was a lovely, breathless silence, and the chair rolled on.
“That is the garden where Ben Weatherstaff works,” said Mary.
“Is it?” said Colin.
A few yards farther on, Mary whispered again.
“This is where the robin flew over the wall,” she said.
“Is it?” cried Colin. “Oh! I wish he would come again!”
“And that,” said Mary, pointing beneath a big lilac bush with solemn delight, “is the spot where he sat on the small mound of earth and showed me the key.”
Then Colin sat up.
“Where? Where? There?” he cried. His eyes were as big as the wolf’s in Red Riding-Hood, when Red Riding-Hood felt she had to remark on them. Dickon stood still, and the wheeled chair stopped.

“And here,” said Mary, stepping onto the flower bed beside the ivy, “is where I stood to talk to him when he chirped at me from the top of the wall. And this is the ivy that the wind blew aside.” She took hold of the hanging green curtain.
“Oh! Is it—is it!” gasped Colin.
“And here is the handle, and here is the door. Dickon, push him in—push him in quickly!”
And Dickon did it with one strong, steady, splendid push.

But Colin had actually sunk back against his cushions, even though he gasped with delight. He covered his eyes with his hands and kept them there, shutting out everything, until they were inside, the chair had stopped as if by magic, and the door was closed. Only then did he take his hands away and look round and round and round, just as Dickon and Mary had done. Over the walls and the earth and the trees, over the swinging sprays and tendrils, the fair green veil of tender little leaves had crept. In the grass under the trees, and in the gray urns in the alcoves, and here and there and everywhere, were touches and splashes of gold and purple and white. The trees above his head were showing pink and snowy blossom, and there was a fluttering of wings, and faint sweet piping, and humming, and scents and scents. The sun fell warm on his face like a hand with a lovely touch. Mary and Dickon stood in wonder and stared at him. He looked so strange and different, because a pink glow of color had actually crept all over him, over his ivory face and neck and hands and everything.
“I shall get well! I shall get well!” he cried out. “Mary! Dickon! I shall get well! And I shall live forever and ever and ever!”

chapters.title: Ben Weatherstaff
paragraphs: Here is one of the strange things about being alive: only now and then do you feel completely sure that you are going to live forever and ever and ever. Sometimes you know it at dawn, in the tender, solemn hour when you get up and go outside and stand alone. You throw your head far back and look up and up, and you watch the pale sky slowly change and glow, and marvelous, unknown things begin to happen. The East almost makes you cry out, and your heart stands still at the strange, unchanging majesty of the sun coming up, which has happened every morning for thousands and thousands and thousands of years. For a moment or two, you know it then. Sometimes you know it when you stand by yourself in a wood at sunset, while the deep gold stillness slants in through the branches and under them, and seems to be saying something slowly, over and over, that you cannot quite hear, however hard you try. Sometimes the huge quiet of the dark blue night, with millions of stars waiting and watching, makes you sure. Sometimes a sound of music far away makes it true, and sometimes a look in someone’s eyes.

It was like that for Colin when he first saw and heard and felt the springtime inside the four high walls of a hidden garden. That afternoon the whole world seemed to give itself up to being perfect, shining and beautiful, and kind to one boy. Perhaps out of pure heavenly goodness, spring had come and packed everything it possibly could into that one place. More than once Dickon stopped what he was doing and stood still, a look of growing wonder in his eyes, shaking his head softly.
“Eh! It’s grand,” he said. “I’m twelve going on thirteen, and there’s a lot of afternoons in thirteen years, but it seems to me I never saw one as grand as this.”
“Aye, it is a grand one,” said Mary, and she sighed with pure joy. “I’ll bet it’s the grandest one that ever was in this whole world.”
“Do you think,” said Colin, with dreamy care, “that maybe it was made like this on purpose, just for me?”
“My word!” cried Mary, full of admiration. “That was a bit of good Yorkshire, that was. You’re coming along first-rate, you are.”
And joy ruled the day.

They pulled the chair under the plum tree, which was snow-white with blossoms and humming with bees. It was like a king’s canopy, a fairy king’s. Flowering cherry trees stood nearby, and apple trees with pink and white buds, and here and there one had burst wide open. Between the blossoming branches of the canopy, patches of blue sky looked down like wonderful eyes.

Mary and Dickon worked a little here and there while Colin watched them. They brought him things to look at: buds that were opening, buds that were still shut tight, bits of twig with their leaves just starting to show green, the feather of a woodpecker that had fallen on the grass, the empty shell of an egg from some bird that had hatched early. Dickon pushed the chair slowly round and round the garden, stopping every few moments to let him look at wonders springing out of the earth or trailing down from the trees. It was like being carried in state around the country of a magic king and queen and shown all the mysterious riches it held.
“I wonder if we’ll see the robin,” said Colin.

“You’ll see him often enough before long,” answered Dickon. “When the eggs hatch out, the little chap will be kept so busy it’ll make his head swim. You’ll see him flying back and forth carrying worms nearly as big as himself, and such a racket in the nest when he gets there that he’s fair flustered and hardly knows which big mouth to drop the first piece in. There’s gaping beaks and squawks on every side. Mother says when she sees the work a robin has to do to keep those beaks filled, she feels like a lady with nothing to do. She says she’s seen the little chaps when it looked like the sweat must be dripping off them, though folk can’t see it.”

This made them giggle so happily that they had to cover their mouths with their hands, because they remembered they must not be heard. Colin had been taught the rule of whispers and low voices several days before. He liked how mysterious it was and did his best, but when you are enjoying yourself and feeling excited, it is rather hard never to laugh louder than a whisper.

Every moment of the afternoon was full of new things, and with every hour the sunshine grew more golden. The wheeled chair had been drawn back under the canopy, and Dickon had sat down on the grass and just taken out his pipe, when Colin noticed something he had not had time to see before.
“That’s a very old tree over there, isn’t it?” he said.
Dickon looked across the grass at the tree, and Mary looked too, and for a short moment everything went still.
“Yes,” answered Dickon, after that moment, and his low voice sounded very gentle.
Mary gazed at the tree and thought.
“The branches are quite gray, and there isn’t a single leaf anywhere,” Colin went on. “It’s dead, isn’t it?”

“Aye,” Dickon admitted. “But those roses that have climbed all over it will nearly hide every bit of the dead wood when they’re full of leaves and flowers. It won’t look dead then. It’ll be the prettiest of all.”
Mary kept gazing at the tree and thinking.
“It looks as if a big branch was broken off,” said Colin. “I wonder how it happened.”
“It’s been that way many a year,” answered Dickon. “Eh!” he said, with a sudden relieved start, laying his hand on Colin’s arm. “Look at that robin! There he is! He’s been hunting food for his mate.”

Colin was almost too late, but he just caught sight of him, a flash of a red-breasted bird with something in his beak. The robin darted through the greenery into the thickly grown corner and was gone. Colin leaned back on his cushion again, laughing a little.
“He’s taking her tea to her. Maybe it’s five o’clock. I think I’d like some tea myself.”
And so they were safe.

“It was Magic that sent the robin,” Mary said secretly to Dickon afterward. “I know it was Magic.” Both she and Dickon had been afraid that Colin might ask something about the tree whose branch had broken off ten years ago. They had talked it over together, and Dickon had stood rubbing his head in a troubled way.
“We must act as if it’s no different from the other trees,” he had said. “We could never tell him how it broke, poor lad. If he says anything about it, we must—we must try to look cheerful.”
“Aye, we must,” Mary had answered.

But she had not felt as if she looked cheerful when she gazed at the tree. In those few moments she wondered and wondered whether there was any truth in that other thing Dickon had said. He had gone on rubbing his rust-red hair in a puzzled way, but a nice, comforted look had begun to grow in his blue eyes.

“Mrs. Craven was a very lovely young lady,” he had gone on, rather hesitantly. “And Mother thinks maybe she’s about Misselthwaite many a time, looking after Mester Colin, same as all mothers do when they’ve been taken out of the world. They have to come back, you see. Maybe she’s been in the garden, and maybe it was her that set us to work and told us to bring him here.”

Mary had thought he meant something to do with Magic. She was a great believer in Magic. Secretly she was quite sure that Dickon worked Magic, good Magic of course, on everything near him, and that this was why people liked him so much and wild creatures knew he was their friend. She even wondered whether his gift might have brought the robin at just the right moment, when Colin asked that dangerous question. She felt that his Magic had been working all afternoon and making Colin look like a completely different boy. It did not seem possible that he could be the wild creature who had screamed and beaten and bitten his pillow. Even his ivory whiteness seemed to change. The faint glow of color that had shown on his face and neck and hands when he first came inside the garden never quite faded away. He looked as if he were made of flesh instead of ivory or wax.
They saw the robin carry food to his mate two or three times. It reminded them so much of afternoon tea that Colin decided they should have some.
“Go and find one of the men servants and have him bring some out in a basket to the rhododendron walk,” he ordered. “Then you and Dickon can carry it the rest of the way.”

It was a pleasant idea and easily done. When the white cloth was spread on the grass, with hot tea and buttered toast and crumpets, they ate a wonderfully hungry meal. Several birds on household errands stopped to ask what was going on, and were soon busily investigating crumbs. Nut and Shell whisked up the trees with pieces of cake. Soot carried off a whole half of a buttered crumpet to a corner, where he pecked at it and examined it and turned it over and made hoarse remarks about it, until he decided to swallow it all in one happy gulp.

The afternoon was drifting toward its mellow hour. The sun was deepening the gold of its spears of light, the bees were going home, and fewer birds were flying past. Dickon and Mary were sitting on the grass, the tea basket was packed up again and ready to go back to the house, and Colin was lying against his cushions with his heavy hair pushed back from his forehead and his face looking a perfectly natural color.
“I don’t want this afternoon to end,” he said, “but I’ll come back tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that, and the day after that.”
“You’ll get plenty of fresh air, won’t you?” said Mary.
“I’ll get nothing else,” he answered. “I’ve seen the spring now, so I’ll see the summer too. I’ll watch everything grow here. And I’ll grow here myself.”
“That you will,” said Dickon. “We’ll have you walking about here and digging, same as other folk, before long.”
Colin turned bright red.
“Walk!” he said. “Dig! Will I?”
Dickon’s glance at him was gently careful. Neither he nor Mary had ever asked whether anything was the matter with his legs.
“For sure you will,” he said firmly. “You—you’ve got legs of your own, same as other folks!”
Mary was rather frightened until she heard Colin’s answer.
“There’s nothing really wrong with them,” he said, “but they’re so thin and weak. They shake so much that I’m afraid to try standing on them.”
Mary and Dickon both let out a relieved breath.
“When you stop being afraid, you’ll stand on them,” Dickon said, with new cheer. “And you’ll stop being afraid before long.”
“Will I?” said Colin, and he lay still as if he were wondering about it all.

They were truly quiet for a little while. The sun was sinking lower. It was the hour when everything grows still, and they had in fact had a busy and exciting afternoon. Colin looked as if he were resting in perfect comfort. Even the creatures had stopped moving about and had gathered close to rest near them. Soot had settled on a low branch, drawn up one leg, and let the gray film slide drowsily over his eyes. Mary privately thought he looked as if he might start snoring any minute.
In the middle of all this stillness it was rather startling when Colin half raised his head and cried out in a loud, suddenly alarmed whisper:
“Who is that man?”
Dickon and Mary scrambled to their feet.
“Man!” they both cried, in low, quick voices.
Colin pointed to the high wall.
“Look!” he whispered excitedly. “Just look!”
Mary and Dickon spun around. There, glaring at them over the wall from the top of a ladder, was Ben Weatherstaff’s furious face! He actually shook his fist at Mary.
“If I wasn’t a bachelor, and you were a lass of mine,” he cried, “I’d give you a hiding!”

He climbed up another step, threateningly, as if he meant to jump down and deal with her right then. But as she came toward him he clearly thought better of it, and he stood on the top step of his ladder shaking his fist down at her.

“I never thought much of you!” he lectured. “I couldn’t stand you the first time I set eyes on you. A scrawny, pale-faced young pest, always asking questions and poking your nose in where it wasn’t wanted. I never knew how you got so thick with me. If it hadn’t been for the robin—drat him—”
“Ben Weatherstaff!” called Mary, who had finally caught her breath. She stood at the bottom and gasped her words up to him. “Ben Weatherstaff, the robin is the one who showed me the way!”
Then it truly seemed that Ben would scramble down on her side of the wall, he was so outraged.

“You young bad one!” he called down at her. “Blaming your badness on a robin! Not that he isn’t cheeky enough for anything. Him showing you the way! Him! Eh! You young good-for-nothing”—she could see his next words burst out because he was overpowered by curiosity—“however in this world did you get in?”
“The robin showed me the way,” she insisted stubbornly. “He didn’t know he was doing it, but he did. And I can’t explain from down here while you keep shaking your fist at me.”
At that very moment he stopped shaking his fist, all at once, and his jaw actually dropped. He was staring past her at something coming across the grass toward him.

At the first sound of Ben’s torrent of words, Colin had been so surprised that he had only sat up and listened as if he were spellbound. But in the middle of it he had recovered himself and beckoned to Dickon like a ruler giving orders.
“Wheel me over there!” he commanded. “Wheel me quite close, and stop right in front of him!”

And this, if you please, is what Ben Weatherstaff saw, and it made his jaw drop. A wheeled chair heaped with rich cushions and robes was rolling toward him, looking something like a State Coach. In it leaned a young Rajah, with royal command in his great black-rimmed eyes and one thin white hand stretched out toward him in a proud gesture. The chair stopped right beneath Ben Weatherstaff’s nose. No wonder his mouth fell open.
“Do you know who I am?” demanded the Rajah.
How Ben Weatherstaff stared! His red old eyes fixed on what was in front of him as if he were seeing a ghost. He gazed and gazed, and swallowed a lump in his throat, and did not say a word.
“Do you know who I am?” demanded Colin, even more commandingly. “Answer!”
Ben Weatherstaff lifted his gnarled hand and passed it over his eyes and over his forehead, and then he did answer, in a strange, shaky voice.
“Who you are?” he said. “Aye, that I do—with your mother’s eyes staring at me out of your face. Lord knows how you came here. But you’re the poor cripple.”
Colin forgot that he had ever had a back. His face flushed scarlet and he sat bolt upright.
“I’m not a cripple!” he cried out furiously. “I’m not!”
“He’s not!” cried Mary, almost shouting up the wall in her fierce anger. “He hasn’t got a lump as big as a pin! I looked, and there wasn’t one there—not one!”

Ben Weatherstaff wiped his hand across his forehead once more and stared as though he could never stare enough. His hand trembled, and so did his mouth and his voice. He was an ignorant old man, and a thoughtless one, and all he could remember were the things he had been told.
“You—you haven’t got a crooked back?” he said hoarsely.
“No!” shouted Colin.
“You—you haven’t got crooked legs?” quavered Ben, more hoarsely still.

It was too much. The strength Colin usually poured into his tantrums rushed through him now in a new way. Never yet had he been accused of crooked legs, even in whispers, and the plain, simple belief in them that came through Ben Weatherstaff’s voice was more than Rajah flesh and blood could stand. His anger and wounded pride made him forget everything except this one moment, and filled him with a power he had never known before, an almost unnatural strength.
“Come here!” he shouted to Dickon. He actually began to tear the covers off his legs and free himself. “Come here! Come here! Right now!”
Dickon was at his side in a second. Mary caught her breath in a short gasp and felt herself turn pale.
“He can do it! He can do it! He can do it! He can!” she gabbled over and over to herself, under her breath, as fast as she could.

There was a short, fierce scramble. The rugs went flying to the ground, Dickon held Colin by the arm, and the thin legs came out and the thin feet touched the grass. Colin stood upright—upright!—as straight as an arrow, looking strangely tall, his head thrown back and his strange eyes flashing lightning.
“Look at me!” he shouted up at Ben Weatherstaff. “Look at me—you! Just look at me!”
“He’s as straight as I am!” cried Dickon. “He’s as straight as any lad in Yorkshire!”
Mary thought Ben Weatherstaff’s reaction was the strangest thing she had ever seen. He choked and gulped, and suddenly tears ran down his weather-wrinkled cheeks as he clapped his old hands together.
“Eh!” he burst out, “the lies folk tell! You’re as thin as a lath and as white as a ghost, but there’s not a knob on you. You’ll make a man yet. God bless you!”
Dickon held Colin’s arm firmly, but the boy had not started to wobble. He stood straighter and straighter and looked Ben Weatherstaff right in the face.

“I’m your master,” he said, “whenever my father is away, and you must do as I say. This is my garden, so don’t you dare breathe a word about it! Come down off that ladder and walk out to the Long Walk. Miss Mary will meet you there and bring you in. I have something to say to you. We never wanted you here, but now you’ll have to share the secret. Hurry up!”

Ben Weatherstaff’s cranky old face was still wet from that one strange rush of tears. It seemed he could not take his eyes off thin, straight Colin, standing on his own feet with his head thrown back.

“Eh! lad,” he said, almost in a whisper. “Eh! my lad!” Then, remembering himself, he suddenly touched his hat the way a gardener does and said, “Yes, sir! Yes, sir!” And he obediently vanished down the ladder.

chapters.title: When the Sun Went Down
paragraphs: As soon as Ben’s head had disappeared, Colin turned to Mary.
“Go and meet him,” he said. Mary raced across the grass to the door under the ivy.
Dickon watched Colin closely. There were bright red spots on his cheeks, and he looked remarkable, but he showed no sign of falling.
“I can stand,” Colin said. He kept his head high, and he said it in a truly grand way.
“I told you you could, as soon as you stopped being afraid,” answered Dickon. “And now you’ve stopped.”
“Yes, I’ve stopped,” said Colin.
Then he suddenly remembered something Mary had told him.
“Are you making Magic?” he asked sharply.
A cheerful grin spread across Dickon’s curving mouth.
“You’re doing Magic yourself,” he said. “It’s the same Magic that made these come up out of the earth.” He nudged a clump of crocuses in the grass with his heavy boot.
Colin looked down at the flowers.
“Yes,” he said slowly, “there couldn’t be any bigger Magic than that. There couldn’t.”
He pulled himself up even straighter than before.

“I’m going to walk to that tree,” he said, pointing to one a few feet away. “I’m going to be standing up when Weatherstaff gets here. I can lean on the tree if I want to. When I want to sit down, I’ll sit down, but not until then. Bring a rug from the chair.”

He walked to the tree, and although Dickon kept hold of his arm, he was wonderfully steady. When he stood against the tree trunk, it was hard to tell that he was holding himself up by it. He kept his back so straight that he looked tall.
When Ben Weatherstaff came through the door in the wall, he saw Colin standing there, and he heard Mary muttering something under her breath.
“What are you saying?” he asked rather crossly, because he did not want anything to pull his attention away from the long, thin, straight figure of the boy and his proud face.
But she would not tell him. What she was saying was this:
“You can do it! You can do it! I told you you could! You can do it! You can do it! You _can!_”

She was saying it to Colin, because she wanted to make Magic and keep him on his feet, looking just like that. She could not stand the thought of his giving in before Ben Weatherstaff. He did not give in. A sudden feeling lifted her up: in spite of how thin he was, he looked really beautiful. He fixed his eyes on Ben Weatherstaff in his odd, commanding way.
“Look at me!” he ordered. “Look at me all over! Am I a hunchback? Have I got crooked legs?”
Ben Weatherstaff had not quite gotten over his feelings, but he had recovered a little, and he answered almost the way he usually did.
“Not you,” he said. “Nothing of the sort. What have you been doing with yourself, hiding out of sight and letting folk think you were a cripple and half-witted?”
“Half-witted!” said Colin angrily. “Who thought that?”
“Lots of fools,” said Ben. “The world’s full of jackasses braying, and they never bray anything but lies. What did you shut yourself up for?”
“Everyone thought I was going to die,” said Colin shortly. “I’m not!”
He said it with such certainty that Ben Weatherstaff looked him over, up and down, and down and up.
