“You, die!” he said, with dry delight. “Nothing of the sort! You’ve got too much pluck in you. When I saw you put your legs on the ground in such a hurry, I knew you were all right. Sit yourself down on the rug a bit, young Master, and give me your orders.”

There was a strange mixture of gruff tenderness and sharp understanding in his manner. Mary had poured out her explanation as fast as she could as they came down the Long Walk. The main thing to remember, she had told him, was that Colin was getting well. He was getting well. The garden was doing it. No one must remind him about humps and dying.
The Rajah graciously lowered himself onto a rug under the tree.
“What work do you do in the gardens, Weatherstaff?” he asked.
“Anything I’m told to do,” answered old Ben. “I’m kept on as a favor, because she liked me.”
“She?” said Colin.
“Your mother,” answered Ben Weatherstaff.
“My mother?” said Colin, and he looked quietly around him. “This was her garden, wasn’t it?”
“Aye, it was that!” Ben Weatherstaff looked around, too. “She was very fond of it.”

“This is my garden now, and I am fond of it. I shall come here every single day,” Colin announced. “But it must stay a secret. I order that nobody is to find out we come here. Dickon and my cousin did the work that made it come alive again. Sometimes I shall send for you to help, but you must come when nobody can see you.”
Ben Weatherstaff’s face twisted into a dry old smile.
“I’ve come here before when no one saw me,” he said.
“What!” exclaimed Colin. “When?”
“The last time I was here,” he said, rubbing his chin and looking around, “was about two years ago.”
“But no one has been in it for ten years!” cried Colin.
“There was no door!”
“I’m no one,” said old Ben dryly. “And I didn’t come through the door. I came over the wall. The rheumatism has held me back these last two years.”
“So you came and did a bit of pruning!” cried Dickon. “I couldn’t make out how it had been done.”

“She was so fond of it, she was!” said Ben Weatherstaff slowly. “And she was such a pretty young thing. She said to me once, ‘Ben,’ she said, laughing, ‘if I’m ever ill or if I go away, you must take care of my roses.’ When she did go away, the orders were that no one was ever to come near. But I came,” he said, with grumpy stubbornness. “Over the wall I came, until the rheumatism stopped me, and I did a bit of work once a year. She’d given her order first.”
“It wouldn’t have been as alive as it is if you hadn’t done it,” said Dickon. “I did wonder.”
“I’m glad you did it, Weatherstaff,” said Colin. “You’ll know how to keep the secret.”
“Aye, I’ll know, sir,” answered Ben. “And it’ll be easier for a man with rheumatism to come in at the door.”

Mary had dropped her trowel on the grass near the tree. Colin stretched out his hand and picked it up. A strange look came over his face, and he began to scratch at the earth. His thin hand was weak, but after a while, as they watched him, with Mary hardly daring to breathe, he drove the end of the trowel into the soil and turned some of it over.
“You can do it! You can do it!” Mary said to herself. “I tell you, you can!”
Dickon’s round eyes were full of eager curiosity, but he did not say a word. Ben Weatherstaff watched with an interested face.
Colin kept at it. After he had turned over a few trowelfuls of soil, he spoke to Dickon in triumph, in his best Yorkshire.

“You said you’d have me walking about here just like other folk, and you said you’d have me digging. I thought you were just lying to please me. This is only the first day, and I’ve walked, and here I am, digging.”
Ben Weatherstaff’s mouth dropped open again when he heard this, but he ended up chuckling.
“Eh!” he said, “that sounds as if you’ve got wits enough. You’re a Yorkshire lad for sure. And you’re digging, too. How would you like to plant something? I can get you a rose in a pot.”
“Go and get it!” said Colin, digging excitedly. “Quick! Quick!”

It was certainly done quickly. Ben Weatherstaff went off, forgetting his rheumatism. Dickon took his spade and dug the hole deeper and wider than a new digger with thin white hands could have managed. Mary slipped out and ran to bring back a watering can. When Dickon had made the hole deeper, Colin went on turning the soft earth over and over. He looked up at the sky, flushed and glowing from the strangely new exercise, slight as it was.
“I want to do it before the sun goes all the way down,” he said.

Mary thought the sun might be lingering a few extra minutes on purpose. Ben Weatherstaff fetched the potted rose from the greenhouse, hobbling over the grass as fast as his legs would take him. He had started to get excited, too. He knelt beside the hole and eased the plant out of its pot.
“Here, lad,” he said, handing the plant to Colin. “Set it in the earth yourself, the way a king does when he goes to a new place.”

The thin white hands shook a little, and Colin’s flush grew deeper as he set the rose in the soil and held it while old Ben packed the earth firm. It was filled in, pressed down and made steady. Mary leaned forward on her hands and knees. Soot had flown down and strutted over to see what was going on. Nut and Shell chattered about it from a cherry tree.
“It’s planted!” Colin said at last. “And the sun is only now sliding down over the rim. Help me up, Dickon. I want to be on my feet when it sets. That’s part of the Magic.”

And Dickon helped him. The Magic, or whatever it was, gave him such strength that when the sun did slip over the edge and end the strange, lovely afternoon for them there, he actually stood on his own two feet, laughing.

chapters.title: Magic
paragraphs: When Colin and Mary got back to the house, Dr. Craven had been waiting there for quite a while. He had even started to wonder whether he ought to send someone out to search the garden paths. When Colin was carried back to his room, the poor man studied him with a worried look.
“You shouldn’t have stayed out so long,” he said. “You must not wear yourself out.”
“I’m not tired in the least,” said Colin. “Being out there has made me well. Tomorrow I’m going out in the morning as well as the afternoon.”
“I’m not sure I can let you,” Dr. Craven answered. “I’m afraid it wouldn’t be wise.”
“It wouldn’t be wise to try to stop me,” Colin said, perfectly serious. “I’m going.”

Even Mary had noticed that one of Colin’s biggest oddities was that he had no idea what a rude little brute he was when he bossed people around. He had spent his whole life on a kind of desert island, and since he was king of it, he had made up his own manners and had never had anyone to compare himself with. Mary had been a good deal like him once. Since coming to Misselthwaite she had slowly found out that her own manners were not the usual kind, and not the kind people liked. Having made that discovery, she naturally thought it interesting enough to share with Colin. So after Dr. Craven left, she sat and gazed at him with curiosity for a few minutes. She wanted him to ask her why she was doing it, and of course he did.
“Why are you staring at me?” he said.
“I’m thinking that I feel rather sorry for Dr. Craven.”
“So do I,” said Colin calmly, though he looked a little pleased with himself. “He won’t get Misselthwaite at all now that I’m not going to die.”

“I’m sorry for him because of that, of course,” said Mary, “but just now I was thinking how awful it must have been to be polite for ten years to a boy who was always rude. I would never have done it.”
“Am I rude?” Colin asked, not bothered in the slightest.
“If you had been his own boy, and he had been the kind of man who slaps,” said Mary, “he would have slapped you.”
“But he wouldn’t dare,” said Colin.

“No, he wouldn’t dare,” answered Mistress Mary, working it out quite fairly. “Nobody ever dared to do anything you didn’t like, because you were going to die and all that. You were such a poor thing.”
“But,” Colin announced stubbornly, “I’m not going to be a poor thing. I won’t let people think I am one. I stood on my own feet this afternoon.”
“It’s always getting your own way that has made you so odd,” Mary went on, thinking out loud.
Colin turned his head and frowned at her.
“Am I odd?” he demanded.

“Yes,” answered Mary, “very. But you needn’t be angry,” she added, quite without taking sides, “because I’m odd too, and so is Ben Weatherstaff. But I’m not as odd as I was before I began to like people and before I found the garden.”
“I don’t want to be odd,” said Colin. “I’m not going to be,” and he frowned again, fiercely determined.
He was a very proud boy. He lay thinking for a while, and then Mary saw his beautiful smile begin and slowly change his whole face.
“I’ll stop being odd,” he said, “if I go to the garden every day. There is Magic in there, good Magic, you know, Mary. I’m sure there is.”
“I am too,” said Mary.
“Even if it isn’t real Magic,” Colin said, “we can pretend it is. _Something_ is there, _something!_”
“It’s Magic,” said Mary, “but not the black kind. It’s as white as snow.”

They always called it Magic, and it truly seemed like magic in the months that followed, those wonderful, shining, amazing months. Oh, the things that happened in that garden! If you have never had a garden, you can’t understand. If you have had one, you will know that it would take a whole book to describe everything that took place there. At first it seemed that green things would never stop pushing up through the earth, in the grass, in the flower beds, even in the cracks of the walls. Then the green things began to show buds, and the buds began to open and show their colors, every shade of blue, every shade of purple, every tint and hue of crimson. In the garden’s happy days, flowers had been tucked into every inch and hole and corner. Ben Weatherstaff had watched it being done, and he had scraped mortar out from between the bricks of the wall himself and made little pockets of earth for lovely climbing things to grow in. Irises and white lilies rose out of the grass in bunches, and the green alcoves filled up with astonishing armies of tall delphiniums, columbines and campanulas, with their blue and white flowers standing like lances.

“She was awful fond of them, she was,” Ben Weatherstaff said. “She liked the things that were always pointing up to the blue sky, she used to say. Not that she was one of those who looked down on the earth. Not her. She loved it just the same, but she said the blue sky always looked so joyful.”

The seeds that Dickon and Mary had planted grew as if fairies had looked after them. Satiny poppies of every shade danced in the breeze by the dozen, boldly defying the flowers that had lived in the garden for years, which, it must be admitted, seemed rather puzzled about how such newcomers had gotten there. And the roses, the roses! They rose out of the grass, tangled around the sun-dial, wound around the tree trunks and hung from the branches, and climbed the walls and spread across them, with long garlands falling in cascades. They came alive day by day and hour by hour. Fresh, lovely leaves appeared, and buds, and more buds. They were tiny at first, but they swelled and worked their Magic until they burst open and uncurled into cups of scent that spilled gently over their rims and filled the air of the garden.

Colin saw all of it, watching every change as it happened. Every morning he was brought out, and he spent every hour of every day in the garden unless it rained. Even gray days pleased him. He would lie on the grass “watching things grow,” he said. If you watched long enough, he declared, you could see buds slip out of their wrappings. You could also get to know strange, busy little insect creatures that scurried about on unknown but clearly serious errands. Sometimes they carried tiny scraps of straw or feather or food, or climbed blades of grass as if they were trees, from whose tops they could look out over the countryside. A mole pushing up its mound at the end of its tunnel, then working its way out at last with its long-nailed paws that looked so much like elf hands, held him spellbound for one whole morning. The ways of ants, beetles, bees, frogs, birds and plants gave him a new world to explore. Then Dickon showed him all of those and added the ways of foxes, otters, ferrets, squirrels, trout, water-rats and badgers, and there was no end to the things to talk about and think over.

And that was not even half of the Magic. The fact that he had really stood on his own feet once had set Colin thinking harder than ever. When Mary told him about the spell she had worked, he was excited and approved of it completely. He talked about it all the time.

“Of course there must be lots of Magic in the world,” he said wisely one day, “but people don’t know what it’s like or how to make it. Maybe the beginning is just to keep saying that nice things are going to happen until you make them happen. I’m going to try an experiment.”

The next morning, when they went to the secret garden, he sent for Ben Weatherstaff at once. Ben came as fast as he could, and he found the Rajah standing on his own feet under a tree, looking very grand, and also smiling beautifully.
“Good morning, Ben Weatherstaff,” he said. “Line up, you and Dickon and Miss Mary, side by side, and hear me out. I have something very important to tell you.”

“Aye, aye, sir!” answered Ben Weatherstaff, touching his forehead. (One of Ben Weatherstaff’s long-hidden charms was that as a boy he had once run away to sea and made voyages. So he could answer like a sailor.)
“I’m going to try a scientific experiment,” the Rajah explained. “When I grow up I’m going to make great scientific discoveries, and I’m going to start right now with this experiment.”
“Aye, aye, sir!” said Ben Weatherstaff at once, even though this was the first he had heard of great scientific discoveries.

It was the first time Mary had heard of them too. But even by now she had begun to realize that, odd as he was, Colin had read about a great many unusual things and was somehow a very convincing sort of boy. When he held up his head and fixed his strange eyes on you, you believed him almost in spite of yourself, though he was only ten years old, going on eleven. At this moment he was especially convincing, because he had suddenly discovered the thrill of making a real speech, like a grown-up.

“The great scientific discoveries I’m going to make,” he went on, “will be about Magic. Magic is a great thing, and hardly anyone knows anything about it, except a few people in old books, and Mary a little, because she was born in India where there are fakirs. I think Dickon knows some Magic, but maybe he doesn’t know that he knows it. He charms animals and people. I would never have let him come to see me if he hadn’t been an animal charmer, which is a boy charmer too, because a boy is an animal. I’m sure there is Magic in everything. We just don’t have the sense to get hold of it and make it do things for us, the way we do with electricity and horses and steam.”
This sounded so impressive that Ben Weatherstaff got quite excited and honestly couldn’t keep still.
“Aye, aye, sir,” he said, and he began to stand up very straight.

“When Mary found this garden, it looked completely dead,” the speaker went on. “Then something began pushing things up out of the soil and making things out of nothing. One day they weren’t there, and the next day they were. I had never watched things before, and it made me very curious. Scientific people are always curious, and I’m going to be scientific. I keep asking myself, ‘What is it? What is it?’ It’s something. It can’t be nothing! I don’t know its name, so I call it Magic. I have never seen the sun rise, but Mary and Dickon have, and from what they tell me I’m sure that is Magic too. Something pushes it up and pulls it. Sometimes since I’ve been in the garden I’ve looked up through the trees at the sky, and I’ve had a strange happy feeling, as if something were pushing and pulling in my chest and making me breathe fast. Magic is always pushing and pulling and making things out of nothing. Everything is made out of Magic: leaves and trees, flowers and birds, badgers and foxes and squirrels and people. So it must be all around us. In this garden, and in every other place. The Magic in this garden has made me stand up and know I’m going to live to be a man. I’m going to try the scientific experiment of getting some of it and putting it inside myself, and making it push and pull me and make me strong. I don’t know how to do it, but I think that if you keep thinking about it and calling it, maybe it will come. Maybe that is the first baby way to get it. When I was about to try standing up that first time, Mary kept saying to herself as fast as she could, ‘You can do it! You can do it!’ and I did. I had to try myself at the same time, of course, but her Magic helped me, and so did Dickon’s. Every morning and evening, and as often in the daytime as I can remember, I’m going to say, ‘Magic is in me! Magic is making me well! I’m going to be as strong as Dickon, as strong as Dickon!’ And you must all do it too. That is my experiment. Will you help, Ben Weatherstaff?”
“Aye, aye, sir!” said Ben Weatherstaff. “Aye, aye!”

“If we keep doing it every day, as regularly as soldiers do their drill, we’ll see what happens and find out whether the experiment works. You learn things by saying them over and over and thinking about them until they stay in your mind forever, and I think it will be the same with Magic. If you keep calling it to come to you and help you, it will become part of you, and it will stay and do things.”
“I once heard an officer in India tell my mother that there were fakirs who said words over and over, thousands of times,” said Mary.

“I’ve heard Jem Fettleworth’s wife say the same thing over thousands of times, calling Jem a drunken brute,” said Ben Weatherstaff dryly. “Something always came of that, sure enough. He gave her a good hiding and went to the Blue Lion and got as drunk as a lord.”
Colin drew his brows together and thought for a few minutes. Then he cheered up.

“Well,” he said, “you see, something did come of it. She used the wrong Magic until she made him beat her. If she’d used the right Magic and said something nice, maybe he wouldn’t have gotten as drunk as a lord, and maybe, just maybe, he might have bought her a new bonnet.”
Ben Weatherstaff chuckled, and there was shrewd admiration in his small old eyes.

“You’re a clever lad as well as a straight-legged one, Master Colin,” he said. “Next time I see Bess Fettleworth I’ll give her a little hint of what Magic can do for her. She’d be mighty pleased if the scientific experiment worked, and so would Jem.”

Dickon had stood listening to the lecture, his round eyes shining with curious delight. Nut and Shell sat on his shoulders, and he held a long-eared white rabbit in his arm, stroking and stroking it softly while it laid its ears flat along its back and enjoyed itself.

Colin asked him, “Do you think the experiment will work?” He was curious what Dickon was thinking. He often was, whenever he caught Dickon gazing at him, or at one of his “creatures,” with that happy, wide smile.
He smiled now, and his smile was wider than usual.
“Aye,” he answered, “I do. It’ll work the same way the seeds do when the sun shines on them. It’ll work for sure. Shall we begin it now?”

Colin was delighted, and so was Mary. Fired up by memories of fakirs and holy men in pictures he had seen, Colin suggested that they should all sit cross-legged under the tree, whose branches made a canopy.
“It will be like sitting in a kind of temple,” said Colin. “I’m rather tired, and I want to sit down.”
“Eh!” said Dickon. “You mustn’t start by saying you’re tired. You might spoil the Magic.”
Colin turned and looked at him, right into his innocent round eyes.
“That’s true,” he said slowly. “I must only think about the Magic.”

It all seemed very grand and mysterious once they had sat down in their circle. Ben Weatherstaff felt as if he had somehow been led into a prayer meeting. Usually he was firmly what he called “against prayer meetings,” but since this was the Rajah’s doing, he didn’t mind, and he was even rather glad to be asked to take part. Mistress Mary felt solemnly thrilled. Dickon held his rabbit in his arm, and perhaps he made some charmer’s signal that no one else could hear. When he sat down cross-legged like the others, the crow, the fox, the squirrels and the lamb slowly drew near and became part of the circle, each settling into a resting place as if by their own choice.
“The ‘creatures’ have come,” said Colin gravely. “They want to help us.”

Colin really did look beautiful, Mary thought. He held his head high, as if he felt like a kind of priest, and his strange eyes had a wonderful look in them. The light shone down on him through the canopy of the tree.
“Now we’ll begin,” he said. “Shall we sway backward and forward, Mary, like dervishes?”
“I can’t do any swaying backward and forward,” said Ben Weatherstaff. “I’ve got the rheumatism.”
“The Magic will take it away,” said Colin in a High Priest voice, “but we won’t sway until it has done that. We’ll only chant.”
“I can’t do any chanting,” said Ben Weatherstaff, a little testily. “They threw me out of the church choir the only time I ever tried it.”
No one smiled. They were all far too serious. Not even a shadow crossed Colin’s face. He was thinking only of the Magic.

“All right, then I’ll chant,” he said. He began, and he looked like some odd little spirit of a boy. “The sun is shining—the sun is shining. That is the Magic. The flowers are growing—the roots are stirring. That is the Magic. Being alive is the Magic—being strong is the Magic. The Magic is in me—the Magic is in me. It is in me—it is in me. It is in every single one of us. It is even in Ben Weatherstaff’s back. Magic! Magic! Come and help!”

He said it many, many times—not a thousand times, but a good number of them. Mary listened, spellbound. It seemed both strange and beautiful to her, and she wanted him to go on and on. Ben Weatherstaff slipped into a kind of dream, which was quite pleasant. The humming of the bees in the blossoms blended with the chanting voice and melted sleepily into a doze. Dickon sat cross-legged with his rabbit asleep on his arm and one hand resting on the lamb’s back. Soot had shoved a squirrel aside and huddled close against his shoulder, with the gray film drawn over his eyes. At last Colin stopped.
“Now I’m going to walk around the garden,” he announced.
Ben Weatherstaff’s head had just dropped forward, and he jerked it back up.
“You were asleep,” said Colin.
“Nowt of the sort,” mumbled Ben. “The sermon was good enough—but I’m bound to get out before the collection.”
He was not quite awake yet.
“You’re not in church,” said Colin.
“Not me,” said Ben, sitting up straight. “Who said I were? I heard every bit of it. You said the Magic was in my back. The doctor calls it rheumatics.”
The Rajah waved his hand.
“That was the wrong Magic,” he said. “You will get better. You have my permission to go back to your work. But come again tomorrow.”
“I’d like to see you walk round the garden first,” grunted Ben.

It was not an unfriendly grunt, but it was a grunt all the same. Ben was a stubborn old fellow and did not have complete faith in Magic. He had made up his mind that if he were sent away, he would climb his ladder and look over the wall. That way he could be ready to hobble back in if anyone stumbled.

The Rajah did not mind his staying, and so the procession was formed. It truly did look like a procession. Colin was at the head of it, with Dickon on one side and Mary on the other. Ben Weatherstaff walked behind, and the “creatures” trailed after them. The lamb and the fox cub stayed close to Dickon, the white rabbit hopped along or stopped to nibble, and Soot followed with the solemn air of someone who felt he was in charge.

It was a procession that moved slowly but with dignity. Every few yards it stopped to rest. Colin leaned on Dickon’s arm, and Ben Weatherstaff kept a sharp, private lookout. But now and then Colin took his hand from its support and walked a few steps alone. He held his head up the whole time, and he looked very grand.
“The Magic is in me!” he kept saying. “The Magic is making me strong! I can feel it! I can feel it!”

It seemed certain that something was holding him up and lifting him along. He sat on the seats in the alcoves, and once or twice he sat down on the grass, and several times he paused on the path and leaned on Dickon. But he would not give up until he had gone all the way around the garden. When he came back to the canopy tree, his cheeks were flushed and he looked triumphant.
“I did it! The Magic worked!” he cried. “That is my first scientific discovery.”
“What will Dr. Craven say?” Mary burst out.

“He won’t say anything,” Colin answered, “because he won’t be told. This is going to be the biggest secret of all. No one is to know a thing about it until I have grown so strong that I can walk and run like any other boy. I’ll come here every day in my chair, and I’ll be carried back in it. I won’t have people whispering and asking questions, and I won’t let my father hear about it until the experiment has completely succeeded. Then, someday when he comes back to Misselthwaite, I’ll simply walk into his study and say, ‘Here I am. I’m like any other boy. I am perfectly well, and I will live to be a man. It was done by a scientific experiment.’”
“He’ll think he’s dreaming,” cried Mary. “He won’t believe his eyes.”

Colin flushed with triumph. He had made himself believe that he was going to get well, which was really more than half the battle, though he did not know it. And the thought that excited him more than any other was imagining his father’s face when he saw that he had a son as straight and strong as other men’s sons. One of the darkest miseries of his unhealthy, gloomy past days had been how much he hated being a sickly, weak-backed boy whose father was afraid to look at him.
“He’ll have to believe them,” he said.
“One of the things I’m going to do, after the Magic works and before I start making scientific discoveries, is to become an athlete.”
“We’ll have you taking up boxin’ in a week or so,” said Ben Weatherstaff. “You’ll end up winnin’ the Belt and bein’ champion prize-fighter of all England.”
Colin fixed his eyes on him sternly.

“Weatherstaff,” he said, “that is disrespectful. You must not take liberties just because you are in on the secret. No matter how well the Magic works, I shall not be a prize-fighter. I shall be a Scientific Discoverer.”

“Beg pardon—beg pardon, sir,” answered Ben, touching his forehead in salute. “I ought to have seen it weren’t a joking matter.” But his eyes twinkled, and secretly he was enormously pleased. He truly did not mind being snubbed, since the snubbing meant the lad was gaining strength and spirit.

chapters.title: “Let Them Laugh”
paragraphs: The secret garden was not the only garden Dickon worked in. Around the cottage on the moor, there was a patch of ground fenced in by a low wall of rough stones. Dickon worked there early in the morning, in the last fading light of evening, and on every day when Colin and Mary didn’t see him. He planted and tended potatoes, cabbages, turnips, carrots, and herbs for his mother. With his “creatures” beside him, he did wonders there, and he never seemed to tire of it. As he dug or weeded, he whistled or sang bits of Yorkshire moor songs, or talked to Soot or Captain or the brothers and sisters he had taught to help him.

“We’d never get along as comfortably as we do,” Mrs. Sowerby said, “if it weren’t for Dickon’s garden. Anything will grow for him. His potatoes and cabbages are twice the size of anyone else’s, and they’ve got a flavor nobody else’s has.”

When she had a moment to spare, she liked to go out and talk to him. After supper there was still a long, clear twilight to work in, and that was her quiet time. She could sit on the low, rough wall, watch him, and hear the stories of his day. She loved this hour. This garden held more than vegetables. Now and then Dickon had bought penny packets of flower seeds and sown bright, sweet-smelling blooms among the gooseberry bushes and even the cabbages. He grew borders of mignonette, pinks, and pansies, and other flowers whose seeds he could save year after year, or whose roots bloomed every spring and spread into fine clumps. The low wall was one of the prettiest sights in Yorkshire. He had tucked moorland foxglove, ferns, rock-cress, and hedgerow flowers into every crack, until only a glimpse of stone showed here and there.

“All a chap has to do to make them thrive, Mother,” he would say, “is to be friends with them, truly. They’re just like the ‘creatures.’ If they’re thirsty, give them a drink, and if they’re hungry, give them a bit of food. They want to live same as we do. If they died, I’d feel I’d been a bad lad and had somehow treated them heartlessly.”

In these twilight hours Mrs. Sowerby heard everything that happened at Misselthwaite Manor. At first she was told only that “Mester Colin” had taken a fancy to going out into the grounds with Miss Mary, and that it was doing him good. But before long the two children agreed that Dickon’s mother might “come into the secret.” Somehow nobody doubted that she was “safe, for sure.”

So one beautiful, still evening Dickon told her the whole story. He told her about the buried key, the robin, and the gray haze that had looked like death, and the secret Mistress Mary had planned never to share. He told her how he had come, and how he had been told about it, how Mester Colin had doubted, and the great scene when Colin was brought into the hidden place. He told her about Ben Weatherstaff’s angry face peering over the wall and Mester Colin’s sudden, furious strength. Mrs. Sowerby’s pleasant face changed color several times as she listened.

“My word!” she said. “It was a good thing that little lass came to the Manor. It’s been the making of her and the saving of him. Standing on his feet! And all of us thinking he was a poor half-witted lad without a straight bone in him.”
She asked a great many questions, and her blue eyes were full of deep thought.
“What do they make of it at the Manor, with him so well and cheerful and never complaining?” she asked.

“They don’t know what to make of it,” answered Dickon. “Every day his face looks different. It’s filling out and doesn’t look so sharp, and that waxy color is going. But he has to do his bit of complaining,” he added, with a delighted grin.
“Whatever for?” asked Mrs. Sowerby.
Dickon chuckled.

“He does it so they won’t guess what’s happened. If the doctor knew he’d found out he could stand, he’d likely write and tell Mester Craven. Mester Colin is saving the secret so he can tell it himself. He’s going to practice his Magic on his legs every day until his father comes home. Then he’s going to march into his room and show him he’s as straight as any other lad. But he and Miss Mary think it’s best to do a bit of groaning and fretting now and then, to throw folks off the scent.”
Mrs. Sowerby was laughing a low, comfortable laugh long before he finished his last sentence.

“Eh!” she said, “I’ll warrant that pair are enjoying themselves. They’ll get plenty of acting out of it, and there’s nothing children like so much as play-acting. Let’s hear what they do, Dickon lad.”
Dickon stopped weeding and sat back on his heels to tell her. His eyes twinkled with fun.

“Mester Colin is carried down to his chair every time he goes out,” he explained. “And he flies at John, the footman, for not carrying him carefully enough. He makes himself look as helpless as he can, and he never lifts his head until we’re out of sight of the house. And he grunts and frets a good deal while he’s being settled into his chair. Both he and Miss Mary have got to enjoying it. When he groans and complains, she says, ‘Poor Colin! Does it hurt you so much? Are you really so weak, poor Colin?’ But the trouble is, sometimes they can hardly keep from bursting out laughing. When we get safe into the garden, they laugh until they have no breath left to laugh with. And they have to stuff their faces into Mester Colin’s cushions so the gardeners won’t hear them, if any are about.”
“The more they laugh, the better for them!” said Mrs. Sowerby, still laughing herself. “Good, healthy laughing is better than pills any day of the year. That pair will plump up, for sure.”

“They are plumping up,” said Dickon. “They’re so hungry they can’t think how to get enough to eat without people talking. Mester Colin says if he keeps sending for more food, they won’t believe he’s an invalid at all. Miss Mary says she’ll let him eat her share, but he says if she goes hungry she’ll get thin, and they must both get fat at the same time.”
Mrs. Sowerby laughed so hard at this problem that she rocked back and forth in her blue cloak, and Dickon laughed along with her.

“I’ll tell you what, lad,” Mrs. Sowerby said when she could speak. “I’ve thought of a way to help them. When you go to them in the mornings, you shall take a pail of good fresh milk, and I’ll bake them a crusty cottage loaf or some buns with currants in them, the kind you children like. Nothing’s so good as fresh milk and bread. Then they could take the edge off their hunger while they’re in their garden, and the fine food they get indoors would finish off the rest.”

“Eh! Mother!” said Dickon admiringly, “what a wonder you are! You always see a way out of things. They were in quite a fuss yesterday. They couldn’t see how they’d manage without ordering up more food. They felt that empty inside.”

“They’re two young ones growing fast, and health is coming back to both of them. Children like that feel like young wolves, and food is flesh and blood to them,” said Mrs. Sowerby. Then she smiled Dickon’s own curving smile. “Eh! But they’re enjoying themselves, for sure,” she said.

She was quite right, that comfortable, wonderful mother of his. She had never been more right than when she said that their “play-acting” would be a joy to them. Colin and Mary found it one of their most thrilling amusements. The idea of protecting themselves from suspicion had come to them without their quite realizing it, first from the puzzled nurse and then from Dr. Craven himself.
“Master Colin, your appetite is improving a great deal,” the nurse had said one day. “You used to eat nothing at all, and so many foods upset you.”

“Nothing disagrees with me now,” replied Colin. Then he saw the nurse looking at him curiously, and he suddenly remembered that perhaps he ought not to seem too well just yet. “At least, things don’t disagree with me so often. It’s the fresh air.”
“Perhaps it is,” said the nurse, still looking at him, puzzled. “But I must talk to Dr. Craven about it.”
“How she stared at you!” said Mary when the nurse had gone. “As if she thought there must be something to find out.”
“I won’t have her finding things out,” said Colin. “No one is to start finding out yet.”
When Dr. Craven came that morning, he seemed puzzled too. He asked a number of questions, to Colin’s great annoyance.
“You stay out in the garden a great deal,” he said. “Where do you go?”
Colin put on his favorite air of dignified indifference to what anyone thought.
“I won’t tell anyone where I go,” he answered. “I go to a place I like. Everyone has been ordered to keep away. I refuse to be watched and stared at. You know that!”
“You seem to be out all day, but I don’t think it has done you any harm. I don’t think so. The nurse says you eat much more than you ever did before.”
“Perhaps,” said Colin, struck by a sudden idea, “perhaps it’s an unnatural appetite.”
“I don’t think so, since your food seems to agree with you,” said Dr. Craven. “You’re gaining weight quickly, and your color is better.”
“Perhaps—perhaps I’m bloated and feverish,” said Colin, putting on a gloomy, discouraging look. “People who aren’t going to live are often—different.”
Dr. Craven shook his head. He was holding Colin’s wrist. He pushed up his sleeve and felt his arm.

“You’re not feverish,” he said thoughtfully, “and the weight you’ve gained is healthy. If you can keep this up, my boy, we needn’t talk of dying. Your father will be happy to hear of this remarkable improvement.”

“I won’t have him told!” Colin burst out fiercely. “It would only disappoint him if I got worse again, and I might get worse this very night. I could come down with a raging fever. I feel as if one might be starting right now. I won’t have letters written to my father. I won’t, I won’t! You’re making me angry, and you know that’s bad for me. I already feel hot. I hate being written about and talked over just as much as I hate being stared at!”
“Hush, my boy,” Dr. Craven said soothingly. “Nothing will be written without your permission. You’re too sensitive about these things. You mustn’t undo the good that has been done.”
He said no more about writing to Mr. Craven. When he saw the nurse, he warned her privately that the patient must never hear any mention of such a thing.

“The boy is extraordinarily better,” he said. “His progress seems almost unnatural. Of course, he is now doing of his own free will what we could not make him do before. Still, he gets excited very easily, and nothing must be said to upset him.”
Mary and Colin were very alarmed, and they talked it over anxiously. From that time on they began their plan of “play-acting.”

“I may have to throw a tantrum,” said Colin regretfully. “I don’t want to have one, and I’m not miserable enough now to work myself into a big one. Perhaps I couldn’t manage one at all. That lump doesn’t come into my throat now, and I keep thinking of nice things instead of horrible ones. But if they talk about writing to my father, I’ll have to do something.”

He made up his mind to eat less. Unfortunately, this brilliant plan was impossible to carry out. Every morning he woke with an amazing appetite, and the table beside his sofa was laid with breakfast: homemade bread and fresh butter, snow-white eggs, raspberry jam, and clotted cream. Mary always ate breakfast with him. When they sat down at the table, especially if there were thin slices of sizzling ham under a hot silver cover, sending up tempting smells, they would look into each other’s eyes in despair.
“I think we’ll have to eat it all this morning, Mary,” Colin always ended up saying. “We can send back some of the lunch and a good deal of the dinner.”
But they never found they could send anything back. The shiny, empty plates that returned to the pantry caused a lot of talk.
“I do wish,” Colin would also say, “I do wish the slices of ham were thicker, and one muffin each isn’t enough for anyone.”

“It’s enough for a person who’s going to die,” Mary answered the first time she heard this, “but it’s not enough for a person who’s going to live. Sometimes I feel I could eat three, when those lovely fresh smells of heather and gorse come pouring in from the moor through the open window.”

One morning, after they had been happily busy in the garden for about two hours, Dickon went behind a big rosebush. He brought out two tin pails. One was full of rich fresh milk with cream on top. The other held cottage-made currant buns wrapped in a clean blue and white napkin, tucked in so well that they were still hot. The children burst into a riot of happy surprise. What a wonderful thing for Mrs. Sowerby to think of! What a kind, clever woman she must be! How good the buns were! And what delicious fresh milk!

“Magic lives in her the same way it lives in Dickon,” said Colin. “It makes her think up ways to do things, and nice things too. She is a Magic person. Tell her we’re grateful, Dickon, extremely grateful.”
He liked using grown-up phrases at times, and he enjoyed them. He liked this one so much that he made it even grander.
“Tell her she has been most bounteous, and our gratitude is extreme.”

Then he forgot his grandeur, dug in, and stuffed himself with buns. He drank milk straight from the pail in great gulps, like any hungry little boy who has been exercising hard and breathing moorland air, and whose breakfast was more than two hours behind him.

This was the beginning of many pleasant moments like it. They realized that Mrs. Sowerby had fourteen people to feed, so she might not have enough left over to satisfy two extra appetites every day. So they asked her to let them send some of their shillings to buy things.

Dickon made an exciting discovery. In the woods of the park outside the garden, where Mary had first found him piping to the wild creatures, there was a deep little hollow. There you could build a tiny oven of stones and roast potatoes and eggs in it. Roasted eggs were a luxury they had never known. Very hot potatoes with salt and fresh butter were fit for a woodland king, and wonderfully filling too. You could buy both potatoes and eggs and eat as many as you liked, without feeling you were taking food out of the mouths of fourteen people.

Every beautiful morning the Magic was worked in the mystic circle under the plum tree. After its short blossom time was over, the tree gave them a canopy of thickening green leaves. After the ceremony, Colin always took his walking exercise, and all through the day he practiced his newly found power now and then. Each day he grew stronger, walked more steadily, and covered more ground. And each day his belief in the Magic grew stronger, as well it might. He tried one experiment after another as he felt his strength growing, and it was Dickon who showed him the best ones of all.

“Yesterday,” he said one morning after being away, “I went to Thwaite for Mother, and near the Blue Cow Inn I saw Bob Haworth. He’s the strongest fellow on the moor. He’s the champion wrestler, and he can jump higher than any other lad and throw the hammer farther. Some years he’s gone all the way to Scotland for the games. He’s known me since I was a little one, and he’s a friendly sort, so I asked him some questions. The gentry call him an athlete, and I thought of you, Mester Colin, and I said, ‘How did you make your muscles stick out like that, Bob? Did you do anything extra to make yourself so strong?’ And he said, ‘Well, yes, lad, I did. A strong man in a show that came to Thwaite once showed me how to exercise my arms and legs and every muscle in my body.’ And I said, ‘Could a delicate chap make himself stronger with them, Bob?’ And he laughed and said, ‘Are you the delicate chap?’ And I said, ‘No, but I know a young gentleman who’s getting well after a long illness, and I wish I knew some of those tricks to tell him about.’ I didn’t say any names, and he didn’t ask for any. He’s friendly, like I said, and he stood up and showed me, good-natured about it, and I copied what he did until I knew it by heart.”
Colin had been listening with great excitement.
“Can you show me?” he cried. “Will you?”
“Aye, of course,” Dickon answered, getting up. “But he says you must do them gently at first and be careful not to tire yourself. Rest in between, take deep breaths, and don’t overdo it.”
“I’ll be careful,” said Colin. “Show me! Show me! Dickon, you are the most Magic boy in the world!”

Dickon stood up on the grass and slowly went through a simple, sensible set of muscle exercises. Colin watched with widening eyes. He could do a few of them while he was sitting down. Soon he was doing a few gently while he stood on his feet, which were already growing steadier. Mary began to do them too. Soot, who was watching the whole performance, became very upset. He left his branch and hopped about restlessly, because he could not do them too.

From that time on, the exercises were as much a part of the day’s duties as the Magic was. Each time they tried, Colin and Mary found they could do more of them. They grew such appetites that they would have been in trouble if Dickon hadn’t put a basket down behind the bush each morning when he arrived. But the little oven in the hollow and Mrs. Sowerby’s generous gifts filled them up so well that Mrs. Medlock and the nurse and Dr. Craven were puzzled all over again. You can pick at your breakfast and seem to turn up your nose at your dinner if you are stuffed to the brim with roasted eggs and potatoes and rich, frothy new milk and oatcakes and buns and heather honey and clotted cream.
“They are eating next to nothing,” said the nurse. “They’ll starve to death if we can’t persuade them to take some nourishment. And yet look at how well they appear.”

“Look at them!” exclaimed Mrs. Medlock angrily. “Eh! I’m worn out with them. They’re a pair of young Satans. One day they’re bursting out of their clothes, and the next they’re turning up their noses at the best meals Cook can tempt them with. Yesterday they didn’t take one bite of that lovely young chicken and bread sauce—and the poor woman practically _invented_ a pudding for them—and back it came. She almost cried. She’s afraid she’ll be blamed if they starve themselves into their graves.”

Dr. Craven came and looked at Colin long and carefully. He looked extremely worried when the nurse talked with him and showed him the almost untouched breakfast tray she had saved for him to see. He looked even more worried when he sat down by Colin’s sofa and examined him. He had been called to London on business and had not seen the boy for nearly two weeks. When young things begin to gain health, they gain it quickly. The waxy look had left Colin’s skin, and a warm rose color showed through it. His beautiful eyes were clear, and the hollows under them and in his cheeks and temples had filled out. His once dark, heavy hair now looked as if it grew healthily from his forehead, and it was soft and warm with life. His lips were fuller and a normal color. In fact, as an imitation of a boy who was a confirmed invalid, he was a disgraceful sight. Dr. Craven held his chin in his hand and thought it over.
“I’m sorry to hear you aren’t eating,” he said. “That won’t do. You’ll lose everything you’ve gained—and you’ve gained a remarkable amount. Not long ago you ate so well.”
“I told you it was an unnatural appetite,” answered Colin.
Mary was sitting on her stool nearby, and she suddenly made a very odd sound. She tried so hard to hold it back that she ended up almost choking.
“What is the matter?” said Dr. Craven, turning to look at her.
Mary became quite stern in her manner.
“It was something between a sneeze and a cough,” she replied with injured dignity, “and it got stuck in my throat.”

“But I couldn’t help it,” she told Colin afterward. “It just burst out of me. All at once I remembered that last big potato you ate, and how wide your mouth stretched when you bit into that thick, lovely crust spread with jam and clotted cream.”
“Is there any way those children could be getting food secretly?” Dr. Craven asked Mrs. Medlock.

“No way at all, unless they dig it up from the ground or pick it from the trees,” Mrs. Medlock answered. “They’re out in the grounds all day and never see anyone but each other. And if they want something other than what’s sent up, all they have to do is ask.”
“Well,” said Dr. Craven, “as long as going without food agrees with them, we need not worry. The boy is a new creature.”

“So is the girl,” said Mrs. Medlock. “She’s started to look downright pretty, now that she’s filled out and lost that ugly, sour little look. Her hair has grown thick and healthy, and she’s got a bright color in her cheeks. She used to be the glummest, most ill-natured little thing, and now she and Master Colin laugh together like a pair of crazy youngsters. Perhaps that’s what’s making them fat.”
“Perhaps it is,” said Dr. Craven. “Let them laugh.”

chapters.title: The Curtain
paragraphs: The secret garden bloomed and bloomed, and every morning brought new wonders. In the robin’s nest there were Eggs, and the robin’s mate sat on them, keeping them warm with her soft little breast and her careful wings. At first she was very nervous, and the robin himself kept a fierce, indignant watch. Even Dickon stayed away from the thickly grown corner in those days. He waited until, through some quiet and mysterious spell, he had made the little pair understand that nothing in the garden was anything but like themselves. Nothing there failed to understand how wonderful it was, what was happening to them—the huge, tender, terrible, heart-breaking beauty and seriousness of Eggs. Suppose there had been one person in that garden who did not know, deep down in every part of his or her being, that if an Egg were taken away or hurt, the whole world would spin around, crash through space and come to an end. Suppose even one person had failed to feel this and act on it. Then there could have been no happiness, even in that golden spring air. But they all knew it and felt it, and the robin and his mate knew that they knew it.

At first the robin watched Mary and Colin with sharp worry. For some mysterious reason, he knew he did not need to watch Dickon. From the first moment his dew-bright black eye landed on Dickon, he knew Dickon was no stranger. He was a kind of robin without a beak or feathers. Dickon could speak robin, which is a language all its own and cannot be mistaken for any other. Speaking robin to a robin is like speaking French to a Frenchman. Dickon always spoke it to the robin himself, so the odd gibberish he used with humans did not matter in the least. The robin figured he used that gibberish with them because they were not clever enough to understand the speech of feathered creatures. Dickon’s movements were robin movements too. They never startled anyone by being sudden enough to seem dangerous or threatening. Any robin could understand Dickon, so having him near was not even upsetting.

But in the beginning it seemed necessary to be on guard against the other two. For one thing, the boy creature did not come into the garden on his own legs. He was pushed in on a thing with wheels, with the skins of wild animals thrown over him. That alone was suspicious. Then, when he began to stand up and move around, he did it in a strange, unpracticed way, and the others seemed to have to help him. The robin used to hide in a bush and watch this anxiously, tilting his head first to one side and then to the other. He thought the slow movements might mean the boy was getting ready to pounce, the way cats do. When cats are about to pounce, they creep along the ground very slowly. The robin talked this over with his mate a great deal for a few days. After that he decided not to mention it again, because she was so terrified that he feared it might harm the Eggs.

When the boy began to walk by himself and even to move faster, it was an enormous relief. But for a long time—or what seemed a long time to the robin—the boy was still a cause for some worry. He did not behave the way the other humans did. He seemed very fond of walking, but he had a habit of sitting or lying down for a while and then getting up again in an unsettling way to start over.

One day the robin remembered that when his own parents had made him learn to fly, he had done much the same thing. He had taken short flights of a few yards and then had been forced to rest. So it occurred to him that this boy was learning to fly—or rather, to walk. He mentioned this to his mate. When he told her that the Eggs would probably act the same way once they had their feathers, she felt much better. She even grew eagerly interested and took great pleasure in watching the boy over the edge of her nest—though she always thought the Eggs would be much cleverer and learn more quickly. Then she added, kindly, that humans were always clumsier and slower than Eggs, and most of them never seemed to learn to fly at all. You never met them in the air or in the treetops.

After a while the boy began to move around the way the others did, but all three children did unusual things at times. They would stand under the trees and swing their arms and legs and heads about in a way that was not walking or running or sitting down. They went through these movements every day, and the robin never managed to explain to his mate what they were doing or trying to do. All he could say was that he was sure the Eggs would never flap around like that. But since the boy who spoke robin so well was doing it with them, the birds could be certain the actions were not dangerous. Of course, neither the robin nor his mate had ever heard of the champion wrestler Bob Haworth and his exercises for making muscles stand out in lumps. Robins are not like human beings. Their muscles are exercised from the very start, so they grow in a natural way. If you have to fly around to find every meal you eat, your muscles do not become atrophied (atrophied means wasted away from lack of use).

Once the boy was walking and running and digging and weeding like the others, a great peace and contentment settled over the nest in the corner. Fears for the Eggs became a thing of the past. You knew your Eggs were as safe as if they were locked in a bank vault, and you could watch so many curious things going on. That made sitting on a nest a very entertaining job. On wet days the Eggs’ mother sometimes felt a little bored, because the children did not come into the garden.

But even on wet days, no one could say that Mary and Colin were bored. One morning the rain poured down without stopping, and Colin was starting to feel a little restless, because he had to stay on his sofa, since it was not safe to get up and walk around. That was when Mary had an inspiration.

“Now that I’m a real boy,” Colin had said, “my legs and arms and my whole body are so full of Magic that I can’t keep them still. They want to be doing things all the time. Do you know, Mary, when I wake up in the morning, when it’s very early and the birds are just shouting outside and everything seems to be shouting for joy—even the trees and the things we can’t really hear—I feel as if I must jump out of bed and shout myself. Just think what would happen if I did!”
Mary giggled helplessly.
“The nurse would come running, and Mrs. Medlock would come running, and they’d be sure you had gone crazy, and they’d send for the doctor,” she said.
Colin giggled too. He could picture how they would all look—how horrified by his outburst, and how amazed to see him standing up straight.

“I wish Father would hurry up and come home,” he said. “I want to tell him myself. It’s all I think about. But we can’t keep this up much longer. I hate lying here pretending, and anyway, I look far too different. If only it weren’t raining today.”
That was when Mistress Mary had her inspiration.
“Colin,” she began, in a mysterious voice, “do you know how many rooms there are in this house?”
“About a thousand, I suppose,” he answered.

“There are about a hundred that no one ever goes into,” said Mary. “One rainy day I went and looked into ever so many of them. No one ever knew, though Mrs. Medlock almost caught me. I lost my way on the way back, and I stopped at the end of your corridor. That was the second time I heard you crying.”
Colin sat straight up on his sofa.
“A hundred rooms no one goes into,” he said. “That sounds almost like a secret garden. Let’s go and look at them. Wheel me there in my chair, and nobody will know we went.”

“I was thinking the very same thing,” said Mary. “Nobody would dare come after us. Some of the galleries are long enough to run in, so we could do our exercises there. And there’s a small Indian room with a cabinet full of ivory elephants. Every sort of room you can imagine is up there.”
“Ring the bell,” said Colin.
When the nurse came in, he gave her his orders.

“Bring my chair,” he said. “Miss Mary and I want to explore the part of the house that isn’t used. John may push me as far as the picture gallery, since there are stairs on the way. After that he must go away and leave us alone until I call for him.”

Rainy days lost their terrors that morning. The footman wheeled the chair into the picture gallery and left the two of them together, as he had been told. Colin and Mary looked at each other, delighted. As soon as Mary was sure that John was really on his way back to his own quarters downstairs, Colin climbed out of his chair.
“I’m going to run from one end of the gallery to the other,” he said, “and then I’m going to jump, and then we’ll do Bob Haworth’s exercises.”
And they did all of these things and many more. They looked at the portraits, and they found the plain little girl in green brocade, holding a parrot on her finger.

“All these,” said Colin, “must be my relatives. They lived a long time ago. I think the one with the parrot is one of my great, great, great, great aunts. She looks a bit like you, Mary—not the way you look now, but the way you looked when you first came here. Now you’re a lot fatter and better looking.”
“So are you,” said Mary, and they both laughed.

They went to the Indian room and had fun with the ivory elephants. They found the rose-colored brocade boudoir and the hole in the cushion that the mouse had left, but the baby mice had grown up and run away, and the hole was empty. They saw more rooms and made more discoveries than Mary had made on her first exploring trip. They found new corridors and corners and flights of steps, and new old pictures they liked, and strange old things they could not guess the use of. It was a wonderfully entertaining morning. It was fascinating to wander through the same house as other people and yet feel as if you were miles away from them.
“I’m glad we came,” Colin said. “I never knew I lived in such a big, strange old place. I like it. We’ll wander around every rainy day. We’ll always be finding new odd corners and things.”
That morning, among other things, they had found such good appetites that when they got back to Colin’s room, they could not possibly send the lunch away untouched.
When the nurse carried the tray downstairs, she banged it onto the kitchen dresser, so that Mrs. Loomis, the cook, could see how clean the dishes and plates were.
“Look at that!” she said. “This is a house of mystery, and those two children are the biggest mysteries in it.”

“If they keep that up every day,” said John, the strong young footman, “it’s no wonder he weighs twice as much today as he did a month ago. I’d have to give up my job before long, for fear of hurting my muscles.”

That afternoon Mary saw that something in Colin’s room had changed. She had spotted it the day before too, but she had kept quiet, thinking it might only be an accident. Today she again said nothing. She just sat staring at the picture over the mantel, which she could see because the curtain had been drawn back. That was the change.

“I know what you’re waiting for me to explain,” said Colin, once she had stared for a few minutes. “I can always tell when you want me to explain something. You’re wondering why the curtain is open. Well, I’m going to leave it that way.”
“Why?” asked Mary.

“Because it doesn’t make me angry anymore to see her laughing. Two nights ago I woke up when the moonlight was bright. I felt as if the Magic were filling the room and making everything so splendid that I couldn’t lie still. I got up and looked out of the window. The room was quite light, and there was a patch of moonlight on the curtain, and somehow that made me go and pull the cord. She looked right down at me, as if she were laughing because she was glad I was standing there. It made me like looking at her. I want to see her laughing like that all the time. I think she must have been a kind of Magic person, maybe.”
“You look so much like her now,” said Mary, “that sometimes I think maybe you are her ghost, made into a boy.”
That idea seemed to affect Colin. He thought it over and then answered her slowly.
“If I were her ghost—my father would be fond of me,” he said.
“Do you want him to be fond of you?” asked Mary.
“I used to hate it that he wasn’t fond of me. If he grew fond of me, I think I would tell him about the Magic. It might make him more cheerful.”

chapters.title: “It’s Mother!”
paragraphs: The children’s faith in the Magic never wavered. After the morning chants, Colin sometimes gave them a lecture on it.

“I like doing this,” he explained, “because when I grow up and make great scientific discoveries, I’ll have to lecture about them, so this is practice. I can only give short lectures now, because I’m very young. Besides, Ben Weatherstaff would feel like he was in church and fall asleep.”
“The best thing about lecturing,” said Ben, “is that a fellow can stand up and say whatever he likes, and no other fellow can talk back. I wouldn’t mind doing a bit of lecturing myself sometimes.”

But whenever Colin spoke from under his tree, old Ben stared at him hungrily and never looked away. He studied the boy with a critical sort of fondness. It was not really the lecture that interested him. It was the legs that looked straighter and stronger every day, the head that held itself so well, the sharp chin and hollow cheeks that had filled out and rounded, and the eyes that were starting to shine with a light he remembered seeing in another pair. Sometimes Colin took Ben’s earnest gaze to mean he was deeply impressed, and he wondered what the old man was thinking. Once, when Ben seemed completely spellbound, Colin asked him.
“What are you thinking about, Ben Weatherstaff?” he asked.
“I was thinking,” answered Ben, “that I’d bet you’ve put on three or four pounds this week. I was looking at your calves and your shoulders. I’d like to get you on a pair of scales.”
“It’s the Magic, and—and Mrs. Sowerby’s buns and milk and things,” said Colin. “You see, the scientific experiment has worked.”

That morning Dickon was too late to hear the lecture. When he arrived, he was red-faced from running, and his funny face looked even more twinkling than usual. There was a lot of weeding to do after the rains, so they got right to work. There was always plenty to do after a warm, soaking rain. The wet that was so good for the flowers was just as good for the weeds, which pushed up tiny blades of grass and little points of leaves. These had to be pulled out before their roots took too firm a hold. Colin was as good at weeding as anyone by now, and he could lecture while he did it.

“The Magic works best when you work too,” he said this morning. “You can feel it in your bones and muscles. I’m going to read books about bones and muscles, but I’m going to write a book about Magic. I’m making it up now. I keep discovering new things.”

Not long after he said this, he put down his trowel and stood up. He had been quiet for several minutes, and they could tell he was thinking up lectures, as he often did. When he dropped his trowel and stood up straight, it seemed to Mary and Dickon that a sudden, powerful thought had made him do it. He stretched himself to his full height and flung his arms out joyfully. Color glowed in his face, and his strange eyes opened wide with happiness. All at once he had understood something completely.
“Mary! Dickon!” he cried. “Just look at me!”
They stopped weeding and looked at him.
“Do you remember that first morning you brought me in here?” he demanded.
Dickon was looking at him very hard. Because he was an animal charmer, he could see more than most people could, and much of what he saw he never talked about. He saw some of it now in this boy.
“Aye, we do,” he answered.
Mary looked hard too, but she said nothing.
“Just this minute,” said Colin, “it all came back to me—when I looked at my hand digging with the trowel—and I had to stand up to see if it was real. And it is real! I’m _well_—I’m _well!_”
“Aye, that you are!” said Dickon.
“I’m well! I’m well!” said Colin again, and his whole face turned red.

In a way he had known it before. He had hoped it, felt it and thought about it. But at that very moment something had rushed through him, a kind of rapturous belief and understanding. It was so strong that he could not help crying out.

“I’ll live forever and ever and ever!” he cried grandly. “I’ll find out thousands and thousands of things. I’ll learn about people and animals and everything that grows—like Dickon—and I’ll never stop making Magic. I’m well! I’m well! I feel—I feel as if I want to shout something—something grateful and joyful!”
Ben Weatherstaff, who had been working near a rose bush, glanced around at him.
“You could sing the Doxology,” he suggested in his driest grunt. He had no great opinion of the Doxology, and he did not offer the idea with any special respect.
But Colin had an exploring mind, and he knew nothing about the Doxology.
“What is that?” he asked.
“Dickon can sing it for you, I’ll bet,” replied Ben Weatherstaff.
Dickon answered with his smile that saw everything, the smile of an animal charmer.
“They sing it in church,” he said. “Mother says she believes the skylarks sing it when they get up in the morning.”
“If your mother says so, it must be a lovely song,” Colin replied. “I’ve never set foot in a church. I was always too sick to go. Please sing it, Dickon. I’d like to hear it.”

Dickon was simple and natural about it. He understood what Colin was feeling better than Colin did himself. He understood it by a kind of instinct so natural that he did not know it was understanding. He pulled off his cap and looked around, still smiling.
“You must take off your cap,” he said to Colin, “and so must you, Ben—and you must stand up, you know.”

Colin took off his cap, and the sun shone on his thick hair and warmed it while he watched Dickon closely. Ben Weatherstaff scrambled up from his knees and bared his head too. He had a puzzled, half-resentful look on his old face, as if he didn’t quite know why he was doing this remarkable thing.
Dickon stood among the trees and rose bushes and began to sing, in a plain, matter-of-fact way and with a fine, strong boy’s voice:

“Praise God from whom all blessings flow,
Praise Him all creatures here below,
Praise Him above, you Heavenly Host,
Praise Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
Amen.”
When he finished, Ben Weatherstaff was standing perfectly still, his jaw set stubbornly, but with a troubled look in his eyes as he stared at Colin. Colin’s face was thoughtful and grateful.

“It is a very nice song,” he said. “I like it. Maybe it means just what I mean when I want to shout that I’m thankful to the Magic.” He stopped and thought, puzzled. “Maybe they’re both the same thing. How can we know the exact names of everything? Sing it again, Dickon. Let’s try, Mary. I want to sing it too. It’s my song. How does it begin? ‘Praise God from whom all blessings flow’?”

And they sang it again. Mary and Colin raised their voices as musically as they could, and Dickon’s swelled out loud and beautiful. At the second line Ben Weatherstaff cleared his throat with a rasp, and at the third line he joined in so vigorously that it sounded almost wild. When the “Amen” ended, Mary saw that the same thing had happened to him that had happened when he found out Colin was not a cripple. His chin was twitching, he was staring and blinking, and his leathery old cheeks were wet.
“I never saw any sense in the Doxology before,” he said hoarsely, “but I may change my mind in time. I’d say you’ve put on five pounds this week, Master Colin—five of them!”
Colin was looking across the garden at something that had caught his attention, and his face had turned startled.
“Who is coming in here?” he said quickly. “Who is it?”

The door in the ivy-covered wall had been pushed gently open, and a woman had come in. She had entered with the last line of their song and had stood still, listening and looking at them. The ivy was behind her, sunlight drifted through the trees and dappled her long blue cloak, and her fresh, kind face was smiling across the greenery. She looked like a softly colored picture in one of Colin’s books. She had wonderful, loving eyes that seemed to take everything in—all of them, even Ben Weatherstaff and the “creatures” and every flower in bloom. Although she had appeared so suddenly, not one of them felt that she was an intruder at all. Dickon’s eyes lit up like lamps.
“It’s Mother—that’s who it is!” he cried, and he ran across the grass.
Colin started toward her too, and Mary went with him. Both of them felt their hearts beat faster.
“It’s Mother!” Dickon said again when they met halfway. “I knew you wanted to see her, and I told her where the door was hidden.”
Colin held out his hand with a flushed, royal sort of shyness, but his eyes drank in her face.
“Even back when I was sick, I wanted to meet you,” he said, “you and Dickon and the secret garden. Before that, I had never wanted to see anybody or anything at all.”
The sight of his lifted face brought a sudden change over hers. She flushed, the corners of her mouth trembled, and a mist seemed to pass over her eyes.

“Eh! Dear lad!” she burst out, trembling. “Eh! Dear lad!” She said it as if she had not known she was going to. She did not say “Master Colin,” but just “dear lad,” quite suddenly. She might have said it to Dickon in the same way if she had seen something in his face that touched her. Colin liked it.
“Are you surprised because I’m so well?” he asked.
She put her hand on his shoulder and smiled the mist out of her eyes.
“Aye, I am!” she said. “But you’re so like your mother that you made my heart jump.”
“Do you think,” said Colin, a little awkwardly, “that it will make my father like me?”
“Aye, for sure, dear lad,” she answered, and she gave his shoulder a soft, quick pat. “He must come home—he must come home.”

“Susan Sowerby,” said Ben Weatherstaff, stepping close to her. “Look at the lad’s legs, will you? They were like drumsticks in stockings two months ago—and I heard folks say they were bandy and knock-kneed both at the same time. Look at them now!”
Susan Sowerby gave a comfortable laugh.

“They’re going to be fine strong lad’s legs before long,” she said. “Let him keep on playing and working in the garden and eating heartily and drinking plenty of good sweet milk, and there’ll not be a finer pair in Yorkshire, thank God for it.”
She put both hands on Mistress Mary’s shoulders and looked over her small face the way a mother would.

“And you too!” she said. “You’ve grown nearly as hearty as our ’Lisabeth Ellen. I’ll bet you’re like your mother too. Our Martha told me Mrs. Medlock had heard she was a pretty woman. You’ll be like a blush rose when you grow up, my little lass, bless you.”

She did not mention that when Martha came home on her “day out” and described the plain, sallow child, she had said she had no confidence at all in what Mrs. Medlock had heard. “It doesn’t stand to reason that a pretty woman could be the mother of such a plain little lass,” she had added stubbornly.

Mary had not had time to pay much attention to how her face was changing. She had only noticed that she looked “different,” that she seemed to have a great deal more hair, and that it was growing very fast. But she remembered how much she had enjoyed looking at the Mem Sahib in the past, so she was glad to hear she might one day look like her.

Susan Sowerby walked around their garden with them, heard the whole story of it, and was shown every bush and tree that had come alive. Colin walked on one side of her and Mary on the other. They kept looking up at her comfortable, rosy face, secretly curious about the lovely feeling she gave them, a warm, supported sort of feeling. It seemed that she understood them the way Dickon understood his “creatures.” She bent over the flowers and talked about them as if they were children. Soot followed her, cawed at her once or twice, and flew onto her shoulder as if it were Dickon’s. When they told her about the robin and the first flight of the young ones, she gave a mellow, motherly little laugh deep in her throat.
“I suppose teaching them to fly is like teaching children to walk, but I’m afraid I’d be in a terrible worry if mine had wings instead of legs,” she said.
She seemed such a wonderful woman, in her kind moorland cottage way, that at last they told her about the Magic.
“Do you believe in Magic?” asked Colin, after he had explained about Indian fakirs. “I do hope you do.”

“I do, lad,” she answered. “I never knew it by that name, but what does the name matter? I’d bet they call it something different in France and something different again in Germany. The same thing that set the seeds swelling and the sun shining made you a well lad, and it’s the Good Thing. It isn’t like us poor fools, who think it matters if we’re called by the wrong name. The Big Good Thing doesn’t stop to worry, bless you. It goes on making worlds by the million—worlds like ours. Never stop believing in the Big Good Thing and knowing the world is full of it—and call it whatever you like. You were singing to it when I came into the garden.”

“I was so happy,” said Colin, gazing at her with his beautiful, strange eyes. “All at once I noticed how different I was—how strong my arms and legs had become, you see—and how I could dig and stand—so I leaped up and wanted to shout something to whatever would hear me.”

“The Magic listened when you sang the Doxology. It would have listened to anything you sang. It was the joy that mattered. Eh! Lad, lad—what are names to the Joy Maker?” And she gave his shoulders a quick, soft pat again.

She had packed a basket that held a real feast this morning. When the hungry hour came and Dickon brought it out from its hiding place, she sat down with them under their tree and watched them gobble up their food, laughing and delighting in their appetites. She was full of fun and made them laugh at all sorts of silly things. She told them stories in broad Yorkshire and taught them new words. She laughed as if she couldn’t help it when they told her how hard it was getting to pretend that Colin was still a fretful invalid.

“You see, we can’t help laughing nearly all the time when we’re together,” explained Colin. “And it doesn’t sound sick at all. We try to choke it back, but it bursts out, and that sounds worse than ever.”

“There’s one thing that comes into my mind so often,” said Mary, “and I can hardly ever hold in my laughter when I suddenly think of it. I keep thinking, what if Colin’s face starts to look like a full moon? It isn’t like one yet, but he gets a tiny bit fatter every day—and what if one morning it looks like one—what would we do!”
“Bless us all, I can see you’ve a good bit of play-acting to do,” said Susan Sowerby. “But you won’t have to keep it up much longer. Master Craven will come home.”
“Do you think he will?” asked Colin. “Why?”
Susan Sowerby chuckled softly.
“I suppose it would nearly break your heart if he found out before you told him in your own way,” she said. “You’ve lain awake nights planning it.”
“I couldn’t stand it if somebody else told him,” said Colin. “Every day I think of a new way to do it. Today I think I’d like to simply run straight into his room.”
“That would be a fine surprise for him,” said Susan Sowerby. “I’d like to see his face, lad. I would indeed! He must come back—he must.”

One of the things they talked about was the visit they would make to her cottage. They planned it all out. They would drive over the moor and eat lunch outdoors among the heather. They would see all twelve children and Dickon’s garden, and they would not come back until they were tired.

At last Susan Sowerby got up to go back to the house and Mrs. Medlock. It was time for Colin to be wheeled back as well. But before he got into his chair, he stood very close to Susan and fixed his eyes on her with a kind of bewildered adoration. Suddenly he caught hold of a fold of her blue cloak and held on tight.
“You are just what I—what I wanted,” he said. “I wish you were my mother—as well as Dickon’s!”

All at once Susan Sowerby bent down and pulled him close, wrapping her warm arms around him against her chest under the blue cloak, as if he were Dickon’s own brother. A quick mist came over her eyes.
“Eh! Dear lad!” she said. “Your own mother is in this very garden, I do believe. She couldn’t keep out of it. Your father must come back to you—he must!”

chapters.title: In the Garden
paragraphs: In every century since the world began, wonderful things have been discovered. In the last century, people found out more amazing things than in any century before it. In this new century, hundreds of things even more astounding will come to light. At first people refuse to believe that a strange new thing can be done. Then they begin to hope it can be done. Then they see that it can be done—and then it is done, and the whole world wonders why nobody did it centuries ago. One of the new things people began to learn in the last century was that thoughts—just plain thoughts—are as powerful as electric batteries. They can be as good for you as sunlight, or as bad for you as poison. Letting a sad or bad thought into your mind is as dangerous as letting a scarlet fever germ into your body. If you let it stay there after it has gotten in, you may never get over it for as long as you live.

As long as Mistress Mary’s mind was full of unpleasant thoughts, she was a yellow-faced, sickly, bored and miserable child. She thought about the things she disliked, and she held sour opinions of people. She was determined not to be pleased or interested by anything. But circumstances were very kind to her, though she had no idea of it. They began to push her along for her own good. Gradually her mind filled up with robins, and with moorland cottages crowded with children. It filled up with queer, crabby old gardeners and ordinary little Yorkshire housemaids, with springtime and with secret gardens coming alive day by day, and with a moor boy and his “creatures.” Then there was no room left for the unpleasant thoughts that had upset her liver and her digestion and made her yellow and tired.

As long as Colin shut himself up in his room, he thought only about his fears and weakness. He hated people who looked at him, and every hour he brooded over humps and early death. He was a hysterical, half-crazy little hypochondriac. He knew nothing of the sunshine and the spring, and he did not know that he could get well and stand on his own feet if he tried. Then new, beautiful thoughts began to push out the old, hideous ones. Life began to come back to him, his blood ran healthily through his veins, and strength poured into him like a flood. His scientific experiment was quite practical and simple, and there was nothing weird about it at all. Much more surprising things can happen to anyone who has the sense, when a disagreeable or discouraged thought comes into his mind, to remember in time and push it out by putting in a pleasant, determinedly courageous one. Two things cannot be in the same place.
“Where you tend a rose, my lad, a thistle cannot grow.”

While the secret garden was coming alive, and two children were coming alive along with it, a man was wandering through certain beautiful, faraway places. He was in the Norwegian fiords and in the valleys and mountains of Switzerland. For ten years he had kept his mind filled with dark, heartbroken thinking. He had not been courageous. He had never tried to put any other thoughts in the place of the dark ones. He had wandered beside blue lakes and thought those dark thoughts. He had lain on mountainsides with sheets of deep blue gentians blooming all around him and the scent of flowers filling the air, and he had thought them there too.
