A terrible sorrow had struck him when he was happy. He had let his soul fill up with blackness and had stubbornly refused to let any crack of light through. He had forgotten and deserted his home and his duties. When he traveled, such darkness hung over him that the sight of him was a wrong done to other people, as if he poisoned the air around him with gloom. Most strangers thought he must be either half mad or a man with some hidden crime on his soul. He was a tall man with a drawn face and crooked shoulders. The name he always wrote in hotel registers was “Archibald Craven, Misselthwaite Manor, Yorkshire, England.”

He had traveled far and wide since the day he saw Mistress Mary in his study and told her she could have her “bit of earth.” He had been to the most beautiful places in Europe, though he never stayed anywhere more than a few days. He had picked the quietest, most remote spots. He had stood on mountaintops with their heads in the clouds and looked down on other mountains as the sun rose and touched them. The light was so wonderful it seemed as if the world were just being born.

But the light never seemed to touch him until one day he realized that something strange had happened, for the first time in ten years. He was in a wonderful valley in the Austrian Tyrol, walking alone through beauty that might have lifted any man’s soul out of shadow. He had walked a long way, and it had not lifted his. But at last he felt tired and threw himself down to rest on a carpet of moss beside a stream. It was a clear little stream that ran quite merrily along its narrow path through the lush, damp greenness. Sometimes it made a sound like very low laughter as it bubbled over and around the stones. He saw birds come and dip their heads to drink from it, then flick their wings and fly away. The stream seemed like a living thing, and yet its tiny voice made the stillness seem deeper. The valley was very, very still.

As he sat gazing into the clear, running water, Archibald Craven slowly felt his mind and body grow quiet, as quiet as the valley itself. He wondered if he was going to fall asleep, but he was not. He sat and gazed at the sunlit water, and his eyes began to notice things growing at its edge. There was one lovely clump of blue forget-me-nots growing so close to the stream that its leaves were wet. He found himself looking at them the way he remembered looking at such things years ago. He was actually thinking, tenderly, how lovely they were and what wonders of blue those hundreds of little blossoms made. He did not know that this one simple thought was slowly filling his mind—filling and filling it until other things were softly pushed aside. It was as if a sweet, clear spring had begun to rise in a stagnant pool, and had risen and risen until at last it swept the dark water away. But of course he did not think of this himself. He only knew that the valley seemed to grow quieter and quieter as he sat and stared at the bright, delicate blueness. He did not know how long he sat there or what was happening to him. But at last he stirred as if he were waking up, and he got up slowly and stood on the carpet of moss. He drew a long, deep, soft breath and wondered at himself. Something seemed to have been untied and set free inside him, very quietly.
“What is it?” he said, almost in a whisper, and he passed his hand over his forehead. “I almost feel as if—I were alive!”

I do not know enough about the wonder of undiscovered things to explain how this happened to him. Nobody else does yet, either. He did not understand it at all himself. But months later he remembered this strange hour, when he was back at Misselthwaite. By pure accident he found out that on this very day Colin had cried out as he went into the secret garden:
“I am going to live forever and ever and ever!”

The unusual calm stayed with him for the rest of the evening, and he slept a new, restful sleep. But it did not stay with him for long. He did not know that it could be kept. By the next night he had flung the doors wide open to his dark thoughts, and they came trooping and rushing back. He left the valley and went on wandering again. But strange as it seemed to him, there were minutes—sometimes half-hours—when, without knowing why, he felt the black burden lift again, and he knew he was a living man and not a dead one. Slowly—slowly—for no reason he could think of, he was “coming alive” with the garden.

As the golden summer turned into the deep golden autumn, he went to Lake Como. There he found a loveliness like a dream. He spent his days on the crystal blueness of the lake, or he walked back into the soft, thick greenery of the hills and tramped until he was tired, so that he could sleep. By this time he had begun to sleep better, he knew, and his dreams had stopped terrifying him.
“Perhaps,” he thought, “my body is growing stronger.”

It was growing stronger. But because of the rare, peaceful hours when his thoughts had changed, his soul was slowly growing stronger too. He began to think of Misselthwaite and wonder whether he should go home. Now and then he wondered vaguely about his boy. He asked himself how he would feel when he went and stood beside the carved four-posted bed again and looked down at the sharply chiseled, ivory-white face while it slept, with the black lashes so startling against the closed eyes. He shrank from the thought.

One marvelous day he walked so far that when he came back the moon was high and full, and the whole world was purple shadow and silver. The stillness of lake and shore and woods was so wonderful that he did not go into the villa where he was staying. He walked down to a little leafy terrace at the water’s edge and sat on a bench and breathed in all the heavenly scents of the night. He felt the strange calm stealing over him, and it grew deeper and deeper until he fell asleep.

He could not tell when he stopped being awake and began to dream. The dream felt so real that it did not seem like dreaming at all. Later he remembered how completely awake and alert he had believed himself to be. As he sat there breathing in the perfume of the late roses and hearing the water lap against the shore below his feet, he thought he heard a voice calling. It was sweet and clear and happy, and it came from far away. It seemed very distant, and yet he heard it as plainly as if the speaker stood right beside him.
“Archie! Archie! Archie!” it said, and then again, sweeter and clearer than before, “Archie! Archie!”
He thought he sprang to his feet, not even startled. It was such a real voice, and it seemed so natural that he should hear it.
“Lilias! Lilias!” he answered. “Lilias! Where are you?”
“In the garden,” it came back, like a sound from a golden flute. “In the garden!”

And then the dream ended. But he did not wake up. He slept soundly and sweetly all through the lovely night. When he finally woke, it was a brilliant morning, and a servant was standing there staring at him. He was an Italian servant. Like all the servants of the villa, he was used to accepting without question any strange thing his foreign master might do. No one ever knew when he would go out or come in, or where he would choose to sleep, or whether he would roam about the garden or lie in the boat on the lake all night. The man held a tray with some letters on it, and he waited quietly until Mr. Craven took them. When he had gone away, Mr. Craven sat a few moments holding the letters in his hand and looking at the lake. His strange calm was still with him, and something more—a lightness, as if the cruel thing that had been done had not happened the way he thought—as if something had changed. He was remembering the dream—the real—real dream.
“In the garden!” he said, wondering at himself. “In the garden! But the door is locked and the key is buried deep.”

A few minutes later he looked through the letters and saw that the one on top was an English letter from Yorkshire. It was addressed in a plain woman’s handwriting, but not one he knew. He opened it, hardly thinking about who had written it, but the first words caught his attention at once.
“_Dear Sir:_

I am Susan Sowerby, the one who made bold to speak to you once out on the moor. It was about Miss Mary that I spoke. I will make bold to speak again. Please, sir, if I was you I would come home. I believe you would be glad you came. And—begging your pardon, sir—I believe your lady would ask you to come, if she was here.
Your obedient servant,
Susan Sowerby.”
Mr. Craven read the letter twice before he put it back in its envelope. He kept thinking about the dream.
“I will go back to Misselthwaite,” he said. “Yes, I’ll go at once.”
And he walked through the garden to the villa and told Pitcher to get ready for his return to England.

In a few days he was in Yorkshire again. On his long railroad journey he found himself thinking about his boy as he had never thought of him in all the ten years before. During those years he had only wanted to forget him. Now, though he did not mean to think about him, memories of the boy kept drifting into his mind. He remembered the black days when he had raved like a madman because the child was alive and the mother was dead. He had refused to see the baby. When he finally went to look at it, it was such a weak, wretched little thing that everyone was sure it would die within a few days. But to the surprise of those who cared for it, the days passed and it lived. Then everyone believed it would grow up deformed and crippled.

He had not meant to be a bad father, but he had not felt like a father at all. He had paid for doctors and nurses and luxuries, but he shrank from the very thought of the boy and buried himself in his own misery. After a year away, he came back to Misselthwaite for the first time. The small, miserable-looking creature lifted its great gray eyes to his face, slowly and without interest. They had black lashes around them, and they were so like the happy eyes he had adored and yet so horribly unlike them. He could not bear the sight of them and turned away, pale as death. After that he hardly ever saw the boy except when he was asleep. All he knew of him was that he was a confirmed invalid with a vicious, hysterical, half-insane temper. He could only be kept from furies that were dangerous to himself by being given his own way in every detail.

None of this was uplifting to remember. But as the train whirled him through mountain passes and golden plains, the man who was “coming alive” began to think in a new way. He thought long and steadily and deeply.
“Maybe I have been completely wrong all these ten years,” he told himself. “Ten years is a long stretch of time. It might be too late to do anything now—far too late. What have I been thinking?”

Of course this was the wrong Magic—to begin by saying “too late.” Even Colin could have told him that. But he knew nothing of Magic, either black or white. That he still had to learn. He wondered whether Susan Sowerby had taken courage and written to him only because the motherly woman had realized that the boy was much worse—that he was fatally ill. If he had not been under the spell of the curious calm that had taken hold of him, he would have been more wretched than ever. But the calm had brought a kind of courage and hope with it. Instead of giving in to thoughts of the worst, he found he was actually trying to believe in better things.
“Could it be that she sees I might be able to help him and handle him?” he thought. “I will stop and see her on the way to Misselthwaite.”

But when he stopped the carriage at the cottage on his way across the moor, seven or eight children who were playing nearby gathered in a group. They bobbed seven or eight friendly, polite curtsies and told him that their mother had gone to the other side of the moor early that morning to help a woman who had a new baby. “Our Dickon,” they offered, was over at the Manor working in one of the gardens, where he went several days each week.

Mr. Craven looked over the group of sturdy little bodies and round, red-cheeked faces, each one grinning in its own special way, and he realized that they were a healthy, likable bunch. He smiled back at their friendly grins. He took a golden sovereign from his pocket and gave it to “our ’Lizabeth Ellen,” who was the oldest.
“Split that eight ways and each of you gets half a crown,” he said.
Then he drove off, leaving behind a crowd of grinning, chuckling children who bobbed curtsies, nudged each other with their elbows, and hopped about with joy.

The ride across the wonderful moor calmed him. Why did it make him feel he was coming home, something he had been sure he could never feel again? He felt the beauty of the land and sky and the purple bloom in the distance, and his heart grew warm as he drew nearer to the great old house where his family had lived for six hundred years. The last time he had driven away from it, he had shuddered to think of its closed rooms and the boy lying in the four-posted bed with the brocade hangings. Was it possible that he might find the boy a little better, and that he might get over his dread of seeing him? How real that dream had been, and how clear and wonderful the voice that called back to him, “In the garden—In the garden!”
“I will try to find the key,” he said. “I will try to open the door. I must, though I don’t know why.”

The servants who greeted him at the Manor with their usual formality noticed that he looked better. He did not head for the remote rooms where he usually lived with Pitcher to look after him. Instead he went into the library and sent for Mrs. Medlock. She came to him a little excited, curious, and flustered.
“How is Master Colin, Medlock?” he asked.
“Well, sir,” Mrs. Medlock answered, “he’s—he’s different, you might say.”
“Worse?” he suggested.
Mrs. Medlock was truly red in the face.
“Well, you see, sir,” she tried to explain, “Dr. Craven and the nurse and I can’t quite make him out.”
“Why is that?”
“To tell the truth, sir, Master Colin might be getting better, or he might be getting worse. His appetite, sir, is beyond understanding—and his ways—”
“Has he become more—more peculiar?” her master asked, knitting his brows anxiously.

“That’s it, sir. He’s getting very peculiar, compared with how he used to be. He used to eat nothing, and then all of a sudden he started eating enormous amounts. Then he stopped again at once, and the meals went back to the kitchen just as they used to. You may never have known, sir, that he would not let himself be taken out of doors. The things we went through to get him out in his chair would leave a person shaking like a leaf. He would work himself into such a state that Dr. Craven said he couldn’t answer for it if we forced him. Well, sir, without any warning, not long after one of his worst tantrums, he suddenly insisted on being taken out every day by Miss Mary and Susan Sowerby’s boy Dickon, who could push his chair. He took a liking to them both, and Dickon brought his tame animals. And if you’ll believe it, sir, he will stay out of doors from morning until night.”
“How does he look?” was the next question.

“If he ate his food the normal way, sir, you’d think he was putting on weight. But we’re afraid it may be a kind of bloating. He laughs sometimes in an odd way when he’s alone with Miss Mary. He never used to laugh at all. Dr. Craven is coming to see you right away, if you’ll let him. He has never been so puzzled in his life.”
“Where is Master Colin now?” Mr. Craven asked.
“In the garden, sir. He’s always in the garden. Not a living soul is allowed to go near it, for fear they’ll look at him.”
Mr. Craven hardly heard her last words.
“In the garden,” he said. After he had sent Mrs. Medlock away, he stood there and said it again and again. “In the garden!”

He had to make an effort to bring himself back to where he was standing. When he felt he was on earth again, he turned and left the room. He took the same way Mary had, through the door in the shrubbery, past the laurels and the fountain beds. The fountain was playing now, ringed with beds of brilliant autumn flowers. He crossed the lawn and turned into the Long Walk beside the ivy-covered walls. He did not walk quickly but slowly, with his eyes on the path. He felt as though he were being drawn back to a place he had abandoned for so long, and he did not know why. As he came closer, his steps grew even slower. He knew where the door was, even though the ivy hung thick over it. But he did not know exactly where it lay, that buried key.
So he stopped and stood still, looking around him. Almost at once he started and listened, asking himself whether he was walking in a dream.

The ivy hung thick over the door, the key was buried under the shrubs, and no human being had passed through that doorway in ten lonely years. And yet there were sounds inside the garden. They were the sounds of running, scuffling feet that seemed to chase round and round under the trees. There were strange sounds of hushed, held-in voices, of exclamations and smothered happy cries. It really seemed like the laughter of young things, the helpless laughter of children trying not to be heard, who in a moment, as their excitement rose, would burst out. What in heaven’s name was he dreaming of? What in heaven’s name did he hear? Was he losing his mind and imagining sounds that were not meant for human ears? Was this what the far, clear voice had meant?

And then the moment came, the helpless moment when the sounds forgot to hush themselves. The feet ran faster and faster and came nearer to the garden door. There was quick, strong, young breathing and a wild outburst of laughing shouts that could not be held back. Then the door in the wall was flung wide open, the sheet of ivy swinging back, and a boy burst through at full speed. He did not see the stranger standing there and dashed almost into his arms.

Mr. Craven had held out his arms just in time to keep the boy from falling after his blind dash into him. When he held the boy away to look at him, amazed to find him there, he truly gasped for breath.

He was a tall boy, and a handsome one. He glowed with life, and his running had brought splendid color leaping into his face. He tossed the thick hair back from his forehead and lifted a pair of strange gray eyes, full of boyish laughter and fringed with black lashes. It was the eyes that made Mr. Craven gasp for breath.
“Who—What? Who!” he stammered.

This was not what Colin had expected, and it was not what he had planned. He had never imagined such a meeting. And yet, to come dashing out, winning a race, was perhaps even better. He drew himself up to his very tallest. Mary, who had been running with him and had dashed through the door too, believed he managed to look taller than he ever had before, inches taller.
“Father,” he said, “I’m Colin. You can’t believe it. I can hardly believe it myself. I’m Colin.”
Like Mrs. Medlock, Colin did not understand what his father meant when he said in a hurry:
“In the garden! In the garden!”

“Yes,” Colin rushed on. “The garden did it—the garden, and Mary and Dickon and the creatures, and the Magic. Nobody else knows. We saved it to tell you when you got home. I’m well now. I can beat Mary in a race. I’m going to be an athlete.”
He said it all like a healthy boy, with his face flushed and his words tumbling over each other in his eagerness. Mr. Craven’s heart shook with a joy he could hardly believe.
Colin put out his hand and laid it on his father’s arm.
“Aren’t you glad, Father?” he finished. “Aren’t you glad? I’m going to live forever and ever and ever!”
Mr. Craven put his hands on both of the boy’s shoulders and held him still. He knew he did not dare try to speak, not for a moment.
“Take me into the garden, my boy,” he said at last. “And tell me all about it.”
And so they led him in.

The place was a wilderness of autumn gold and purple and violet blue and flaming scarlet. On every side stood sheaves of late lilies, growing together, white or white streaked with ruby. He remembered well when the first of them had been planted, so that their late glory would show itself at just this time of year. Late roses climbed and hung and clustered, and the sunshine deepened the color of the yellowing trees until one felt one was standing in a leafy temple of gold. The newcomer stood silent, just as the children had when they first came into the garden’s grayness. He looked round and round.
“I thought it would be dead,” he said.
“Mary thought so at first,” said Colin. “But it came alive.”
Then they sat down under their tree. Only Colin stayed on his feet, because he wanted to stand while he told the story.

Archibald Craven thought it was the strangest thing he had ever heard, as it poured out in headlong boy fashion. There was Mystery and Magic and wild creatures, and the eerie midnight meeting. There was the coming of the spring, and the burst of insulted pride that had dragged the young Rajah to his feet to defy old Ben Weatherstaff to his face. There was the odd friendship, the play-acting, and the great secret so carefully kept. The listener laughed until tears came into his eyes, and sometimes tears came into his eyes when he was not laughing. The Athlete, the Lecturer, the Scientific Discoverer was a funny, lovable, healthy young human being.

“Now,” he said when the story was over, “it doesn’t need to be a secret anymore. I dare say it will frighten them nearly into fits when they see me. But I am never going to get into that chair again. I shall walk back to the house with you, Father.”

Ben Weatherstaff’s work rarely took him away from the gardens. But this time he found an excuse to carry some vegetables to the kitchen. Mrs. Medlock invited him into the servants’ hall for a glass of beer, so he was on the spot, as he had hoped to be, when the most dramatic event Misselthwaite Manor had seen in a generation actually took place.

One of the windows overlooking the courtyard also gave a glimpse of the lawn. Mrs. Medlock knew Ben had come from the gardens, and she hoped he might have caught sight of his master, and perhaps even of his meeting with Master Colin.
“Did you see either of them, Weatherstaff?” she asked.
Ben took his beer mug from his mouth and wiped his lips with the back of his hand.
“Aye, that I did,” he answered, looking very knowing.
“Both of them?” suggested Mrs. Medlock.
“Both of ’em,” replied Ben Weatherstaff. “Thank you kindly, ma’am, I could drink another mug of it.”
“Together?” said Mrs. Medlock, so excited that she hastily filled his mug to overflowing.
“Together, ma’am,” and Ben gulped down half of his new mug in one swallow.
“Where was Master Colin? How did he look? What did they say to each other?”

“I didn’t hear that,” said Ben, “seein’ as I was only on the stepladder lookin’ over the wall. But I’ll tell you this. There’s been things goin’ on outside that you house people know nowt about. And what you’ll find out, you’ll find out soon.”
And within two minutes he had swallowed the last of his beer and solemnly waved his mug toward the window, which showed a piece of the lawn through the shrubbery.
“Look there,” he said, “if you’re curious. Look what’s comin’ across the grass.”

When Mrs. Medlock looked, she threw up her hands and gave a little shriek. Every man and woman servant within hearing rushed across the servants’ hall and stood at the window, staring out with their eyes almost popping out of their heads.

Across the lawn came the Master of Misselthwaite, looking as many of them had never seen him. And at his side, with his head held high and his eyes full of laughter, walking as strongly and steadily as any boy in Yorkshire, came Master Colin!
